found.angle: Physics-aware, simulation-ready object reconstruction: methods that add stability, support-plane contact, non-penetration or simulator feasibility as constraints or losses on shape and pose. Main finding: our two hand-made patches are special cases of general constraints in the literature. "Flatten the underside along one episode's up vector" is a crude form of the support constraint: a surface the object is seen resting on bounds its geometry from below and must touch it (Vysics calls this "physible" geometry; Atlas3D adds a flat-bottom term; ARM has an extrusion baseline). "Carve slots from the co-located overlap" is a crude form of hard multi-object non-penetration (S2MDF; HoloScene's SDF-penetration energy; SPARCS's separating planes). Floating and tipping objects are handled in the literature by physics-aware pose refinement and settling, not by shape edits (PhysPose, RoboSnap, SimuScene, phi-Scene). The robust version needs no per-object or per-episode parameters. It is one automatic stage between TSDF reconstruction and reference building, run identically on public and eval episodes, in four steps. (A) Ground-truth-free diagnostics for every object and rest segment: an assist-off drop test, support gap, centre-of-mass margin inside the support polygon, pairwise penetration volume at co-located frames, and hand penetration. (B) Shape fixes that may only change voxels that are unknown or contradicted by physics. They use all rest frames' support planes, hard non-penetration between objects (contested volume assigned by observation evidence and insertion direction), and mask (silhouette) carving for narrow concavities. (C) Pose fixes: gravity and collision refinement, then bottom-up settling along a support tree (table, then rack, then cup) with supports frozen. (D) Re-verify the physics and that the visual fit (masks, depth residual) did not degrade. Heavy joint optimisers (SPARCS takes 46-540 CPU-minutes per scene and no code link was found; HoloScene takes about 8 GPU-hours per scene and uses a generative prior) do not fit in 13 days. Their constraint formulations are cheap to reuse on our TSDF grids, CoACD hulls and CPU MuJoCo. Everything below runs on CPU; GPU is needed only to retrain and evaluate policies, about $3-4 per episode at current offers. All reported numbers are the papers' own claims, not measured by us. All ideas are hypotheses.

sources.title: Vysics: Object Reconstruction Under Occlusion by Fusing Vision and Contact-Rich Physics (Bianchini, Zhu, Sun, Jiang, Taylor, Posa; RSS 2025)
sources.method: BundleSDF tracks the object and reconstructs its visible SDF from RGB-D video. PLL (a contact-dynamics learner) then infers geometry from the trajectory: whenever the object touches a known plane (the table) or the robot, the contact gives a support point and normal ('physible' geometry). These are injected back into the SDF as constraints: zero SDF at support points, signed distance bounded from below by the supporting hyperplane, plus a convexity bias where no data exists. No pretraining, no tactile sensors.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 1 (unseen sweeper underside) and the rounded board edges in problem 2. At every frame where our track has an object resting on the table, the table plane in the object frame is a supporting hyperplane: nothing may lie beyond it, and the object must touch it. Taking this over ALL rest frames (and the standing pose in the assembled X) replaces flatten_base.py's single up vector and 8 mm band with a constraint derived from our own observations. A simplified version that skips PLL works for static rests: plane carve plus a minimal fill of unknown voxels down to the plane.
sources.evidence: Average chamfer distance under heavy occlusion: BundleSDF 2.98 cm vs Vysics 1.45 cm. Learned shape-completion baselines scored 2.45-3.06 cm, no better than vision-only. Open-loop dynamics rollouts stay within 10 cm / 45 deg longer than with vision-only geometry. Data: 7 objects on a table with a Franka arm.
sources.code: Project page https://vysics-vision-and-physics.github.io/ links github.com/DAIRLab/vysics; the page also shows a 'coming soon' note and the repo contents and licence were not verified.
sources.adoption_effort: Adopt the concept, not the code. About 1-2 days CPU: a three-state voxel grid (occupied / free / unknown) in recon_mesh.py; rest-segment detection from our tracks; per-rest plane carve plus fill of unknown voxels between the plane and the observed surface, inside the mask visual hull. Then retrain ep18/ep24 (about 2.2 h of GPU each).
sources.rule_risk: Low. Uses only our perception (tracks, table plane, depth) and no pretrained prior. It changes the mesh only in unobserved regions, which the hidden-scan registration may weigh slightly differently; check on public episodes.

sources.title: SPARCS: Simulation-Ready Cluttered Scene Estimation via Physics-aware Joint Shape and Pose Optimization (Huang, Han, Ye, Pan, Hauser; RSS 2026)
sources.method: Each object is a union of convex hulls whose vertices are optimisation variables, with an SE(3) pose. An augmented-Lagrangian solve enforces quasi-static force and torque balance, using a separating-plane log-barrier contact potential between every pair of hulls (globally differentiable, collision-free at every iterate) and friction cones. The objective is ICP-like: observed points fit to the hull union (large weight), hull vertices kept near the input mesh, and a weak prior mesh term for unseen regions. A Woodbury/Schur structured solver gives up to 8.7x speedup.
sources.solves_for_us: The principled formulation of problems 1-3 together. Our CoACD hulls are already this representation. Force balance would reshape the sweeper's unseen underside until it stands. Hull non-penetration plus point fit would open the ep24 slots where the depth data allows, and force balance makes the assembled X a valid resting state.
sources.evidence: Five scenes (up to 5 objects and 22 hulls) stay in force equilibrium for 1 minute of MuJoCo simulation. The SAM3D+FoundationPose initialisations always blew up the simulation. PSNR is comparable to the initialisation. Wall time 46-540 min per scene on CPU (Intel Core Ultra 9 285K).
sources.code: No code link found on the project page https://rory-weicheng.github.io/SPARCS/.
sources.adoption_effort: Too heavy for 13 days: weeks of implementation, no code, hours of CPU per scene. A cheap subset is usable: the separating-plane test between hulls and a centre-of-mass-in-support-polygon check on our CoACD pieces.
sources.rule_risk: Their initialisation uses SAM3D (a generative prior, grey zone). The optimiser itself is prior-free if initialised from our TSDF mesh.

sources.title: S2MDF: A Plug-And-Play Layer for Intersection-Free Multi-Object Signed Distance Fields (Sayin Mercadier et al., arXiv 2026)
sources.method: Defines a hard constraint on a vector of per-object SDFs: at every point, the smallest plus the second-smallest signed distance must be at least zero, so at most one object is 'inside'. The constraint is enforced by projecting each grid sample (a QP, or the closed-form 'Shift-All' heuristic, exact for K=2: subtract (d1+d2)/2 from both). It is proven to stay intersection-free under linear interpolation, so per-object marching cubes gives intersection-free meshes. Works as a post-processing step on any SDF grid.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 2 (ep24 boards overlapping by 13.5 cm^3 in the assembled pose; slots filled in). Transform board B's TSDF into board A's frame at the assembled frames and project, and the overlap goes to zero by construction. Caution: the symmetric split cuts the contested box along equal-distance planes, which would give V-shaped full-height notches, not cross-halving half-depth notches. We need an asymmetric split, by observation evidence and by insertion direction (see ideas).
sources.evidence: Reduces intersection volume 'to numerical precision' (several orders of magnitude) on MedTet, ObjectSDF++ and PartSDF while preserving reconstruction metrics. Soft penalty losses reduce intersection only marginally (their Table 4).
sources.code: No code link found in the paper or on the abstract page.
sources.adoption_effort: Hours: a numpy operation on our TSDF voxel grids at the co-located frames, plus a day for evidence-weighted ownership and checks. CPU only.
sources.rule_risk: None: a pure geometric constraint on our own reconstruction.

sources.title: Atlas3D: Physically Constrained Self-Supporting Text-to-3D for Simulation and Fabrication (NeurIPS 2024)
sources.method: Adds three terms to SDS text-to-3D. (1) A standability loss: rotation drift after a differentiable rigid-body simulation (NVIDIA Warp), ||R(T)-I||^2. (2) A cheap stable-equilibrium (potential-well) loss: small tilts phi about horizontal axes must raise the centre-of-mass height. (3) A bottom-Laplacian loss that flattens vertices below a height threshold, plus normal consistency. Robustness is tested under random initial tilts.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 1 and the board edges in problem 2. The potential-well test is a closed-form, simulation-free stability check usable as a fast gate in the inner loop. The bottom-Laplacian term is the smooth, principled version of our flatten_base.py, applied only to the support band. Warp-based differentiable simulation matches our Newton/Warp stack if gradient-based shape refinement is ever wanted.
sources.evidence: Generated models stand where Magic3D/MVDream baselines fall over. Higher standing success under random perturbations (their Fig. 7 / Table 1). Eight 3D-printed figures, 800 user trials plus robot trials. Quantitative values are in tables not extracted here.
sources.code: Not verified (project page atlas3dphys.github.io did not return a code link).
sources.adoption_effort: Potential-well check: a few hours with trimesh on our meshes. Bottom-Laplacian smoothing restricted to the support band: about half a day.
sources.rule_risk: The SDS generative part is a grey zone, but we would only reuse the physics terms, which are prior-free.

sources.title: SimuScene: Simulation-Ready Compositional 3D Scene Reconstruction from a Single Image (Lee et al., arXiv 2606.03994, NeurIPS 2026)
sources.method: Uses the simulator as a diagnostic instrument. Objects are processed one by one in ascending order of their lowest point: earlier objects are frozen as static colliders, the active one first gets its penetration resolved, then is dropped and stopped at first contact. The normalised gravity-axis displacement rho (displacement over the object's extent along gravity) chooses the fix: below 0.15, stretch the shape along the gravity-aligned box axis; above, resample the shape (fine-tuned SAM3D). A final joint settle follows. Tables get a RANSAC-plane top-surface snap. Collision geometry is MuJoCo plus V-HACD.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 3 (objects floating 1-4 cm and dropping at the start; the ep12 cup in the rack tipping 23 deg) and the QA gate. The sequential, frozen-support, first-contact protocol is a direct recipe for a stable initial state. rho is a ground-truth-free metric for automatically deciding whether a pose fix or a shape fix is needed.
sources.evidence: Ablation on GenWild: adding stabilised gravity simulation lowers mean displacement 0.395 -> 0.197; adding shape correction lowers it to 0.128, and strict ABO rises 0.218 (SAM3D) -> 0.507. Lowest penetration ratios on GraspClutter6D and GenWild (e.g. 2.5% for theirs in one column of Table 1).
sources.code: github.com/snuvclab/SimuScene (linked from the project page; licence not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: About 0.5-1 day CPU: extend our contact_retarget --rest_settle into sequential settling along a support tree, with supports frozen and a first-contact stop, using our CPU MuJoCo and CoACD pieces.
sources.rule_risk: The resampling stage uses a fine-tuned SAM3D generative prior (grey zone); skip it and use only the diagnostic and settling protocol (prior-free). The related phi-Scene (arXiv 2606.21596) does the same topology-ordered SDF-then-simulation settling.

sources.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints (Malenicky, Cifka, Fourmy, Montaut, Carpentier, Sivic, Petrik; arXiv 2503.23587, 2025)
sources.method: Post-processes estimated 6D poses by gradient optimisation of three weighted costs. A pose cost keeps the result near the image estimate, weighted by uncertainty. A collision cost penalises pairwise penetration between convex sub-parts of movable and static objects. A gravity cost is the positive distance of each convex sub-part to the nearest static support along gravity; it is switched off when the object is already supported by contact. The table pose is estimated from two views (MASt3R plus RANSAC).
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 3 directly, and our score: pose errors in depth (floating) are exactly what ADD-type metrics punish. Applies to every rest segment of every object without per-object tuning, using our CoACD pieces and table plane.
sources.evidence: YCB-Video BOP average recall: MegaPose 0.620 -> 0.707, FoundPose 0.690 -> 0.775. HOPE-Video: 0.353 -> 0.395 and 0.286 -> 0.324. Gains are mainly in MSSD/VSD, the depth-sensitive metrics. Higher real pick-and-place success.
sources.code: Project page https://data.ciirc.cvut.cz/public/projects/2025PhysPose/ (no GitHub link found).
sources.adoption_effort: About 1 day CPU, reusing the MuJoCo collision queries we already use in contact_retarget.py; restrict to frames our tracks mark as static.
sources.rule_risk: None: our own meshes and poses only. Must not use mocap; the gravity direction comes from our table plane.

sources.title: HoloScene: Simulation-Ready Interactive 3D Worlds from a Single Video (Xia et al., NeurIPS 2025)
sources.method: Energy-based scene-graph reconstruction from a video. Terms: observation (RGB, depth, mask, normal); completeness (Wonder3D virtual views); geometry (SDF penetration: the sum over points of max(0, -g_k(x) - g_i(x)), plus a mesh-intersection indicator); physics (an E_stable pose drift after a gravity simulation, plus E_touch Chamfer distance between support pairs). The support relations form a tree. Three stages: gradient optimisation, generative sampling plus structured tree search over shape hypotheses, appearance fine-tuning.
sources.solves_for_us: Problems 2-3 conceptually: a support tree (table, then rack, then cup), an SDF non-penetration term for co-located objects, and stability measured by simulated drift. The closest setting to ours (video input), but for static scenes.
sources.evidence: Stable (All) %: Replica 81.7 vs PhyRecon 5.6, DP-Recon 8.5, ObjSDF++ 39.4. ScanNet++ 70.6 vs 9.4 / 9.4 / 28.2. iGibson 71.1. Runtime about 4 h + 4 h + 20 min on one A6000.
sources.code: github.com/xiahongchi/HoloScene (per search results; licence not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: Full method not adoptable: about 8 GPU-hours per scene, neural SDF plus Gaussians, Wonder3D. Reuse only the energy formulations (hours).
sources.rule_risk: High for the full method: it uses Wonder3D and LaMa generative priors to complete unseen geometry (grey zone, and arguably not 'our own reconstruction'). The geometry and physics terms alone are fine.

sources.title: Real-to-Sim for Highly Cluttered Environments via Physics-Consistent Inter-Object Reasoning (Xiang et al., arXiv 2602.12633, 2026)
sources.method: Builds a contact graph: a support parse tree scored by normalised support gap and centre-of-mass-in-support-polygon consistency, plus proximity edges. Stage 1 refines poses with an SDF contact loss: no penetration plus at least K near-contact samples for support pairs, and only non-penetration for proximal pairs. Stage 2 runs hierarchical, root-to-leaf differentiable rigid-body simulation (DiffSDFSim, Frank-Wolfe SDF-mesh collision) that drives velocities to zero, jointly optimising pose, centre of mass, mass and friction.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 3 and the cup-in-rack case: support-gap and centre-of-mass-margin scores are cheap ground-truth-free diagnostics. The idea of identifying the centre of mass (not just shape) from observed static rests is a rule-safe fallback for objects whose mass distribution is not uniform.
sources.evidence: Stability ratio improves on average by 38% over SAM3D+ICP across GSO/YCB simulated clutter (4-15 objects). Real world: about 72% physical stability, average initial UCD 40 mm.
sources.code: Project page https://physics-constrained-real2sim.github.io/ links github.com/physics-constrained-Real2Sim/physics-constrained-Real2Sim (contents and licence not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: Scores and the support tree: hours. Differentiable simulation with centre-of-mass identification: days; not needed in full.
sources.rule_risk: Their initialisation is SAM3D (grey zone); the physics stages are prior-free. Changing the simulator's centre of mass is not a mesh change, but disclose it.

sources.title: RoboSnap: One-Shot Real-to-Sim Scene Generation (Zhang et al., arXiv 2607.06699, 2026)
sources.method: After per-object reconstruction (SAM3D, VGGT, ICP), a physical scene graph guides alternating rounds of an SDF phase and a physics phase. The SDF phase uses 128^3 Open3D SDF grids and minimises penetration, support, contact and regularisation losses on residual SE(3) poses. The physics phase builds V-HACD hulls, teleports the poses into SAPIEN with roots kinematic and the rest dynamic, settles, and reads the poses back. About 20 rounds. Includes voxel morphological watertight repair (dilate, flood-fill from outside, erode) before computing SDFs.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 3: a ready recipe for alternating geometric depenetration with physical settling, which avoids explosive starts when meshes overlap. The watertight repair recipe is relevant to our hole-closing step.
sources.evidence: Scenes stay stable over 300 frames in Isaac Sim (Table 1 of the paper), whereas the unrefined ones float or interpenetrate. Reliable trajectory replay on DROID scenes. The full pipeline takes 12-25 min per scene, mostly in non-physics stages.
sources.code: GitHub org github.com/robosnap linked from https://robosnap.github.io (contents not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: About 1 day CPU, mostly already covered by rest_settle plus contact_retarget's MuJoCo; add SDF-phase depenetration before settling.
sources.rule_risk: The asset generation uses SAM3D (grey zone); the refinement stage is prior-free.

sources.title: ARM: Amodal 3D Reconstruction for Robotic Manipulation via Stability and Connectivity (Agnew et al., CoRL 2020)
sources.method: Adds two differentiable priors to a learned voxel reconstructor (GenRE). A stability loss gives the probability that the object is unstable in each horizontal direction (the centre of mass must be within the base of support), with gradients that raise the occupancy of any voxel that would make the object stable; deliberately not biased toward simply adding a base. A connectivity loss fills gaps between disjoint observed parts and inferred bases. Baselines include ray carving and an 'extrusion' baseline.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 1: evidence that stability reasoning beats naive extrusion of the visible surface down to the table. Our flatten or fill approach is close to that extrusion baseline. The probabilistic directional stability test is a cheap voxel-level diagnostic and a guide for minimal fills.
sources.evidence: Chamfer distance improves 28% overall vs GenRE. Manipulation task success improves 42% over the baseline and 25% over the extrusion baseline. Task success correlates with target-object stability.
sources.code: github.com/wagnew3/ARM (per search results; licence not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: The network is trained on ShapeNet (not usable as is). The stability-loss logic on our occupancy grid: about half a day.
sources.rule_risk: The trained network would be a pretrained shape prior (grey zone); the analytic stability test alone is fine.

sources.title: Make It Stand: Balancing Shapes for 3D Fabrication (Prevost, Whiting, Lefebvre, Sorkine-Hornung; ACM TOG / SIGGRAPH 2013)
sources.method: Given a mesh, desired contact points and gravity direction, minimises an energy that moves the centre-of-mass projection into the support polygon. It trades off carving interior voids against small surface deformations that preserve detail. Supports multiple bases and delicate balance poses.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 1 as a last resort: the classic minimal-change stability fix. Relevant mainly as the template 'change as little as possible, only where unobserved, until the COM is over the support'. Interior carving maps to setting the simulator's COM, which avoids distorting the mesh.
sources.evidence: Qualitative: printed characters and everyday objects stand in surprising poses without glue or pedestals.
sources.code: Unofficial libigl implementation github.com/MultiW/make-it-balance (assumes solid objects; licence not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: About 1-2 days if needed; probably unnecessary if the support-plane completion (Vysics-style) fixes the footprint.
sources.rule_risk: None for COM or interior changes. Surface deformation of observed regions could hurt scan registration; restrict it to unobserved voxels.

sources.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction (Ni et al., NeurIPS 2024)
sources.method: A neural SDF scene reconstruction trained jointly with a differentiable particle-based simulator (DiffTaichi). Surface-points marching cubes (SP-MC) extracts surface points differentiably. The physics loss penalises motion of contact points under gravity. A physical-uncertainty grid accumulates where contact points move (missing support) and re-weights rendering losses and ray sampling toward thin supporting structures.
sources.solves_for_us: Mainly the idea of 'physical uncertainty': localise where support is missing, e.g. the dish rack's thin wires under the ep12 cup, and spend reconstruction effort there. Their object-ground-only assumption fails for stacked objects such as a cup in a rack.
sources.evidence: Claims at least a 40% stability improvement over baselines in Isaac Gym across Replica, ScanNet and ScanNet++. In HoloScene's re-evaluation, PhyRecon's Stable (All) is only 5.6% on Replica and 9.4% on ScanNet++.
sources.code: github.com/PhyRecon/PhyRecon and github.com/bigai-ai/differentiable-rigid-body-simulator (linked from phyrecon.github.io).
sources.adoption_effort: Full method not adoptable (a different reconstruction paradigm, GPU days). The missing-support heat-map idea from our MuJoCo settling: about half a day.
sources.rule_risk: Uses monocular geometry priors (pretrained depth and normal networks); a mild grey zone, comparable to our use of FoundationStereo.

sources.title: Physically Compatible 3D Object Modeling from a Single Image (Guo et al., NeurIPS 2024; PhysComp)
sources.method: Splits an object into mechanical properties, external forces and rest-shape geometry. It optimises the rest shape (through per-element deformation gradients, using finite-element static equilibrium as a hard constraint, solved by implicit differentiation) so that the shape under gravity matches the image and its centre-of-mass projection hits a stability target.
sources.solves_for_us: Weakly relevant: our objects are rigid, so the elastic rest-shape problem does not arise. Its centre-of-mass-target stability constraint is the same as the simple support-polygon check.
sources.evidence: Standability: Wonder3D baseline 6.9% -> 72.4%, LGM 20.3% -> 85.9% on 100 Objaverse shapes. Fewer connected components and lower mean stress.
sources.code: github.com/gmh14/PhysComp (linked from the project page).
sources.adoption_effort: Not worth adopting (finite-element simulation plus tetrahedral meshing, single-image setting).
sources.rule_risk: The inputs come from single-image generative reconstructors (grey zone); the method itself is physics-only.

ideas: H1 - Support-plane ('physible') completion from all rest frames, replacing flatten_base.py. Keep a three-state voxel grid (occupied / free / unknown) in recon_mesh.py. Detect rest segments from our own tracks (object speed < ~5 mm/s for >= 0.5 s within ~1 cm of the table plane). For each, transform the table plane into the object frame: carve beyond it (as below_carve does), then mark as occupied only the UNKNOWN voxels between the plane and the observed surface, inside the mask visual hull. Then check, per rest pose: contact-patch area, centre-of-mass margin inside the support polygon, and the Atlas3D potential-well test. If a pose is still unstable, extend the fill minimally within unknown voxels (ARM / Make It Stand style). No per-object parameters. Falsified if, run on all 11 objects of all public episodes with one fixed setting: (a) the assist-off 2 s drop-test failure rate over all rest segments is not lower than with library_v3; or (b) ep18's sweeper footprint at its perceived rest is not >= ~5 cm^2 (real 11.7 cm^2; now 0.3 cm^2) with its centre of mass inside; or (c) ep18's mean registered AUC over 6 evaluations falls below library_v3's 0.715; or (d) the diagnostics-only mesh-vs-scan registration AUC drops by more than 0.01 on any object.

H2 - Hard inter-object non-penetration at co-located frames, with an asymmetric ownership rule. For object pairs within ~5 mm of each other in any frame (ep24 boards, cup in rack, lid on pot), resample B's TSDF into A's frame at those frames and enforce d_A + d_B >= 0 (S2MDF; HoloScene's E_pene_sdf). Do not split the contested volume symmetrically. Assign it by observation evidence (TSDF integration weight per voxel). Break ties by insertion direction: the object that moved into the contact along direction n keeps the part of the overlap on its arrival side, which for cross-halving gives the inserting board the upper half. Falsified if: ep24's assembled-pose overlap does not drop from 13.5 cm^3 to < 0.5 cm^3; or the assembled X does not stay together and upright in an assist-off 2 s simulation; or the change alters meshes of objects that never co-locate (it must be a no-op there); or, after retraining, ep24's mean registered AUC does not exceed the current ~0.31.

H3 - Mask (silhouette) carving for narrow concavities. The ep24 notches are probably visible as gaps in the board outline whenever a board lies flat, even when FoundationStereo depth smooths over them. Carve voxels that project outside confident instance masks in at least k frames (a visual hull with a confidence threshold), alongside the depth free-space carving. This is Picasso's 'object-free-space non-penetration' constraint applied to shape (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08058). Falsified if: the board meshes still show no notch (notch width within ~3 mm of the width measured in images); or the carve removes real geometry elsewhere (any object's volume shrinks > 5% or its diagnostics-only scan-registration AUC drops > 0.01).

H4 - Physics-aware pose refinement plus bottom-up settling for every rest segment (PhysPose costs, then SimuScene / RoboSnap protocol). Minimise the pose change subject to: no penetration with the table or other objects, zero support gap, centre of mass inside the support polygon. Then settle in CPU MuJoCo in support-tree order (table, then rack, then cup), with already-placed objects frozen and a first-contact stop, and use the settled pose for the segment's frames with a short blend into motion. Falsified if, on public episodes: the first-0.5 s assist-off displacement of resting objects is not < 3 mm and < 3 deg; or the floats (1-4 cm today) do not fall below 2 mm; or ep12's cup still tips > 5 deg; or the diagnostics-only ADD vs mocap on static segments gets worse; or the mean registered AUC on ep12 (0.790 with contact retargeting) or ep27 (0.942 base) drops.

H5 - If the ep12 cup still tips after H4, the rack's thin wires (the support) are missing from the rack mesh; the cup is not to blame. Test: replace the rack by an infinite plane at the cup's observed contact height (diagnostic only). If the cup then stands, the rack geometry is the cause, and the fix is a local minimum thickening of the rack at the cup's expected contact points (PhyRecon-style missing-support localisation from settling drift). Falsified if the cup still tips on the ideal plane, which would point to the cup's own underside (apply H1) or its pose.

H6 - A ground-truth-free physical QA gate for every reconstructed object and episode (SimuScene's rho, HoloScene's E_stable, the support gap, the centre-of-mass margin, pairwise penetration volume, hand-penetration p95). It triggers H1-H4 automatically and logs everything in qa.py. It runs identically on eval episodes, with no tuning on their results. Falsified if, across public episodes, gate flags do not predict low scores (registered AUC < 0.5) better than chance, or flagged-and-fixed episodes do not improve on average.

H7 - The Atlas3D potential-well test (tilt by phi in 8 directions about the support; the centre-of-mass height must rise) as a cheap stand-in for the MuJoCo drop test inside H1's fill loop. Falsified if it disagrees with the 2 s MuJoCo drop test on > 5% of the public rest segments.

H8 - For planar wooden boards, fit a primitive model (an oriented box from RANSAC planes, minus notch boxes) instead of TSDF marching cubes, giving sharp, flat standing edges and exact slots. This comes from outside the physics-aware literature (PolyFit / CSG-fitting family; not reviewed here). Falsified if the primitive's residual to our observed depth points exceeds the TSDF mesh's, or if trimesh.poses.compute_stable_poses still finds no stable standing-on-edge pose.

H9 - Fallback that leaves the mesh alone: identify the simulator's centre of mass and inertia so that every observed rest pose is stable (as arXiv 2602.12633 optimises centre of mass, mass and friction). Expected to fail on ep18 with the rounded mesh, because a 0.3 cm^2 point contact has no stable centre of mass; that failure would confirm that a shape fix (H1) is required. Falsified as a useful fallback if no object on the public episodes becomes stable with the centre of mass alone. Disclose any centre-of-mass edits.
gaps: No work found on reconstructing interlocking or joinery parts (cross-halving notches) from video. Every non-penetration method found splits contested volume symmetrically or by optimisation against a prior; how to assign the overlap correctly (evidence plus insertion direction, H2) is our own hypothesis and untested.

Almost all physics-aware reconstruction papers (SimuScene, SPARCS, the cluttered Real2Sim paper, RoboSnap, Picasso, phi-Scene) are single-image or static-scene and start from SAM3D or other generative priors; only Vysics and HoloScene use video. Their stability numbers do not transfer to our moving-object, TSDF-in-object-frame setting.

Code could not be checked: the GitHub search API is blocked in this session, and repository pages returned no readable content via curl. SPARCS, Atlas3D, PhysPose and S2MDF have no code link I could find; Vysics' page shows 'coming soon' next to its repo link. Licences for all repos are unverified.

Unknown how the challenge's hidden-scan registration weighs geometry in regions we change on physical grounds (underside fill, slot carving). The impact on registered AUC has to be measured on public episodes (diagnostics only), not assumed.

Not verified whether the challenge FAQ treats physics-constrained completion of unobserved geometry (plane fill, centre-of-mass identification) as 'own reconstruction'. It uses no ground truth and no pretrained prior, but the owner may want to confirm with the organisers.

Thin structures (the plastic dish rack's wires supporting the cup) are covered only indirectly (PhyRecon's physical uncertainty); I found no physics-aware method that reliably recovers thin supports from noisy stereo depth.
I did not extract exact quantitative tables for Atlas3D (perturbation success rates) or RoboSnap (Isaac Sim stability metrics); their evidence is summarised qualitatively above.

Hand-object video reconstruction work (AGILE arXiv 2602.04672; zero-shot in-scene manipulation arXiv 2512.19684) relies on generative mesh synthesis and was not reviewed in depth; the generative-prior grey zone makes it unsuitable for our submitted meshes.

verified.angle:
Fact-check of the "physics-aware-recon" survey. I read the arXiv full text (HTML) of Vysics, S2MDF, SimuScene, SPARCS, PhysPose and Atlas3D. For HoloScene I read only the runtime line and confirmed the repo exists; for phi-Scene I checked only the abstract. Code status comes from the project pages and from read-only git clones of the repos. The GitHub web pages and API are blocked for this session, so licences were read from the cloned files. All six papers exist and their methods are described broadly correctly. The corrections that matter are these.
(1) PhysPose's headline gains (0.620->0.707 and 0.690->0.775 AR) assume a KNOWN scene. When the table is estimated from two views the gains are only 0.620->0.650 and 0.690->0.715, and with one view the scores get worse.
(2) SimuScene's rho does NOT choose between a pose fix and a shape fix. Both of its branches are shape edits (gravity-axis stretch or generative resample), and the pose is always corrected first. Its diagnostic is translation-only (no rotation for free objects), so it cannot detect our sweeper toppling. Its last ablation gain (D_mean 0.197->0.128) comes from the fine-tuned SAM3D resampling, which we would skip. The prior-free stages stop at 0.197.
(3) SimuScene's central claim contradicts the colleague's framing that floating is handled "by pose refinement, not by shape edits". SimuScene argues that hovering and sinking need shape correction too.
(4) Code status was wrong in three places. Vysics code IS released (DAIRLab/vysics, NVIDIA Source Code License, research/evaluation-only). Atlas3D code exists under Apache-2.0 (github.com/yunuoch/Atlas3D; the colleague's project URL returns 404). The SimuScene repo is a placeholder README ("Will be updated"). SPARCS says "Code (To be released soon)". S2MDF and PhysPose have no code link.
(5) Vysics: three of the four learned shape-completion baselines DID beat BundleSDF (2.45-2.80 vs 2.98 cm). Vysics's contact geometry comes from a known robot sphere plus proprioception, so its dynamics inference does not transfer to human hands. Its convexity bias would fill our slots and cavities.
(6) Our recon_mesh.py already implements the Vysics hyperplane carve (--below_carve, 4 mm per-frame table-plane carve). What is missing is the support-point / contact half.
Everything below is the papers' own numbers. Nothing has been measured by us, and every adaptation is a hypothesis.

checked.title: Vysics: Object Reconstruction Under Occlusion by Fusing Vision and Contact-Rich Physics (Bianchini, Zhu, Sun, Jiang, Taylor, Posa; RSS 2025)
checked.claim_checked: Method (support points, hyperplane bound, convexity bias). Chamfer 2.98 -> 1.45 cm. Shape-completion baselines 2.45-3.06 cm and 'no better than vision-only'. 10 cm / 45 deg divergence metric. 7 objects with a Franka. Code 'coming soon / not verified'.
checked.verdict: partly
checked.what_source_actually_says: Method confirmed. BundleSDF tracks the object and reconstructs its visible SDF. PLL (a deep support function, which can represent only CONVEX shapes) infers contact forces from the trajectory, where contacts are with a table plane and a spherical robot end-effector whose position is KNOWN from the joint states. Support/normal pairs whose inferred force is above a threshold become 'physible' data, and BundleSDF is rerun with three losses: SDF = l along the support ray (support point loss, eq. 8); SDF >= (q - s)·n (hyperplane loss, eq. 10-11, sampled in a cylinder around the support points); and a convexity upper bound between near-surface and support points (eq. 12-13), assuming one object at a time. Table I confirms the per-object-average chamfer: BundleSDF 2.98, Vysics 1.45, 3DSGrasp 3.06, V-PRISM 2.80, IPoD 2.47, OctMAE 2.45 cm. Correction: three of the four completion baselines are BETTER than BundleSDF; the paper says they are 'similar or slightly lower' and fall far behind Vysics. Setup: 7 objects, RealSense D455, sessions of about 10 s, Franka with a spherical tip. Dynamics: time-before-divergence uses 10 cm / 45 deg thresholds, with the gains shown in figures (no single number). Code: the repo github.com/DAIRLab/vysics is populated (BundleTrack, the dair_pll submodule, docker, run_all.sh; last commit 2025-09-29). It needs CUDA, Docker, ROS Noetic and pretrained XMem and LoFTR weights. Licence: NVIDIA Source Code License (section 3.3, research/evaluation use only).
checked.code_status: Released: github.com/DAIRLab/vysics, NVIDIA Source Code License (non-commercial). Inherits the BundleSDF stack and pretrained XMem/LoFTR weights.
checked.applicability: Use the formulation, not the code. PLL needs known pusher geometry and proprioception. Our hands are MANO estimates, and the objects mostly move while held, so dynamics inference has almost nothing to use. Only rest-on-table frames transfer. Note that recon_mesh.py already applies the hyperplane half: every frame's table plane carves voxels more than 4 mm below it (--below_carve). The missing half is the support-point constraint, meaning the object must actually reach the plane with enough footprint at each rest segment. A rest in a different orientation adds another supporting plane: the ep24 boards standing in the assembled X give an edge plane that should flatten the rounded edges. Do NOT adopt the convexity loss: it would fill the ep24 notches, cup interiors and dish-rack gaps. That is exactly the failure we have.

checked.title: S2MDF: A Plug-And-Play Layer for Intersection-Free Multi-Object Signed Distance Fields (Sayin Mercadier, Stella, Bizeau, Talabot, Fua; arXiv 2605.29761, v2 16 Sep 2026)
checked.claim_checked: min1 + min2 >= 0 constraint. QP or Shift-All. Closed form exact for K=2. Intersection-free under linear interpolation, so per-object marching cubes. Post-processing. 'Numerical precision'. Table 4: soft losses help only marginally. No code.
checked.verdict: confirmed
checked.what_source_actually_says: Theorem 1: for true SDFs, 'second-smallest >= 0' is equivalent to 'smallest + second-smallest >= 0'. Theorem 2: the latter survives linear interpolation, so independent marching cubes on the shared grid gives intersection-free meshes. Projection is a QP (pairwise d_i + d_j >= 0). For K=2 the analytic optimum adds -(min1 + min2)/2 to every entry (Shift-All), and for K>2 Shift-All is feasible but not optimal. It works during training or as post-processing (PP). It was tested on MedTet (organs), ObjectSDF++ (scenes) and PartSDF (parts), all neural SDFs. Table 4 (MedTet, training): with the soft loss the intersection volume goes from 2.28e-5 to 2.07e-5; with S2MDF it is about 1e-9 (QP) or 7e-12 (Shift-All), and MCD is unchanged. No code link in the paper or on the abstract page.
checked.code_status: No code link found (arXiv abstract and full text).
checked.applicability: Usable for ep24 on CPU in hours, with three caveats. (a) It needs real, untruncated signed distances on ONE shared grid. Our TSDF clamps at ±TRUNC, and two clamped insides give a flat 0 band after the shift. So compute full SDFs from the two board meshes (e.g. an EDT on the voxel grids), resample board B into A's grid at the assembled relative pose, project, mesh both, and map B back to its own frame. (b) A symmetric K=2 split puts the surface at d_A = d_B inside the crossing column. For two crossed plates that is a diagonal split in plan view that hardly varies with height, so each board is pinched to about zero thickness along the full height. That is not a cross-halving joint. Because the split is roughly the same at every height, vertical insertion stays collision-free, so it is a valid cheap BASELINE for simulation, but it is less faithful than the true half-depth notch. (c) First check how much of the 13.5 cm^3 lies OUTSIDE the crossing column. That part is pose error and must be fixed by pose, not by carving.

checked.title: SimuScene: Simulation-Ready Compositional 3D Scene Reconstruction from a Single Image (Lee, Baik, Kim, Kim, Cha, Joo; arXiv 2606.03994, NeurIPS 2026 per repo README)
checked.claim_checked: Sequential lowest-first protocol with frozen supports and first-contact stop. rho < 0.15 stretch, otherwise resample. D_mean 0.395 -> 0.197 -> 0.128. Strict ABO 0.218 -> 0.507. Penetration 2.5%. MuJoCo + V-HACD. Code on GitHub. 'rho decides pose fix vs shape fix'.
checked.verdict: partly
checked.what_source_actually_says: The numbers are confirmed. Objects are processed in ascending order of the bottom corner of their world bounding box along gravity. Earlier objects are frozen static colliders. The active object first has its penetration resolved, then is released and frozen at the first contact frame. For FREE objects the rotation change is the identity, so the diagnostic is translation-only. rho = |g·(dt_pen + dt_grv)| / OBB extent along gravity. If rho >= 0.15 the shape is resampled by SAM3D fine-tuned with flow-matching DPO (LoRA, 16.6K pairs, 4 RTX PRO 6000 GPUs). Otherwise the mesh is stretched along the gravity-aligned OBB axis with the top face held fixed. A final joint 6-DoF settle follows, and any object that moves more than a divergence bound is reverted. Table 2 (GenWild): +Pen D_mean 0.395 -> +Grv 0.197 -> +Resample 0.128; strict ABO_fh/fo 0.218 -> 0.406 (+Grv) -> 0.507 (full). ABO is 2D mask overlap. GenWild penetrated-object ratio 2.5%. MuJoCo + V-HACD confirmed. The table snap is a category-gated top-plane alignment for table/desk MESHES in single-image scenes. Corrections: (1) rho chooses between two SHAPE fixes, not between a pose fix and a shape fix; pose is always corrected first. (2) The last gain (0.197 -> 0.128, 0.406 -> 0.507) is the generative resampling we would skip. (3) The paper explicitly argues that hovering and sinking come from shape errors that pose-only correction leaves unresolved.
checked.code_status: github.com/snuvclab/SimuScene contains only a README ('Will be updated', last commit 2026-09-26). No code and no licence.
checked.applicability: Adopt the protocol: lowest-first sequential settling, supports frozen as static colliders, first-contact stop, final joint settle, and revert on divergence. It fits our CPU MuJoCo and CoACD pieces in about a day. Do not use rho as a pose-vs-shape oracle, and do not use its gravity-axis stretch. Our depth is metric stereo, and stretching the whole mesh would distort the visible geometry that the hidden-scan registration uses. It also cannot catch ep18-type toppling, because the drop test is translation-only. The prior-free part of their evidence is the +Pen/+Grv rows, not the full model.

checked.title: SPARCS: Simulation-Ready Cluttered Scene Estimation via Physics-aware Joint Shape and Pose Optimization (Huang, Han, Ye, Pan, Hauser; RSS 2026)
checked.claim_checked: Hull vertices plus SE(3) as variables. Augmented Lagrangian with separating-plane contact and friction cones. Woodbury/Schur solver up to 8.7x faster. 1-minute MuJoCo equilibrium. 46-540 CPU-min on a Core Ultra 9 285K. SAM3D+FoundationPose initialisation. No code.
checked.verdict: confirmed
checked.what_source_actually_says: All confirmed. Table III wall times are 46.1, 259.7, 224.2, 202.15 and 539.92 min for scenes of 6-22 hulls. Everything runs on CPU except texture refinement on an RTX 5090. Table IV gives a 1.43-8.71x linear-solve speedup over LU. Reconstructions stay in equilibrium over 1 minute of MuJoCo, while SAM3D+FoundationPose initialisations blow up. PSNR is comparable to the initialisation. It is single-view and static. Unseen regions are regularised toward the SAM3D mesh. Mass and friction are set by hand. Baselines are simulated with CoACD collision meshes. 'Separating plane aggregation' uses one plane per object pair to smooth occluded contact regions.
checked.code_status: Project page says 'Code (To be released soon)'. Not released.
checked.applicability: Too heavy for the freeze date, as the colleague said. Its unseen-region term depends on a generative prior. Our existing MuJoCo assist-off settle is a cheaper equilibrium oracle. Keep only the concepts: a quasi-static equilibrium check for the assembled X and cup-in-rack states, and a non-penetration test between hulls.

checked.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints (Malenicky, Cifka, Fourmy, Montaut, Carpentier, Sivic, Petrik; arXiv 2503.23587; project supplementary is labelled ICCV 2025)
checked.claim_checked: Pose + collision + gravity costs on convex parts. Gravity cost switched off when supported. Table from two views (MASt3R + RANSAC). AR 0.620 -> 0.707 and 0.690 -> 0.775, HOPE 0.353 -> 0.395 and 0.286 -> 0.324.
checked.verdict: partly
checked.what_source_actually_says: Costs confirmed. Collision cost: a hinge on negative signed distance between convex parts. Gravity cost: the mean positive distance of ALL the movable object's convex parts to the nearest static part below it. It is disabled when the object is 'in collision with any other object'. Gravity is taken from the table normal. Meshes are known BOP CAD models, so there are no shape errors. The quoted numbers are real but come from Table 1, 'Results in KNOWN environments', where the scene geometry is given. With ESTIMATED geometry (Table 2, YCB-V): support-view estimate 0.620 -> 0.650 and 0.690 -> 0.715; single view 0.597 and 0.658 (worse than the initial poses); known gravity no consistent help. Gains are mostly in MSSD and VSD (depth), as the colleague said.
checked.code_status: The project page links only the arXiv paper and a supplementary PDF. No code found.
checked.applicability: Useful for problem 3 when the float is a POSE error. Our table plane is fitted from many metric stereo frames, which may be closer to their 'known' case, but expect about +0.03 AR-like gains, not +0.085. It cannot fix ep18: with a rounded underside, pose refinement can only tilt or drop the sweeper onto a point. Restrict it to rest segments, use our CoACD pieces, and keep the uncertainty-weighted pose prior to the visual track.

checked.title: Atlas3D: Physically Constrained Self-Supporting Text-to-3D for Simulation and Fabrication (Chen, Xie, Zong, Li, Gao, Yang, Wu, Jiang; NeurIPS 2024)
checked.claim_checked: Warp differentiable-sim standability loss, potential-well loss, bottom Laplacian. Eight printed figures, 800 user trials. Code not verified.
checked.verdict: confirmed
checked.what_source_actually_says: Method confirmed. Values the colleague did not extract: 800 user trials (10 users x 5 trials, over the printed figures and their baselines), success 7% for the baseline vs 92.25% for Atlas3D. Robot arm: 64 trials, 6.25% vs 90.6%. Stability-loss ablation on one model (goose): with vs without the loss, 0.69 vs 0.62 at 0.04 rad perturbation and 0.40 vs 0.23 at 0.08 rad. In the code (threestudio/systems/loss_func.py), the potential-well loss tilts the mesh up to 0.1 rad over 20 azimuths and penalises any drop in the centre-of-mass height above the lowest vertex. The bottom Laplacian acts only on vertices in the lowest 2% of height and only on the z component, with z as the canonical up.
checked.code_status: Released: github.com/yunuoch/Atlas3D, Apache-2.0, 2024-06-07. Bundles its own Warp fork. The project page is yunuoch.github.io/Atlas3D (atlas3dphys.github.io returns 404).
checked.applicability: For a rigid body on a plane, the potential-well test is the same as 'the centre-of-mass projection lies inside the support polygon with a margin set by the tilt'. Implement one check, not two, using our perceived up per rest. The bottom Laplacian only flattens vertices that already exist in a band. It cannot grow the sweeper's 0.3 cm^2 tip into an 11.7 cm^2 base, so it is no more principled than flatten_base.py's 8 mm band. A footprint has to come from evidence-based filling of unknown voxels down to the support plane.

checked.title: HoloScene (Xia et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2510.05560) - runtime and code only
checked.claim_checked: About 8 GPU-hours per scene. Uses a generative prior.
checked.verdict: confirmed
checked.what_source_actually_says: 'Approximately 4 hours, 4 hours, and 20 minutes for stages 1, 2, and 3 ... on a single A6000 GPU', which is about 8.3 GPU-hours per scene. The energy combines observations, physical constraints and generative priors.
checked.code_status: github.com/xiahongchi/HoloScene exists (git ls-remote). Licence not read.
checked.applicability: Too slow for the freeze date. Not adopted.

corrected_ideas: Hyperplane carve: recon_mesh.py already does this. Its --below_carve option makes voxels more than 4 mm below each frame's table plane free. The missing piece is Vysics's other half, the support-point constraint. Hypothesis H-support: for each rest segment found from our own tracks (low speed, near the table), fill only the voxels that are never observed (fewer than --min_obs updates) and lie between the observed surface and that rest's table plane. Restrict the fill to the object's mask visual hull, and only where the column below the voxel was never seen to be empty. Each additional rest orientation adds another plane; for the ep24 boards, the standing frames in the assembled X give a plane for the board edge. Falsify on public episodes after inference: compare the filled underside with the scans (Chamfer of the bottom region, footprint area) and run the assist-off standing test. If objects with concave bottoms (cup foot rings, pot) get worse, H-support is wrong as stated.

Do not adopt Vysics's convexity loss or Atlas3D's bottom-band Laplacian. The convexity loss fills notches, cup interiors and rack gaps. The band Laplacian only flattens vertices that already exist and cannot create a footprint. Neither removes the per-object band parameter in flatten_base.py.

Pose fix or shape fix for floating objects: SimuScene's rho does not answer this; both of its branches are shape edits. Use a rule based on our own evidence instead. If depth rays passed through the gap between the mesh bottom and the table plane (seen empty), it is a pose error: lower the object with a PhysPose-style gravity, collision and pose-prior refinement. If the gap was never observed, it is a shape error: apply H-support. This matters for scoring. Dropping an object whose mesh is missing its bottom adds the full gap to the ADD error after the hidden-scan registration. Validation on public episodes, diagnostics only: split each rest gap into pose error (our track vs mocap) and shape error (our mesh vs scan bottom), then measure how often the rule picks correctly.

One stability diagnostic, not two. Atlas3D's potential-well test equals the centre-of-mass margin inside the support polygon. The support polygon is the convex hull of the vertices within a small distance of the plane at the rest pose, and the margin is the signed distance from the projected centre of mass to its edge. Use one global tilt or margin setting (Atlas3D's code uses 0.1 rad), and keep an assist-off MuJoCo drop test as the final check. SimuScene's translation-only drop test cannot detect ep18-type toppling.

ep24 overlap. Steps:
(1) Measure how much of the 13.5 cm^3 lies outside the crossing column; fix that part by pose.
(2) Cheap baseline: S2MDF Shift-All on full (untruncated) SDFs resampled into one grid at the assembled relative pose. It gives a diagonal split of the crossing column that hardly varies with height, so it is free of intersections and allows vertical insertion, but it is not the real joint.
(3) More faithful: an asymmetric split. Hypothesis: the board lowered from above gets the slot opening downward and the other board gets the slot opening upward. The split height is H/2, a cross-halving convention, not observed; refine it only if a slot is visible in the masks in some frame.
Compare (2) and (3) by: overlap volume -> 0, both boards' rendered masks still match the assembled frames, and the policy's ep24 score. If neither improves the score, the bottleneck is the reference or the policy, not the geometry.

Pose stage: SimuScene/phi-Scene-style sequential settling. Order: lowest object first. Supports: frozen as static colliders. Stop: at first contact. Then one final joint settle, reverting any object that moves more than a set bound. Apply only to rest segments and keep a pose prior to our visual tracks. Use PhysPose's estimated-environment gains (about +0.03 AR), not the known-scene +0.085, as the realistic expectation.

ep12 cup tipping 23 deg (unmeasured hypothesis): the cause may be the rack's collision geometry. Thin plastic bars, 4 mm voxels and CoACD hulls that fill the gaps between bars give the cup a wrong seat, which pose settling cannot fix. Check: compare the volume of the rack's CoACD hull union with its mesh volume near the cup contact, then re-settle with a finer decomposition.

Keep it general. Run the stage with the same global thresholds on ALL public episodes, not only ep18 and ep24. Gate on two things: no object's Chamfer-to-scan gets worse beyond a fixed tolerance, and the stability, overlap and gap diagnostics pass. Otherwise we only tune to two episodes. Record the results per object and per rest segment.

Code and licences: Vysics's code is released but carries a research/evaluation-only NVIDIA licence and needs robot proprioception, so reimplement only its losses. Atlas3D's code is Apache-2.0 and its stability/Laplacian functions are small enough to read and reimplement on CPU. SimuScene and SPARCS have no usable code, and S2MDF and PhysPose have no code link. None of this changes the plan: every planned piece is a few hundred lines of numpy/trimesh/MuJoCo on our own grids.

found.angle: Unseen-geometry completion: undersides, back faces, edges and narrow slots. Bottom line: the two hand-made fixes (flatten the underside along one up vector, carve the slot from the final overlap) apply the right physics, but each was tuned to a single episode. The literature points to a sturdier route. Build one mesh per object from all its episodes. Label each voxel as observed-surface, observed-free or unknown. Resolve unknown voxels only with constraints that come from our own tracks: (a) an object resting on the table touches it with a flat patch; (b) an object seen resting untouched must be stable in the simulator; (c) the object never shares space with the table, the hands or the other object at any frame. Simple shape families can help (surface of revolution, mirror symmetry, flat extruded slab), chosen by how well they fit. Gate every object and episode, eval included, with a physics check that needs no ground truth. PhyRecon is the closest evidence: adding the rule 'resting means stable' lifted the stability ratio on real ScanNet++ objects from about 25% to 78%. Generative priors (SAM 3D, TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D, Zero123 family) complete real objects only to about 1 cm Chamfer or about 0.5 volume IoU. Even for images of stable objects, TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D-2.0 produce about 30% and 15% unstable meshes. SAM 3D's coarse shape grid is 64^3, too coarse for an 8 mm notch. So a generative mesh can only be a candidate for unknown voxels, accepted after the same physics checks; it cannot be the fix. Repo-specific finding (from reading pipeline/recon_mesh.py, not from the papers): depth samples within 15 mm of the table never vote as surface (`--table_band` 0.015). Thin objects then use 'near' closing with 3 voxels of 4 mm (12 mm). So the bottom 1-1.5 cm of every resting object is unknown, which can produce rounded undersides and part of the 1-4 cm floats. The boards are 7.5-9 mm thick (from our eval survey note 15), which is thinner than the 12 mm truncation band. That is the regime where the thin-structure papers report thickening and rounded edges, and it explains why the boards cannot stand on an edge. These are hypotheses with tests below. Today's numbers come from STATUS and the work log, not from new measurements.

sources.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction (Ni et al., NeurIPS 2024)
sources.method: Trains a neural SDF with differentiable rendering plus a differentiable particle-based rigid-body simulator. SP-MC turns the SDF into surface points for the physics loss. A physical-uncertainty map steers pixel sampling toward slender structures. Only object-ground support is modelled, and objects that move when dropped onto their support are penalised.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 1, and the standing poses in problem 2. Their baselines show the same failure we measured: real objects that rest on a support come out unstable. Adding the constraint 'seen resting means stable' to the reconstruction fixes most cases. We should adopt the principle and the metric (a drop test per static segment), not the neural pipeline.
sources.evidence: ScanNet++ object stability ratio (Isaac Gym drop; stable if under 5 deg and 5 cm after 200 steps at 60 Hz): RICO 26.43%, ObjectSDF++ 25.28%, PhyRecon 78.16%. Object Chamfer 4.08 to 3.28 cm. Abstract claims at least 40% stability improvement on all datasets.
sources.code: https://github.com/PhyRecon/PhyRecon (licence not verified; GitHub API blocked from this session)
sources.adoption_effort: Full port: weeks (neural SDF, custom differentiable simulator, multi-view RGB), not feasible in 13 days. Discrete version (MuJoCo drop test plus constrained completion of unknown voxels): 1-2 days CPU.
sources.rule_risk: None for the principle. It uses only our own static segments, table plane and meshes.

sources.title: Physically Compatible 3D Object Modeling from a Single Image (PhysComp; Guo et al., NeurIPS 2024)
sources.method: Takes a mesh from any image-to-3D model and optimises its rest shape (TetSphere/FEM volumetric mesh), with static equilibrium as a hard constraint. The stability loss is ||proj_z(CoM) - target||: it pulls the projected centre of mass inside the contact support.
sources.solves_for_us: Problems 1 and 2. This is the same criterion as our ep18 diagnosis (CoM 3 cm outside a 0.3 cm^2 footprint). It also shows that raw generated meshes are usually not standable.
sources.evidence: Objaverse, share of shapes that can stand, before vs after optimisation: Wonder3D 6.9 to 72.4%, LGM 20.3 to 85.5%, MeshLRM 29.6 to 74.5%, TripoSR 24.2 to 80.6%, TetSphere 32.8 to 92.2%. Image loss stays the same or improves.
sources.code: https://github.com/gmh14/PhysComp (licence not verified)
sources.adoption_effort: Not worth porting: FEM/tet pipeline; the DSO authors report it is slow on CPU and sometimes fails numerically. Reusing the CoM-projection loss on unknown voxels only: hours.
sources.rule_risk: None for the idea. Changes should stay inside never-observed regions so the mesh remains our own reconstruction.

sources.title: DSO: Aligning 3D Generators with Simulation Feedback for Physical Soundness (Li, Zheng, Rupprecht, Vedaldi, ICCV 2025)
sources.method: Fine-tunes TRELLIS (LoRA; DPO or a new DRO objective) using stability labels from a non-differentiable MuJoCo simulator: upright drop, uniform density, stable if tilt is under 20 deg. Training data is self-generated, with no 3D ground truth.
sources.solves_for_us: Mainly evidence. A generative completion of the sweeper or a board would still need our stability check. It also supports using a simulator as the judge that picks among several candidate meshes.
sources.evidence: TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D-2.0 produce about 30% and 15% unstable assets even for training-set images of stable objects. On 65 Objaverse objects: TRELLIS 85.1% stable (mean tilt 14.14 deg) vs DSO-DRO 99.0% (1.88 deg); CD 0.0485 to 0.0440; F-score 73.12 to 76.17. About 10 s per object on an A100.
sources.code: Project page https://ruiningli.com/dso (code link not verified)
sources.adoption_effort: Not worth adopting. It only tests the canonical upright pose, not our observed resting poses, and the TRELLIS stack carries a Blackwell build risk.
sources.rule_risk: Pretrained generator (grey zone).

sources.title: SAM 3D: 3Dfy Anything in Images (SAM 3D Objects, Meta, 2025)
sources.method: Single image plus object mask goes to a coarse 64^3 occupancy (flow transformer), then a structured latent, then a mesh or Gaussian splats, plus layout (pose and scale). Trained on 2.7M synthetic meshes and real images annotated with humans in the loop. Optional pointmap conditioning.
sources.solves_for_us: A candidate filler for never-seen undersides and back faces (problem 1) where the TSDF has no evidence. The official V2D ego baseline already uses it. It does not solve slots (problem 2) or stability.
sources.evidence: SA-3DAO real images: F1@0.01 0.2344 vs TRELLIS 0.1475 and Hunyuan3D-2.1 0.1399; Chamfer 0.0400 vs 0.0902 and 0.1126; human preference at least 5:1. Pointmap conditioning barely changes shape (each variant preferred 48% of the time). The authors list as limitations that the 64^3 coarse shape loses thin structures and that the model is not trained for contact, stability, interpenetration or a shared ground plane. Their Art-3DO data 'suppresses bottomless meshes'.
sources.code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sam-3d-objects (SAM License, gated weights on HF, about 13 GB)
sources.adoption_effort: 0.5-1 day of environment setup on an RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell build risk); seconds per object. Then about 1 day for Sim(3) registration to our TSDF and fusion into unknown voxels only.
sources.rule_risk: Grey zone: pretrained generative prior. The FAQ allows pretrained models and the organisers' baseline uses SAM 3D. The SAM licence sits awkwardly with the Apache-2.0 release that winners must make.

sources.title: Hunyuan3D-Omni: Unified Framework for Controllable Generation of 3D Assets (Tencent, 2025)
sources.method: Hunyuan3D-2.1 (VecSet VAE decoded to an SDF, then iso-surface) with one control encoder for image plus point cloud, voxel, bounding box or skeleton. The point-cloud control is trained with random point drop and noise to mimic partial RGB-D or LiDAR scans.
sources.solves_for_us: The closest off-the-shelf tool that could complete our own fused partial cloud instead of a single image. SDF decoding gives closed meshes, and bounding-box control could impose the measured aspect ratio (board thickness). A candidate for undersides (problem 1) and sharp board edges (problem 2); how well it keeps slots is unknown.
sources.evidence: Qualitative only. Figures show better alignment with complete, depth-projected and scanned point clouds than image-only. The paper has no quantitative table for point control. 3.3B parameters, 10 GB VRAM.
sources.code: https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hunyuan3D-Omni. Tencent Hunyuan 3D Omni community licence, which excludes the EU, UK and South Korea. torch 2.5.1/cu124.
sources.adoption_effort: About 1 day of setup and a test on the ep18 sweeper and ep24 boards; under 1 GPU hour (about $1-2). The output is in a normalised canonical frame, so it needs scale and pose registration to our TSDF.
sources.rule_risk: Grey zone: pretrained generative prior. Territorial, non-Apache licence.

sources.title: ReconViaGen: Accurate Multi-view 3D Object Reconstruction via Generation (Chang et al., ICLR 2026)
sources.method: VGGT multi-view features condition both diffusion stages of TRELLIS. A rendering-aware velocity correction keeps the generation consistent with the input views, so only unseen parts are hallucinated.
sources.solves_for_us: Shows that 'reconstruct what is seen, generate only the rest' beats either part alone, which is the architecture we would want for undersides. But it expects a few clean object-centred views, not hand-occluded egocentric stereo.
sources.evidence: OmniObject3D (real scanned objects), 4 views: CD 0.059 and F-score 0.959 vs TRELLIS-M 0.072/0.932, VGGT 0.091/0.900, Hunyuan3D-2.0-mv 0.124/0.871 (normalised units). Dora-bench: CD 0.0895, F 0.953.
sources.code: https://github.com/GAP-LAB-CUHK-SZ/ReconViaGen (v0.2 training and inference; under 24 GB for 16 images). Depends on torch 2.4/cu121, spconv, kaolin and nvdiffrast (non-commercial licence).
sources.adoption_effort: 1-2 days of setup (Blackwell risk). Needs masked crops with the hands inpainted. Gains at our 4 mm scale are uncertain.
sources.rule_risk: Grey zone: pretrained generative prior; nvdiffrast licence.

sources.title: MagicHOI: 3D Priors for Hand-object Reconstruction from Short Monocular Clips (Wang et al., ICCV 2025)
sources.method: A neural object field fitted to the observed RGB, regularised in unseen regions by a Zero-1-to-3 novel-view diffusion prior built from an inpainted reference frame. Occlusion-aware weighting, plus hand alignment from visible contacts.
sources.solves_for_us: The same setting as ours (hand occlusion, limited viewpoints), and it measures how much a prior adds for unseen regions. Even with the prior the error is about 0.9 cm, coarser than stability needs: the sweeper's real base is a flat 11.7 cm^2 and the board edges are 8 mm.
sources.evidence: HO3D (14 sequences): object CD 0.87 cm, F5 69.7%, F10 92.2% vs HOLD 1.31 cm, 57.2%, 80.2%. Ablation: RGB only 1.37 cm, prior only 1.54 cm, RGB plus prior 0.91 cm.
sources.code: https://github.com/byran-wang/MagicHOI (v1.0.0, Nov 2025)
sources.adoption_effort: Days. An RGB-only neural pipeline that would throw away our stereo; not worth it in 13 days.
sources.rule_risk: Grey zone: pretrained diffusion prior.

sources.title: SceneComplete: Open-World 3D Scene Completion for Robot Manipulation (MIT/Brown, 2024-2025)
sources.method: Single RGB-D input: a VLM lists the objects, Grounded-SAM masks them, the masks are inpainted, InstantMesh generates each mesh, scale comes from the partial cloud (isotropic), FoundationPose registers it. Meshes are then made watertight (ManifoldPlus) and decomposed with CoACD for simulation and grasping.
sources.solves_for_us: A real-world measurement of how accurate generative completion plus registration is on household tabletop objects, using a pipeline like ours, plus the post-processing they needed to make the meshes simulation-ready.
sources.evidence: GraspNet-1B (real RealSense data, 88 objects): MIoU 0.478 (OctMAE 0.445, ZeroGrasp 0.440, partial cloud alone 0.166); CD 1.54 (x1e-4); 16% of grasps collide with the ground truth; about 73% real-robot pick success. The authors call isotropic scaling naive and report registration failures on uniformly textured objects.
sources.code: https://github.com/scenecomplete/SceneComplete
sources.adoption_effort: Not for adoption; evidence only.
sources.rule_risk: n/a

sources.title: Scalable Real2Sim: Physics-Aware Asset Generation via Robotic Pick-and-Place (Pfaff et al., 2025)
sources.method: A robot regrasps each object so a static RGB-D camera sees every side, bottom included. Meshes come from BundleSDF, Neuralangelo or Frosting; collision geometry from convex decomposition; inertia from joint torques via convex optimisation.
sources.solves_for_us: The simulation-ready recipe closest to ours (mesh, convex decomposition, physics), and the clearest evidence that millimetre-level meshes come from actually seeing the underside. For us: fuse every episode of an object, and keep near-table depth samples in frames where the object is lifted, so undersides seen during lifts vote as surface.
sources.evidence: BundleSDF vs YCB scanner meshes with regrasps: Chamfer 0.93, 1.68, 5.58 and 0.80 mm on 4 objects. BundleSDF meshes have non-manifold vertices and stray boundary faces (not watertight). 3D-printed mustard bottle: mass error 1.23%, CoM 6.33%, inertia 358.6%.
sources.code: https://github.com/nepfaff/scalable-real2sim
sources.adoption_effort: Nothing to port; design lessons only (hours).
sources.rule_risk: None.

sources.title: Thin structures in TSDF fusion: Directional TSDF (Splietker & Behnke, 2019) and RoutedFusion (Weder et al., CVPR 2020)
sources.method: The directional TSDF keeps surfaces facing opposite directions in separate channels and adapts marching cubes, so a thin plate seen from both sides keeps both faces. RoutedFusion (https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04388) learns non-linear fusion updates that remove thickening at edges and on thin objects.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 2. Our boards are 7.5-9 mm plates fused at 4 mm voxels with a 12 mm truncation (recon_mesh.py defaults): thinner than the band, which is the regime both papers flag for thickening, wrong surfaces and rounded edges. This explains why the board meshes have no stable standing pose.
sources.evidence: DTSDF abstract: TSDF plus marching cubes 'has severe issues with thin structures: not only does it lead to loss of accuracy, but it can generate completely wrong surfaces'. Voxel size and truncation set the minimum thickness, and thin objects 'blow up' when seen from opposite sides. RoutedFusion: the original fusion 'suffers from thickening artifacts' at edges and thin objects. No numbers at our scale found.
sources.code: DTSDF code not checked. Cheap version for us in recon_mesh.py: 2 mm voxels, 4-5 mm truncation and per-normal-direction channels; 0.5-1 day CPU.
sources.adoption_effort: 0.5-1 day CPU; the field grows 8x at 2 mm voxels unless restricted to a band around the object.
sources.rule_risk: None.

sources.title: Mind the Gap: Robotic Grasping under Incomplete Observation (Bohg et al., ICRA 2011)
sources.method: For unknown objects on a table, searches for the symmetry plane (perpendicular to the table) that best explains the visible points, subject to a visibility constraint: mirrored points may not land in observed free space. Then mirrors the cloud, meshes it, and plans grasps in simulation.
sources.solves_for_us: Cheap, CPU-only completion of back faces for mirror-symmetric objects (sweeper, dust pan, rack, pitcher, pot), using our own free-space evidence as the visibility test. No ground truth needed. It complements the table-contact fill, which makes the flat base.
sources.evidence: Abstract: predictions are 'valid approximations of the real object shape', shown on two robot platforms; 106 citations. No numbers retrieved.
sources.code: None; about 1 day to implement on our TSDF field.
sources.adoption_effort: About 1 day CPU.
sources.rule_risk: None (geometric prior).

sources.title: A volumetric fusion technique for surface reconstruction from silhouettes and range data (Yemez & Wetherilt, CVIU 2007)
sources.method: Builds a volumetric (octree) visual hull from silhouettes, then carves and refines it with range data. Silhouettes give a hole-free envelope where range data miss surfaces; range data recover the concavities that silhouettes cannot.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 2. An 8-9 mm notch in a board's edge is visible in the silhouette when the board is seen face-on, so mask carving removes it even if stereo depth smears across the gap. Masks also give a cleaner envelope where the table and hand bands drop depth samples. Our perception runs SAM2 only at frame 0, so this needs per-frame masks (SAM2 video propagation, or masks seeded from the rendered mesh).
sources.evidence: Qualitative, abstract level; the full text was not retrievable here.
sources.code: None. About 1 day CPU for carving, plus SAM2 video masks on GPU (minutes per episode).
sources.adoption_effort: 1-1.5 days.
sources.rule_risk: None (SAM2 is already used).

ideas: STAGE 0, a physics check before training that needs no ground truth (hypothesis: it catches every geometry failure we found by hand). For every object, episode and static segment (no hand within about 3 cm and low velocity in our track), run 1 s of CPU MuJoCo on the same CoACD pieces. Measure drift (fail above 3 mm or 3 deg), the gap to the table plane (fail above 2 mm or below -2 mm), and pairwise penetration with the other object over all frames (fail above 1 cm^3). Also check that the CoACD pieces keep at least 50% of the mesh's support area at each resting pose. Run it on public and eval episodes. Falsified if, on ep12/18/24/27 with library_v2 meshes, it misses one of the known failures (ep18 sweeper falls; ep24 boards cannot stand; ep12 cup tips 23 deg; 1-4 cm floats), or if it flags more than 20% of objects in episodes that already score well (ep27, 0.94). Cost: about 1 day CPU.

H1, cause of rounded undersides and floats (from reading recon_mesh.py, unmeasured). Depth samples within table_band = 15 mm of the frame-0 table plane never vote as surface, and auto closing picks 'near' (3 voxels, 12 mm) for thin objects. So the bottom 1-1.5 cm of every resting object stays unknown and comes out rounded or short. Test on CPU: for each object, take the gap between the mesh's lowest point at its static poses and the table plane. Then rebuild with table_band 0.006 for static frames, and keep near-table samples whenever the object is more than 3 cm above the table. Falsified if the gap and the contact area at rest do not change. In that case the floats are a pose or table-plane error, not geometry.

STAGE 2, fill the gap down to the table, automatically (replaces flatten_base's single up vector). In every static frame of every episode, unknown voxels between the table plane and the observed object, inside the object's footprint (vertical projection of the observed lower surface, or the visual hull), become inside. Each distinct resting orientation then gets its own flat contact face at exactly the table plane. Never change observed-free or observed-surface voxels. Falsify on GPU (about $3-4 per episode): ep18 must reach at least 0.70 registered AUC without the manual patch (manual was 0.715), and ep12/ep27 must not drop by more than 0.02. Diagnostic only, on public episodes: footprint area at the scan's mocap rest pose within 30% of the scan's (sweeper scan 11.7 cm^2).

STAGE 2b, completion driven by the stability check (PhyRecon/PhysComp, discrete). If an object still fails the drop test at a static pose after the table fill, grow only unknown voxels inside the footprint's convex hull, at the table plane, until the projected CoM falls inside the support polygon with at least 5 mm margin. If unknown voxels cannot fix it, flag it instead of hacking the inertia. Falsified if it fixes fewer than 3 of the flagged public cases, or if it changes CD-O vs scan (diagnostic) by more than 1 mm for objects that were already stable.

STAGE 3a, boards as extruded slabs (thin objects detected automatically: two dominant parallel planes and PCA thickness under 15 mm). Fit the two planes (thickness should come out at 7.5-9 mm). Take the 2D outline from points and face-on masks projected into the plane (alpha shape or polygon, so the notch is kept). Extrude to get sharp edges and flat edge faces. Falsify on CPU: the standing poses at ep24 f150/f250 must pass the drop test, and the notch width and depth must be within 2 mm of the scan (diagnostic). Then a GPU A/B with 6 evaluations: registered AUC must exceed 0.36 (now 0.31 +/- 0.01) or the policy must stand the boards, otherwise reject. Generalises to eval ep25.

H2, what fills the notch. Register the public wooden_piece scan to our mesh (diagnostic only) and label the voxels inside the scan's notch as observed-free, observed-inside, or unknown-then-closed. If more than 50% are unknown-then-closed, the cause is the closing step: forbid 'near' closing next to free-space evidence and use 2 mm voxels with 4-5 mm truncation (directional TSDF). If more than 50% are observed-inside, stereo depth is smearing across the notch and needs mask carving: SAM2 video masks with silhouette carving (Yemez & Wetherilt). The hypothesis that closing is the cause is falsified by the second outcome.

STAGE 2c, the boards must not overlap anywhere, at any frame. Carve each object with the other's volume at every frame, weighted by pose confidence, not only at the final pose. Assign shared volume by free-space and mask evidence from frames before assembly. Without such evidence, fall back to the insertion direction: the board that moves down in the last approach keeps the upper part, split at the column's mid-height. Each board must stay one connected piece, and the end state must overlap by under 1 cm^3 (now 13.5 cm^3). Falsified if the slot lands on the wrong board or at the wrong height vs the public scans (diagnostic), or if a board splits into two pieces. Rule note: this must stay an algorithm applied the same way to eval ep25. Editing eval meshes by hand, guided by the public scans, risks the Kaggle no-hand-labelling rule.

STAGE 3b, shape families picked by fit. Surface-of-revolution fit for the cup, pot, lid and pitcher bodies (axis from normals or RANSAC, profile from observed points, base from the table fill). Mirror symmetry under a visibility check (Bohg 2011) for the sweeper, dust pan and rack. Keep the family only if it fits observed depth and masks at least as well as the TSDF and passes the stage-0 check; otherwise keep the TSDF. Falsify on public objects with CD-O (Sim(3) Chamfer vs scan, diagnostic) and footprint error at rest: reject a family that does not improve CD by at least 1 mm or that fails stability.

STAGE 4, low priority, generative prior only as a candidate. Run Hunyuan3D-Omni with point-cloud control on our fused partial cloud (or SAM 3D on the best frame) for the ep18 sweeper and the ep24 boards. Fuse only into unknown voxels, after Sim(3) alignment, and accept only if it passes stage 0 with Chamfer to observed points under 3 mm. The literature predicts failure: 15-30% of TRELLIS/Hunyuan outputs are unstable, raw baselines can stand only 7-33% of the time, SAM 3D's 64^3 grid loses an 8 mm notch, and real-object completion IoU is about 0.48. Worth keeping only if it passes on both objects with no manual edits. Budget about 1 day and $5. Also the most plausible route for the unscanned wooden_spoon if it is thin or under-observed (not tested here).

Validation protocol for all stages. Develop and score only on public episodes; use scans and mocap only for diagnostics after inference. Report the per-voxel evidence class, the stage-0 pass rates and the registered AUC together. Then run the same code unchanged on eval episodes 19/30 (sweeper), 25 (boards) and 14/15/16/28/30 (rack), and on 1 (lid on pot), using only the stage-0 report to decide which objects need attention. No tuning on eval results.
gaps: No quantitative evaluation of Hunyuan3D-Omni's point-cloud control exists in the paper (figures only). Its benefit on partial, noisy, hand-occluded clouds is unmeasured.
No paper found that reconstructs assembly joints (cross-halving slots, interlocking parts) from video. The insertion-direction and swept-volume assignment is our own hypothesis.

No published numbers on how FoundationStereo behaves across 8-9 mm gaps at our 40-60 cm working distance. Whether the notch is filled by stereo smearing or by our closing step is unmeasured (test H2).

Full-text numbers not retrieved for Bohg 2011 or Yemez & Wetherilt 2007; arXiv HTML tables for CAD-Recode's CC3D results were incomplete. CAD-Recode (https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14042) reports only relative gains on real scans: 89% lower median CD and 30% higher IoU vs CAD-SIGNet. It is a possible learned extrude prior for the boards, but a hand-coded slab fit looks simpler and safer.

GitHub API and github.com pages were blocked (403) from this session; licences were checked only through raw READMEs and licence files (TRELLIS.2 MIT; SAM License; Tencent community licence excluding EU, UK and South Korea). Licences for PhyRecon, PhysComp, MagicHOI, SceneComplete and ReconViaGen were not verified. DSO's code link was not found.
