Not verified whether the TRELLIS-family dependencies (torch 2.4/cu121, spconv, kaolin, flash-attn, nvdiffrast) build on RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell, sm_120). This is a real risk for any generative-prior experiment.
Real mass distribution is unknown (for example a heavier sweeper head). Uniform density in our simulation assets could itself make objects tip; estimating it from video was not resolved.
Not confirmed that the official evaluator uses exactly our CoACD pieces and contact settings, so the stage-0 check may differ slightly from the evaluator's physics.

No organiser statement on whether shape-family priors (revolution, slab) or generative completions count as 'own reconstructed meshes'. FAQ: pretrained models allowed and CD-O must use own meshes. The organisers' baseline uses SAM 3D. Manual per-object edits for eval objects carry Kaggle no-hand-labelling risk.
Not checked: in which public or eval episodes each object is lifted far enough for its underside to be seen. That decides how much stage 2 matters compared with simply fusing more episodes.

verified.angle:
Fact-check of the "unseen-geometry-completion" findings. I read the arXiv HTML full text with curl, because WebFetch could not resolve arxiv.org. Licences and READMEs came from raw.githubusercontent.com, because the GitHub API is blocked in this session. I checked the repo claim against pipeline/recon_mesh.py and docs/professor-package/notes/15-eval-video-survey.md. No repo files were modified.

Verdict: every quoted number I checked is real and correctly transcribed (PhyRecon, PhysComp, DSO, SAM 3D, MagicHOI, Hunyuan3D-Omni licence). Some framing needs correcting:
1. PhyRecon scores Chamfer only on visible areas. Its own paper reports bulges in barely observed regions when the physics loss acts there, and our undersides are exactly such regions. The physics loss alone gives most of the stability gain (25.3 to 69.0%).
2. The "64^3 is too coarse for an 8 mm notch" argument starts from a wrong width. Our own note 15 measured the halving slot at about 19 mm wide; 7.5 to 9.1 mm is the board thickness.
3. The repo finding is right in mechanism but overstated as "every resting object". Combining the code with the measured thicknesses gives a stronger version: a board lying flat (7.5 to 9.1 mm thick) sits entirely inside the 15 mm table band, so it gets no surface votes in any frame where it lies flat. Separately, both closing modes fill an unobserved 19 mm pocket: near-closing grows 12 mm from each wall, which covers it, and fill-closing turns any enclosed unknown pocket into solid.
4. PhysComp's benchmark (100 Objaverse plants, animals and characters, elastic tet-FEM) and DSO's benchmark (65 objects, upright drop, lenient 20 deg threshold) do not transfer numerically to our rigid household objects at their observed resting poses.

checked.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction (Ni et al., NeurIPS 2024)
checked.verdict: confirmed (numbers), partly (interpretation)
checked.claim_checked: Object stability ratio on ScanNet++ is RICO 26.43%, ObjectSDF++ 25.28%, PhyRecon 78.16%. The drop test is in Isaac Gym, stable if under 5 deg and 5 cm after 200 steps at 60 Hz. Object Chamfer goes from 4.08 to 3.28 cm. The abstract claims at least 40% improvement. Only object-ground support is modelled.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Table 1 matches exactly. ScanNet++ object CD/F/NC/SR: RICO 4.29/85.91/85.45/26.43, ObjectSDF++ 4.08/86.32/85.32/25.28, Ours 3.28/87.21/86.16/78.16. ScanNet SR: 29.68, 26.56, 70.31. Replica SR: 32.89, 30.26, 77.63. The test: T=200 steps at dt=0.016 s (60 Hz); stable if within 5 deg rotation and 5 cm translation. Objects are dropped at their reconstructed in-scene pose with the reconstructed background ('relative positions ... preserved'), not in a canonical upright pose. Appx. D.1: 'focused solely on object-ground support'. Caveats the colleague left out: (1) Appx. D.2: 'evaluate reconstruction only on the visible areas', so the Chamfer gain says nothing about unseen undersides. (2) Ablation Tab. 2 on ScanNet++: the physical loss alone already lifts SR from 25.28 to 68.96% (CD 4.13 to 3.97), but the paper says that alone 'will overshadow the rendering losses, leading to degenerated object shapes'. The full model reaches 78.16% only with uncertainty-guided sampling, which recovers thin parts such as chair legs. (3) Failure cases (Fig. 8): 'in regions scarcely observed ... the physical loss may lead to degenerated object shapes, e.g., bulges'. (4) 22% of objects are still unstable. Data is 7 ScanNet++ scenes, input is multi-view RGB plus monocular depth/normal priors (not metric stereo), and training takes 12.56 h per scene on an A100 (Tab. A4) vs 8.70 h for RICO. Its simulator is a DiffTaichi particle simulator with max 100 steps during training.
checked.code_status: github.com/PhyRecon/PhyRecon exists; LICENSE.txt is Apache-2.0. README: python 3.9, torch 2.0.1/cu118 (a Blackwell risk), Isaac Gym needed only for the stability-ratio eval script. Not run.
checked.applicability: Adopt the protocol, not the method: a per-static-segment drop test at the perceived pose, run in our own MuJoCo/Newton scene with the same CoACD hulls the policy uses, as a ground-truth-free gate for public and eval episodes. Their 5 deg / 5 cm threshold is too lenient for our ADD scoring; we should pick something like 3 deg / 1 cm and calibrate it on public episodes. The bulge failure is the warning for us: a stability objective on unknown voxels must be confined to a low-dimensional family (support-plane extrusion, flat base), not free-form voxel edits, or it will invent wrong geometry that is merely stable. Porting the neural pipeline is not justified.

checked.title: Physically Compatible 3D Object Modeling from a Single Image (PhysComp; Guo et al., NeurIPS 2024)
checked.verdict: confirmed (numbers), partly (relevance)
checked.claim_checked: Standability before vs after: Wonder3D 6.9 to 72.4, LGM 20.3 to 85.5, MeshLRM 29.6 to 74.5, TripoSR 24.2 to 80.6, TetSphere 32.8 to 92.2. Static equilibrium is a hard constraint, the stability loss pulls the CoM projection to a target, and the image loss stays the same or improves.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Table 1 matches exactly. Img. Loss means go down slightly for every method (e.g. Wonder3D 0.073 to 0.069, TetSphere 0.061 to 0.057). The stability loss is the distance between the xy-projection of the CoM of the static shape and a target position. The hard constraint is elastic static equilibrium (FEM on a tet mesh, the rest shape is the variable, with predefined Young's modulus and external forces); stability itself is only an objective term. The evaluation set is 100 Objaverse shapes picked from the plants, animals and characters categories, mostly inside the baselines' own training data. 'Standable' means staying upright without toppling, a canonical-pose test, not a test at an observed resting pose. Listed limitations: needs predefined material and forces, and a tetrahedralised input. DSO (Sec. 4) independently measured PhysComp at 15 min per object on a 24-core CPU vs the 80 s its authors report. On DSO's 11-object unstable subset it produced output in only 46.2% of runs (stable 80.3%) and worsened geometry (CD 0.0529 to 0.0698, F 72.48 to 53.73).
checked.code_status: github.com/gmh14/PhysComp README reachable. No LICENSE, LICENSE.md or LICENSE.txt at the repo root (404), so the licence is unclear. Built on libpgo plus tetgen, CPU (tbb/mkl).
checked.applicability: Only the criterion transfers, and it is the same one we already measured on ep18: the CoM projection must lie inside the support polygon. That check takes a few lines on our mesh plus the table plane and needs no FEM. Do not port: the method is elastic, slow and numerically fragile, and it was tested on non-rigid-looking categories. It also changes the whole shape, which would move observed surfaces we reconstructed ourselves.

checked.title: DSO: Aligning 3D Generators with Simulation Feedback for Physical Soundness (Li, Zheng, Rupprecht, Vedaldi, ICCV 2025)
checked.verdict: confirmed, with an internal inconsistency in the source
checked.claim_checked: TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D-2.0 make about 30% and 15% unstable assets even for training-set images of stable objects. MuJoCo upright drop, uniform density, 20 deg threshold. On 65 objects: TRELLIS 85.1% stable / 14.14 deg vs DSO-DRO 99.0% / 1.88 deg, CD 0.0485 to 0.0440, F 73.12 to 76.17. About 10 s per object on an A100. No 3D ground truth.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Sec. 3: 'Even when taking images of stable objects in their training set as input, TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D-2.0 generate about 30% and 15% unstable assets respectively.' The Introduction instead says 'The failure rate is 15% even for objects seen during training', and the Table 1 TRELLIS row (85.1% stable) also implies about 15%. So 30% is the high end, and quoting '~15-30%' is safer. The test runs MuJoCo for 10 s from an upright pose on flat ground, rigid with uniform density, stable if final tilt is under 20 deg. Eval: 65 objects x 12 images (780). Training data comes only from the 'Human-Shape', 'Animals' and 'Daily-Used' GObjaverse categories (slender, two-legged shapes). CD and F-score are computed after unit-cube normalisation plus ICP, with F at threshold 0.05. All Table 1 numbers match. Also: DPO 95.1% / 5.42 deg; on the 11-object unstable subset TRELLIS 54.5% / 39.18 deg vs DRO 95.5% / 5.58 deg; 10 s per model on an A100. The self-generated data uses no 3D ground truth (it renders Objaverse, excluding objects whose ground truth is unstable).
checked.code_status: github.com/RuiningLi/dso exists. Checkpoints are on HF (rayli/DSO-finetuned-TRELLIS, DRO and DPO LoRA) and the eval set is on HF (rayli/image-to-3D-eval-stability-under-gravity). No LICENSE file at the repo root, so the licence is unclear. Needs torch 2.4.0/cu124 plus the full TRELLIS stack (spconv, kaolin, nvdiffrast, flash-attn, diffoctreerast), a Blackwell build risk.
checked.applicability: Evidence only. Generic generators fail stability at a measurable rate even under a lenient 20 deg upright test, so any generated completion must pass our own drop gate at the observed resting poses. Our objects (cups, pot, pitcher, rack) are mostly bulky and low, so these failure rates should not be read as predictions for them. If the owner accepts a generative prior at all, the DSO LoRA on TRELLIS is a ready-made, more stable drop-in than plain TRELLIS. It still knows nothing about our observed poses, contact or the slot, and its licence is unclear.

checked.title: SAM 3D: 3Dfy Anything in Images (SAM 3D Objects, Meta, arXiv 2511.16624)
checked.verdict: confirmed (numbers), partly (the notch argument is wrong in its premise)
checked.claim_checked: 64^3 coarse shape. SA-3DAO F1@0.01 0.2344 vs TRELLIS 0.1475 and HY3D-2.1 0.1399; Chamfer 0.0400 vs 0.0902 and 0.1126; at least 5:1 human preference. Pointmap conditioning barely changes shape (48% each). Limitations: thin structures, no contact, stability, interpenetration or ground plane. Art-3DO suppresses bottomless meshes. Too coarse for an 8 mm notch. SAM License.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Table 2 matches exactly (SAM 3D F1 0.2344, vIoU 0.2311, Chamfer 0.0400, EMD 0.1211). The metrics normalise ground truth and prediction separately into [-1,1] and then ICP-align them, so they are scale- and pose-free shape scores, not metric accuracy of hidden faces. Sec. 2: O in R^{64^3} coarse shape; the Texture & Refinement stage adds detail within those voxels. Appx. E.5: pointmap vs no-pointmap versions are 'each selected 48% of the time' on LVIS. Sec. 3: Art-3DO 'helps suppress common failures, e.g. floaters, bottomless meshes, and missing symmetry'. Appx. F: the 64^3 grid can lose 'thin structures'. The model 'isn't trained to reason about physical interactions, such as contact, physical stability, interpenetration, or co-alignment (e.g. on the same ground plane)'. That sentence is about multi-object layout, but it applies to our use. Correction to the notch argument: our own measurement (note 15, public scan, diagnostic only) puts the halving slot at about 19 mm wide, with boards 139x227 mm and 7.5/9.1 mm thick. At 64 cells over 227 mm a cell is about 3.5 mm, so the slot spans about 5 cells and is representable. The marginal dimension is the plate thickness (about 2-2.6 cells), not the slot. Our own TSDF grid (4 mm voxels, 12 mm truncation) is no finer than SAM 3D's coarse grid for these boards.
checked.code_status: github.com/facebookresearch/sam-3d-objects; the LICENSE is the custom 'SAM License' (Last Updated Nov 19, 2025), confirmed. I did not verify the gated HF weights or the ~13 GB size.
checked.applicability: At most a candidate for unknown voxels, accepted only after the drop and no-overlap gates; it is not the fix. For the boards the binding problem is our own thickness and closing, not resolution, and a single egocentric image will not reliably produce a cross-halving slot. A generated mesh needs Sim(3) registration to our partial TSDF, and anything it puts into observed-free space must be rejected. Licence and rule risk stand: grey-zone pretrained prior, and a SAM-licensed component sits awkwardly with an Apache-2.0 release.

checked.title: MagicHOI: 3D Priors for Hand-object Reconstruction from Short Monocular Clips (Wang et al., ICCV 2025)
checked.verdict: confirmed
checked.claim_checked: HO3D object CD 0.87 cm, F5 69.7%, F10 92.2% vs HOLD 1.31 / 57.2 / 80.2. Ablation: RGB only 1.37, prior only 1.54, RGB plus prior 0.91 cm.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Table 1: Ours 0.87 / 69.72 / 92.15, HOLD 1.31 / 57.20 / 80.23 (EasyHOI 1.86, DiffHOI 2.30). The ablation rows 1.37, 1.54 and 0.91 are present. The data is HO3D-v3 RGB video with YCB objects.
checked.code_status: github.com/byran-wang/MagicHOI; the LICENSE at the root is Apache-2.0. It depends on Zero-1-to-3 weights, whose licence I did not check.
checked.applicability: Confirms that even the best hand-occlusion-aware prior method is about 0.9 cm off on average. That is coarser than what stability needs (a flat base or a square board edge), so a prior cannot replace explicit support-plane constraints. Not worth adopting: it is RGB-only and would discard our stereo depth.

checked.title: Hunyuan3D-Omni (Tencent, arXiv 2509.21245): licence and requirements only
checked.verdict: confirmed (licence, VRAM, torch); paper numbers not checked
checked.claim_checked: Tencent Hunyuan 3D Omni community licence excludes the EU, UK and South Korea; 10 GB VRAM; torch 2.5.1/cu124.
checked.what_source_actually_says: License.txt: 'Territory shall mean the worldwide territory, excluding the territory of the European Union, United Kingdom and South Korea.' The HF model card sets license: other, tencent-hunyuan-community, extra_gated_eu_disallowed: true. README: 'It takes 10 GB VRAM for generation'; pip install torch==2.5.1 ... cu124.

checked.title: Repo claim: pipeline/recon_mesh.py table band, truncation and closing (and note 15 board measurements)
checked.verdict: partly (mechanism confirmed, 'every resting object' overstated, a stronger board-specific consequence missed)
checked.claim_checked: Depth samples within 15 mm of the table never vote as surface. 'near' closing uses 3 voxels of 4 mm. So the bottom 1-1.5 cm of every resting object is unknown, which causes rounded undersides and part of the 1-4 cm floats. Boards 7.5-9 mm are thinner than the 12 mm truncation.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Defaults are --table_band 0.015, --trunc 0.012, --voxel 0.004, --near_vox 3, --below_carve 0.004, --close auto (near if the unknown share exceeds 0.5, else fill). Lines 156-157 and 184-187 flag samples whose observed point lies at most 15 mm above the per-frame refitted plane, or anywhere below it. Those samples only carve (sdf > trunc) and never update surface or inside voxels. Lines 252-253: fill makes every enclosed unknown voxel solid, and near dilates observed-inside by 3 voxels (12 mm) and then fills holes. Corrections: (a) the band applies per frame, so the lower 15 mm is unknown only for faces never seen while the object is lifted; 'every resting object' is too strong. (b) Missed and more important: per note 15 the boards are 7.5 mm and 9.1 mm thick, so a board lying flat sits entirely inside the 15 mm band, and while it lies flat the board contributes no surface or inside votes at all. Only lifted or tilted frames build its mesh. (c) The slot is about 19 mm wide (note 15). If its interior is never observed as free, near-closing (12 mm from each wall, 24 mm > 19 mm) or fill-closing (an enclosed unknown pocket) will solidify it. So the closing, not only TSDF averaging, can explain the filled notch. (d) The band can explain floats of at most about 1.5 cm; the 2-4 cm board floats need another cause (pose height or plane error).
checked.code_status: Read only; nothing run or changed.
checked.applicability: Highest-value, cheapest checks, each a few minutes of CPU on existing caches. (1) Count surface and inside votes per frame for board voxels in ep24, split by whether the board is resting or lifted. (2) In the saved ep24 grid, label the slot region as unknown, observed-inside or observed-free. If unknown, the fix belongs in the closing step; if observed-inside, it belongs in the truncation or averaging. (3) For ep18 sweeper base voxels, check whether the rounded underside comes from unknown voxels shaped by fill or near closing.

corrected_ideas: Keep the colleague's core architecture (observed-surface / observed-free / unknown voxels, with unknowns resolved only by constraints from our own tracks), but restate the evidence. PhyRecon shows a 'resting means stable' loss alone takes ScanNet++ stability from 25.3 to 69.0% (78.2% with uncertainty sampling). It also shows the same loss creates bulges where observations are scarce, which is our underside case. So the stability constraint must act through a low-dimensional parameter, never through free voxel edits. Hypothesis: constrained completion keeps observed-surface error unchanged and makes every public static segment pass the drop gate. Falsified if any public object still tips at a perceived resting pose, or if the completed region moves observed surfaces by more than 1 voxel.

Replace 'flatten the underside along one episode's up vector' with a support-plane extrusion computed from all resting segments of all episodes of that object. For each static segment, transform the table plane into the object frame. Mark voxels below that plane as free (the below_carve rule already does this per frame). Fill unknown voxels between the lowest observed cross-section and the plane by extruding that cross-section straight down, so the contact patch is the object's own cross-section, not a rounded cap. If different segments give different 'down' directions (an object resting on different faces), each one carves its own plane, and their intersection gives the shape. Test on ep18: footprint area against the 11.7 cm^2 measured from the public scan (diagnostic only), and the drop test at every sweeper static segment.

Fix the table band before any completion work, because it disables the boards. A 15 mm band swallows a 7.5-9.1 mm board lying flat. Make it object-aware: keep a sample as surface evidence when it lies inside the object's tracked footprint and more than about 3 mm above the plane, or shrink the band to about 4 mm and rely on the per-frame plane refit (lines 146-155). Falsify by counting board surface votes in resting frames before and after, and by comparing reconstructed board thickness and edge squareness to the public-scan values (7.5 / 9.1 mm) on ep24 only.

For the slot, generalise 'carve from the final overlap' to 'every voxel that the other tracked object's observed-surface or inside region occupies at any frame is free', applied before closing. Also forbid near or fill closing from filling any unknown pocket that intersects the other object's swept volume. Note 15 puts the slot at about 19 mm, so a 3-voxel near-closing from both walls (24 mm) fills it unless the slot is explicitly carved. First test whether the slot voxels are unknown or observed-inside in the ep24 grid; that decides whether to fix the closing or the truncation. Only if co-location carving is insufficient, fit a parametric cross-halving slot (width = mating board thickness plus clearance, depth = overlap depth) and accept it only if the final assembled pose has no overlap above, say, 1 cm^3 in our CoACD hulls.

Run the ground-truth-free gate on the simulation geometry the policy actually uses (CoACD hulls), not on the raw mesh. Note 15 measured hulls up to about 6 mm thicker than the scan, which changes footprints and slot clearance. Gate per object and per episode, on eval episodes too: (a) drop at every perceived static pose, stable if under about 3 deg and under 1 cm after about 3 s (PhyRecon used 5 deg / 5 cm, too loose for our ADD scoring; calibrate the threshold on public episodes); (b) zero hull-hull and hull-table penetration at perceived resting and assembled poses; (c) a CoM-in-support-polygon check (the PhysComp criterion, a closed-form check, no FEM).

Treat floats separately from mesh completion. The band explains at most about 1.5 cm of missing base. The 2-4 cm board floats need a pose or plane cause. Measure each episode's float from our own perceived poses (lowest hull vertex minus table plane at static frames). If it exceeds the missing-base estimate, snap the static segments to contact with the table, which already exists as nearest stable pose snapping. Do not stretch the mesh to close a pose error.

Downgrade generative priors to optional candidates, and state the correct reason. 64^3 is not too coarse for the 19 mm slot (about 5 cells on a 227 mm board), but it is marginal for the 7.5-9 mm plate thickness. More importantly, none of these models is trained for contact or stability. DSO measured about 15-30% unstable outputs even for stable training-set images under a lenient 20 deg upright test. If used at all, a generated mesh may only fill unknown voxels, must agree with observed free space, and must pass the same gate. DSO-finetuned TRELLIS weights exist on HF, but no licence file was found. SAM 3D carries the SAM License and Hunyuan3D-Omni a territory-excluded licence, which is a problem for an Apache-2.0 release. Flag any of them to the owner as a grey-zone prior before use.

Do not port PhyRecon (12.6 h per scene on an A100, torch 2.0.1/cu118, Isaac Gym) or PhysComp (elastic FEM, unclear licence, 15 min per object on CPU, and only 46% of runs produced output on DSO's hard subset). Their published numbers come from ScanNet++ furniture or Objaverse characters, not rigid tabletop objects, so do not cite them as expected gains for us.

Rule check before multi-episode fusion: fusing all eval episodes of the same object (names come from the kit) is our own reconstruction and should be fine. Using meshes built from public-episode videos to complete eval-episode objects is a separate question to put to the owner and the FAQ. Public scans stay diagnostic-only (as in note 15), and no completion parameter may be tuned on eval scores.

found.angle:
hoi-physical-plausibility. I looked at how recent work makes a hand-object trajectory reconstructed from video physically feasible in simulation, including rest phases and contact between objects. Main finding: physics-in-the-loop refinement of the trajectory (sampling MPC: SPIDER, Do as I Do; RL tracking: DexMachina, ManipTrans, InterMimic, RePHO) absorbs hand-side noise well (penetration, floating or missed contacts, unstable grasps). None of these methods repairs object geometry that makes the target state impossible.
- Do as I Do, the closest system to ours, retargets to the Sharpa hand in MuJoCo Warp. Its released code adds stabilising pedestals and welded supports under resting objects that would otherwise fall. Our evaluator has no such supports.
- PhyRecon reports that a physics loss applied where the surface was never observed produces bulges and degenerate shapes.
- RePHO's physics refinement lowers floating and penetration but raises object Chamfer error (BEHAVE 8.73 to 11.06). This matches our measured ep12 loss of -0.05 from rest settling.
So our per-object patches are instances of the right constraints but are not robust as written. The robust version, assembled from this literature, has five stages:
(A) Label interaction phases per frame from our own tracks only (hand-object, object-table and object-object contact; held vs rest from object acceleration plus hand proximity, with neutral bands as in InterMimic and PhysHOI).
(B) Make each mesh valid in simulation from all its rest and co-location evidence: a support patch plus static equilibrium at every perceived rest pose, no overlap at co-located frames. Edit only never-observed regions, and only with constrained shape families (planar cut, box primitives, boolean subtraction).
(C) Refine rest poses PhysPose-style, per rest segment: anisotropic stereo prior, collision cost on convex pieces, gravity cost switched off when another object supports it. Check each result with a simulated settle.
(D) Generate physics-grounded hand references by sampling MPC (Do as I Do or SPIDER), with the transition reward on and pedestals off.
(E) Train RL tracking with contact-graph rewards that include table and object-object edges, and start-state selection.
Validate every stage in the collision representation the evaluator actually uses (CoACD hulls), and apply a correction only where an assist-off drop test fails. Object-object assembly geometry (ep24 slots) is not covered by any published HOI method I found.

sources.title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
sources.method: Reconstructs hand-object interaction from monocular RGB, then retargets it to a dexterous hand by MPPI-style annealed sampling MPC in MuJoCo Warp, built on SPIDER. Additions: (a) warmup steps that weld the object in place while the hand finds a feasible pre-pose, then release it; (b) random force perturbations in rollouts; (c) a constant transition penalty when the reference says 'rest' but the object has no floor contact, or says 'in hand' but has no hand contact. The released code also adds a penetration penalty (scale 3000, margin 5 mm). It injects pedestals plus support geoms welded to the object under objects that are not in hand at the trajectory endpoints (resolve_pedestal.py).
sources.solves_for_us: Problems (3) and (1), the rest phases: the transition reward directly penalises an object that leaves its support during reference rest frames. ep24 and ep18 hard segments: the physics search yields a feasible hand+object reference and nominal controls. The default robot_type is 'sharpa' and the system was deployed on Sharpa Wave hands, so it is our embodiment. The pedestal code is evidence that even this pipeline must invent support when reconstructed objects cannot rest. For us pedestals must be disabled and the meshes fixed instead.
sources.evidence: Table 3, success on reconstructed in-the-wild references: annealed sampling 0.25, +warmup 0.66, +perturbation 0.67, +transition reward 0.71 (position error 0.08 -> 0.05 m). OakInk2: 0.72 -> 0.77 -> 0.79 -> 0.81. The authors say warmup is the main differentiator. Success uses loose thresholds (SPIDER/ManipTrans style), not comparable to ADD-AUC. The published numbers include the pedestal/support mechanism; results without it are unknown.
sources.code: https://github.com/malik-group/do-as-i-do (MIT; built on SPIDER, which is CC BY-NC 4.0). Retargeting stages: process_dataset (clean + gravity-align) -> CoACD -> MJCF -> mink IK -> pedestal -> optimize_physics (MuJoCo Warp). Defaults: 1024 samples, 32 iterations, horizon 3.0 s, sim_dt 5 ms.
sources.adoption_effort: About 1-2 days. Write an adapter from our MANO tracks, own meshes and object poses to their reconstruction output format, and map their Sharpa joint order and limits to FlashCHORD's. Needs a GPU (MuJoCo Warp); RTX PRO 6000 is fine. Runtime per episode not measured; estimate under 1 GPU-hour (about $1.4). Risks: contact parameters differ between their MJCF scene and Newton/FlashCHORD; their scene adds a UR3 wrist-cylinder collider; pedestals must be switched off (use_pedestal=False).
sources.rule_risk: Retargeting uses only our meshes and tracks: fine. Their reconstruction stage uses SAM 3D (generative image-to-3D): pretrained-generative grey zone that also conflicts with the own-mesh rule; do not use it. Non-commercial licence inherited from SPIDER.

sources.title: SPIDER: Scalable Physics-Informed Dexterous Retargeting
sources.method: Treats retargeting as trajectory optimisation, solved by MPPI-style sampling in a parallel simulator with covariance annealed across iterations and along the horizon. Virtual contact guidance: a constraint holds the relative position of intended hand-object contact pairs early on and is relaxed as optimisation proceeds. A contact filter disables guidance for contacts that are short or drift. A min-max robustification over domain-randomised parameters follows. Output is a feasible trajectory plus nominal controls; RL can then learn only a residual (u = u_SPIDER + pi).
sources.solves_for_us: Produces dynamically feasible references for ep24 (lift and stand-up) and ep18 (tool use) before RL. Residual RL on its nominal controls is a way past the ep24 learning ceiling (~0.31). The contact filter is a principled version of our 'snap only reliable fingertip contacts'.
sources.evidence: Annealed sampling + virtual contact guidance beats annealed-only by about 18% success (Oakink 8 trajectories + GigaHands 5, 5 seeds); 2.5 Hz vs 3.0 Hz. Full-dataset success (Inspire hand): Oakink 0.479 (1022 trajectories), GigaHands 0.879 (756). Against RL: Oakink 47.9% vs ManipTrans 39.5% at 2.5 vs 0.1 frames/s; ARCTIC 42.0% vs DexMachina 67.1% at 1.5 vs 0.05 frames/s, so RL is still better on complex long-horizon clips. Settings: H = 1.2 s, N = 1024, 16 iterations, 100 Hz physics / 50 Hz control in MuJoCo Warp, RTX 4090. Success thresholds are loose (rotation < 0.5 rad, average position < 10 cm).
sources.code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/spider (CC BY-NC 4.0); supports MuJoCo Warp, Genesis and IsaacGym; 7,876 retargeted trajectories released 2026-09-22.
sources.adoption_effort: Same as Do as I Do, which already wraps SPIDER for Sharpa; take Do as I Do first. GPU needed. Residual RL needs FlashCHORD to accept a feed-forward action term (estimate: about 1 day).
sources.rule_risk: None for retargeting with our own references. Non-commercial licence: check that challenge use is acceptable.

sources.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints
sources.method: Post-hoc optimisation of all object poses jointly. Costs: (i) a Mahalanobis pose cost to the initial estimate, with covariance larger along the camera ray; (ii) a collision cost: hinge on negative signed distance between every pair of convex-decomposition pieces of objects and the static scene (differentiable GJK, DiffCol); (iii) a gravity cost: positive distance of each piece to the nearest static support below. The gravity cost is disabled (delta term) for an object in contact with another object, so stacks work. Table plane from two views.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem (3), floating 1-4 cm and interpenetration at rest, in a form that generalises beyond our vertical-shift rest_settle. It covers the stacked case that rest_settle skips (ep12 cup in the plastic dish rack, which tips 23 deg). The anisotropic prior matches stereo depth error. It does not check static equilibrium (torque/COM), so it does not fix (1) alone; it needs a simulated settle check afterwards.
sources.evidence: YCB-Video AR: MegaPose 0.620 -> 0.707, FoundPose 0.690 -> 0.775. HOPE-Video: 0.353 -> 0.395 and 0.286 -> 0.324. With an estimated two-view table: 0.650 / 0.715. Real Panda grasping, 5 trials x 3 objects: initial poses 0% / 60% / 0% success -> 80% on all three. Reported failures: large initial collisions can reorder objects along the optical axis, and false detections push others away.
sources.code: None found (the project page links only the paper and supplementary PDF).
sources.adoption_effort: Hours on CPU. Reimplement on our existing convex pieces with MuJoCo mj_collision distances (already used in contact_retarget.py) and our LM solver; one constant pose per rest segment plus a 1-2 s assist-off settle check.
sources.rule_risk: None (own poses, own meshes, own table plane).

sources.title: RePHO: Recovering Physically Plausible Human-Object Interactions from Monocular Videos
sources.method: Starts from a noisy kinematic HOI reconstruction (VisTracker) and trains a per-sequence RL tracking policy in physics. Adaptive reset sampling favours frames whose rollouts survive longer (reliable frames: visible contacts, slow motion). Dual forward/backward propagation with a kinematics self-update replaces noisy reference states with physically obtained ones.
sources.solves_for_us: A recipe for noisy references: it finds reliable start frames automatically, and the reference self-update can replace our floating or tipping rest poses with simulator-consistent ones. Its results also quantify the accuracy cost of physical correction, which supports applying corrections only where needed.
sources.evidence: BEHAVE: ObjFloat 0.30 -> 0.10, penetration 6.64 -> 3.91, hand contact rate 0.52 -> 0.89, but object Chamfer 8.73 -> 11.06 (worse). InterCap: ObjFloat 0.49 -> 0.06, penetration 3.11 -> 1.76, object Chamfer 11.07 -> 12.32 (worse).
sources.code: Project page https://dingbang777.github.io/RePHO/ (code release not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: Concept-level changes in FlashCHORD (reset-frame weights from rollout length; optional reference self-update loop). About 1-2 days plus GPU retrains (~$3-6 per episode for a 2-seed A/B). Risk: self-update drifts away from the true motion and lowers ADD-AUC.
sources.rule_risk: None (own estimates only).

sources.title: InterMimic: Towards Universal Whole-Body Control for Physics-Based Human-Object Interactions
sources.method: Teacher policies imitate imperfect MoCap HOI and thereby correct it. Reference contact markers come from the object's acceleration (forces from the human), not only distances, with three levels: promote, neutral buffer, penalise. Physical State Initialization (PSI) resets from a buffer of reference states and successful simulated states. Interaction early termination fires when a required contact is lost for more than 10 frames. Refined teacher rollouts become references for a student (reference distillation).
sources.solves_for_us: A better rest/held labeller than distance alone: when the object accelerates and no gravity or support explains it, a hand is acting on it. Neutral bands avoid enforcing uncertain contacts. PSI avoids training resets from floating or unsupported states, the failure mode of our 1-4 cm floating references.
sources.evidence: Qualitatively corrects floating contacts and penetration that PhysHOI cannot track (BEHAVE). Reference distillation improves all metrics in Table 2, more so on the test set. I did not extract exact numbers, and could not verify the '68% / 81% fewer pops / frozen frames' figure from secondary summaries in the v2 text.
sources.code: Project page https://sirui-xu.github.io/InterMimic (code release reported, not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: Ideas only: hours each in FlashCHORD reward and reset code; GPU A/B to validate.
sources.rule_risk: None.

sources.title: PhysHOI: Physics-Based Imitation of Dynamic Human-Object Interaction
sources.method: Physics-based HOI imitation with a contact graph. Nodes are aggregated body-part groups, the object and the table; edges are per-frame binary contact labels. A multiplicative contact-graph reward penalises contact-state mismatches, on top of body, object and interaction-graph rewards.
sources.solves_for_us: Lets FlashCHORD reward object-table contact during reference rest phases and object-object contact during the ep24 assembly. It can also penalise wrong contacts, for example a board lying flat on the table when the reference stands it on its edge (our observed ep24 failure: the policy always lays the boards flat).
sources.evidence: BallPlay ablation, success without -> with the contact-graph reward: Toss 7.7% (20.7% without the interaction graph) -> 84.8%; Cross leg 8.2% -> 88.2%; Backspin 21.7% -> 70.3%; Pass 16.2% -> 71.2%.
sources.code: Isaac Gym implementation reported on GitHub (not verified in this session).
sources.adoption_effort: Hours: add 2-4 edges from Newton contact buffers to the FlashCHORD reward. Needs a GPU A/B (2 seeds x 6 evals, ~$5-8).
sources.rule_risk: None (contact labels come from our reference).

sources.title: DexMachina: Functional Retargeting for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
sources.method: PPO with virtual object controllers (PD on 6 virtual base joints plus articulation) that drive the object along the demonstration. Their gains decay exponentially, gated on learning progress (reward history), down to zero. Hybrid actions: residual wrist on the retargeted base, absolute fingers. Keypoint imitation, behaviour-cloning and contact rewards. Object-aware retargeting post-process: the object is held at its target and the simulator resolves hand penetration. Metric: ADD-AUC.
sources.solves_for_us: Training side of the ep24 stand-up: the assist decay is gated on progress rather than a fixed schedule. Its retargeting post-process matches our contact-anchored retargeting, which supports that design. Their finding that 'kinematics only' barely lifts objects matches our ep24 behaviour.
sources.evidence: Per-task success is in figures only. SPIDER reports DexMachina at 67.1% vs SPIDER 42.0% on ARCTIC (Inspire). In DexMachina's re-implementation, the ManipTrans physics-relaxation curriculum 'initially achieves high task reward, but performance drops ... and cannot recover'.
sources.code: https://github.com/MandiZhao/dexmachina (MIT; Genesis + rl_games).
sources.adoption_effort: FlashCHORD already has an object assist with curriculum stages and a 20-step post-reset assist, so the increment is small: a progress-gated decay schedule (hours) plus a GPU A/B.
sources.rule_risk: None; the assist is training-only and the official evaluation runs unassisted.

sources.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction
sources.method: Neural SDF multi-view reconstruction coupled to a differentiable particle-based rigid simulator (DiffTaichi) through differentiable surface-point extraction (SP-MC). The physical loss penalises motion of contact points during a drop simulation. A physical uncertainty field down-weights rendering losses and steers sampling toward unstable regions.
sources.solves_for_us: The principle behind problem (1): stability as a reconstruction constraint for unseen support structure. Its failure analysis is the key caution: in scarcely observed regions the physics loss creates bulges and degenerate shapes, and disconnected parts can look stable. Never-observed regions (our undersides) therefore need a constrained shape family (planar support patch), not free-form physics optimisation.
sources.evidence: Object stability (Isaac Gym drop test) at least 40% better than all baselines on ScanNet, ScanNet++ and Replica, with no loss of reconstruction quality reported. The failure cases above are from the paper.
sources.code: Project page https://phyrecon.github.io (code release not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: The full method is too heavy for 13 days (neural SDF + DiffTaichi). Adopt the drop-test stability check and uncertainty-guided edits in our TSDF post-process (CPU, about 1 day).
sources.rule_risk: None (own multi-view data).

sources.title: In-Hand 3D Object Reconstruction from a Monocular RGB Video (contact-constrained surface under occlusion)
sources.method: NeuS-style SDF of a hand-held object with physical contact losses in occluded contact regions. Penetration loss: hand vertices with negative object SDF are penalised. Attraction loss: object surface points in the contact region are pulled to the nearest hand surface along the normal. Smoothness in the contact region. Also uses an amodal mask completion network.
sources.solves_for_us: A template for 'meshes built from interactions', the owner's plan. Fingertip contacts must lie on the surface (hand-object). The table contact patch at rest must lie on the underside (object-table, problem 1). The other object's volume at co-located frames must be outside (object-object, the ep24 slots, problem 2). Penetration plus attraction must be used together, as their ablation shows.
sources.evidence: Surface quality +52% on HO3D and +20% on HOD over prior methods. The contact loss alone lowers Chamfer by 0.115. Penetration-only reduces intersection volume but gives worse quality; both terms are needed.
sources.code: Project page https://east-j.github.io/ihor (code not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: As post-hoc constraints on our TSDF/mesh output: about 1-2 days CPU. Risk: MANO fingertip error (~1 cm) overfits the surface; use only high-confidence contacts and only in low-observation regions.
sources.rule_risk: Hand estimates are already in our pipeline (fine). Their amodal-completion network is a pretrained prior (grey zone): skip it.

sources.title: Newton 1.0: SDF-based collision and hydroelastic contact (NVIDIA technical blog, 2026-03-16)
sources.method: Newton 1.0 GA adds SDF-based collision for meshes used directly, with no convex approximation, plus hydroelastic contact patches. Both can bypass MuJoCo Warp's native collision pipeline. Configured with mesh.build_sdf(max_resolution=...) and ShapeFlags.HYDROELASTIC with a HydroelasticSDF config. Earlier SDF-collision work, Factory (RSS 2022): GPU SDF collisions with contact reduction simulate 1000 nut-bolt pairs in real time, but allow penetration on large flat low-tessellation surfaces.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem (2): narrow cross-halving notches could be simulated exactly instead of through CoACD hulls that may bridge them; also thin boards standing on an edge. This only helps if the official evaluator uses the same collision path; otherwise it creates a training/evaluation mismatch.
sources.evidence: Vendor claims only (tight-tolerance connector insertion; Skild uses it to bypass MJWarp contacts). No numbers relevant to our objects.
sources.code: Newton (open source on GitHub; licence and version support in FlashCHORD's pinned Newton not verified).
sources.adoption_effort: Hours to test whether FlashCHORD's pinned Newton exposes the SDF path. Blocked on knowing how the official evaluator collides submitted meshes.
sources.rule_risk: None, but a mismatch with the evaluator's collision model would make training gains illusory.

sources.title: CAST: Component-Aligned 3D Scene Reconstruction from an RGB Image (physics-aware correction)
sources.method: Single-image scene reconstruction with generative meshes, followed by a physics-aware pose correction. A relation graph (from GPT-4v) is mapped to Contact (bilateral: no penetration and at least one contact point) and Support (unilateral: the supporter is fixed and only the supported object moves) costs. Costs are evaluated by SDF queries of sampled surface points (Open3D + PyTorch). For flat supports it regularises SDF values near the contact region, which handles partially reconstructed objects. The authors state it does not model full dynamics, so stability over time is not guaranteed.
sources.solves_for_us: Gives a clean formal split for multi-object rest states. Cup in dish rack (ep12) is unilateral support. Boards in an X (ep24) are bilateral contact with no overlap. The flat-support regularisation for partial objects corresponds to our flatten_base. We can derive the relations from our tracks instead of a VLM.
sources.evidence: Better than baselines on 3D-FRONT geometry and on VLM / user-study physical plausibility; no stability numbers extracted.
sources.code: Not checked.
sources.adoption_effort: Formulation only (hours), merged into a PhysPose-style refiner.
sources.rule_risk: The generative mesh and GPT-4v parts are excluded (own meshes, no priors). The correction formulation itself is fine.

sources.title: ManipTrans: Efficient Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation Transfer via Residual Learning
sources.method: Pre-trained hand-trajectory imitator plus a residual module for object interaction. Reference state initialization, early termination and curriculum thresholds (finger 6 -> 4 cm; object 90 deg / 6 cm -> 30 deg / 2 cm). Physics relaxation: gravity starts at 0, friction starts high. Contact force as observation, reward and termination: terminate if the mocap shows a firm grasp but the simulated contact force is low. Unknown masses set from 200 kg/m^3; friction set slightly above real to compensate for missing skin compliance.
sources.solves_for_us: Minor: a contact-termination rule and friction/mass handling for gripping the ep24 boards. Mostly overlaps with what FlashCHORD already does.
sources.evidence: OakInk-V2 success, single / bimanual: 58.1 / 39.5% vs Retarget+Residual 47.8 / 13.9, RL-only 34.3 / 12.1, Retarget-only 4.6 / 0.0. Third-party results: DexMachina found its curriculum unstable on long-horizon tasks; Grasp-and-Lift (arXiv 2601.18121) reports ManipTrans 45.9% vs 71.7% success for their CMA-ES simulation-in-the-loop refinement on DexYCB.
sources.code: https://maniptrans.github.io (Isaac Gym; licence not checked).
sources.adoption_effort: Ideas only (hours).
sources.rule_risk: None.

ideas: H1, interaction phase graph as the single source of all physical constraints (stage A). From our own tracks only, label per frame: hand-object contact (fingertip SDF < 1.5 cm, neutral band 1.5-3 cm, InterMimic style); object-table contact (lowest point within 1 cm and object static); object-object contact or co-location; 'held' when the object accelerates beyond what gravity or support explains. Every later fix (flatten, carve, settle, rewards) reads this graph instead of per-episode hand parameters. Falsify: on the 12 public two-object episodes, compare the graph with the same labels computed from mocap after inference (diagnostic only). If rest/held agreement is below 90% of frames, the labeller is not good enough to drive automatic mesh edits.

H2, generalise flatten_base into a static-equilibrium completion over all rest evidence (stage B). For each library object, gather every perceived rest orientation across all public episodes where it appears. For each, require a planar support patch at the lowest point and the centre of mass projecting inside the support polygon with at least 5 mm margin, using the COM the simulator actually uses. Edit only vertices whose TSDF observation weight is about zero (PhyRecon warns that free-form physics edits in unobserved regions produce bulges). Falsify: (a) any library object still fails the assist-off drop test (> 2 deg tilt or > 3 mm drift in 2 s) at any perceived rest pose, or (b) registered AUC on episodes where the object never fell drops by more than 0.005 relative to library_v3.

H3, centre-of-mass mismatch (found while reading our code; hypothesis, not measured). pipeline/contact_retarget.py:stable_ups() computes stable poses with the COM as the volume-weighted centroid of the convex pieces. pipeline/make_assets.py writes the URDF COM/inertia of a thin uniform surface shell, with a placeholder 0.3 kg for every object. The stability analysis and the simulator may therefore disagree on where the COM is, which matters most for the open cup and the sweeper. Test (CPU, minutes): print both COMs for all 11 objects, and check which one Newton/FlashCHORD (and, if knowable, the official evaluator) actually applies. Falsified if |delta COM| < 3 mm for every object, or if the simulator recomputes inertia from the same convex pieces.

H4, slot carving must be validated in the collision representation, not the mesh (problem 2). Even with notches carved into the mesh, CoACD hulls can bridge a narrow notch and keep the assembled boards overlapping. Test: at ep24's assembled frames, measure hull-hull penetration depth (mj_collision on the exact CoACD pieces FlashCHORD builds) before and after carving, with a CoACD concavity-threshold sweep. Falsified if penetration is < 1 mm at default settings after carving. If it is not falsified, decompose boards explicitly: a near-planar object (thickness/length < 0.15) becomes an oriented box minus notch boxes, which is exactly 3 convex boxes per board (cuboid idea as in Shao et al. 2014, 'Imagining the Unseen'). That gives sharp standing edges and exact slots. Falsify the box approach if board registered ADD-AUC drops > 0.01 vs the TSDF meshes, or a board cannot stand on its edge in the drop test.

H5, PhysPose-style rest-segment refinement replaces the vertical-shift rest_settle (stage C). One constant pose per rest segment. Costs: anisotropic stereo prior (larger sigma along the camera ray), hinge collision cost between convex pieces and the table or other objects, gravity cost disabled when another object is the support (PhysPose delta / CAST unilateral support). Accept the result only after a 1-2 s assist-off simulated settle. Target: ep12's cup in the dish rack, which rest_settle currently skips because it rests on another object. Falsify: the cup still tips > 5 deg in the drop test, or ep12 registered AUC < 0.77 over 2 seeds x 6 evals (k baseline 0.790 +- 0.023). Diagnostic: if rest-frame ADD to mocap rises by > 3 mm median after refinement, exclude those segments.

H6, physical corrections should be gated by a failing drop test. Evidence: RePHO's object Chamfer gets worse after physics refinement (8.73 -> 11.06 on BEHAVE), and our ep12 rest settling cost -0.05 while helping ep18 only together with a standable mesh. Rule: correct an object or segment only if it fails the assist-off drop test with no hand within 3 cm. Falsify: on ep12/18/24/27, the gated variant scores below max(no correction, ungated) by more than 0.01 on any episode (2 seeds x 6 evals).

H7, sampling-MPC references for the hard segments (stage D). Run do-as-i-do retargeting stage 5 (MuJoCo Warp, Sharpa, MIT) on our ep24 and ep18 tracks with our fixed meshes, pedestals and supports disabled, transition reward on. Train FlashCHORD on the result, or as a residual on its nominal controls. Falsify: (a) the MPC itself fails to track the ep24 stand-up segment (~f95-f130) within 3 cm / 30 deg in at least 3 of 5 seeds. That would mean the bottleneck is geometry or the contact model, not RL exploration, and the mesh work must come first. Or (b) the resulting policy does not lift ep24 registered AUC from ~0.31 to >= 0.40 (2 seeds x 6 evals). Estimated cost < 1 GPU-hour per episode for the MPC (unmeasured) plus normal training.

H8, contact-graph and transition rewards in FlashCHORD (stage E). Add PhysHOI-style edges for object-table (reference rest) and object-object (ep24 assembly). Add Do as I Do penalties for a missing support contact during rest and a missing hand contact during in-hand frames, plus ManipTrans contact termination (reference shows a firm grasp but the simulated contact force is about 0). Falsify: with fixed meshes, ep24 mean registered AUC improves by < +0.03 over 2 seeds x 6 evals (noise is about +-0.02), or the 'boards laid flat' failure persists in more than 4 of 6 rollouts.

H9, start-state selection (InterMimic PSI / RePHO adaptive sampling). Add successful simulated states to FlashCHORD's reset buffer, and weight reset frames by surviving rollout length, so training stops restarting from floating or unsupported reference states. Falsify: no faster rise in the learning curve on ep24 and no AUC gain beyond +0.02 at equal training budget.
gaps: No published HOI or retargeting method I found recovers object-object assembly geometry (notches, slots) from interaction video. SPIDER and ManipTrans test two-object bimanual tasks but assume correct meshes. Carving from co-located overlap looks novel, with no benchmark to compare against.

Official evaluator details that decide which fixes count are unknown to me. How are submitted meshes turned into collision geometry: CoACD, convex hull or SDF? Where do mass, COM and inertia come from: our URDF or recomputed? Is the initial object state taken from our reference frame 0 or set elsewhere? Which contact parameters are used?

PhysPose code is not released (the project page has only the paper and supplementary), so it must be reimplemented. CAST, PhyRecon, RePHO, InterMimic and PhysHOI code availability was not verified in this session.
SPIDER is CC BY-NC 4.0, and Do as I Do (MIT) builds on it. Whether non-commercial terms are fine for the challenge was not checked.
Do as I Do's published success numbers include pedestal and welded-support geoms under resting objects. Its performance without them, the setting that matches our evaluator, is unknown.
The success thresholds in SPIDER, Do as I Do and ManipTrans (3-10 cm, 30 deg or 0.5 rad) are far looser than ADD-AUC, so their numbers do not predict our score.

Transfer from Do as I Do's MuJoCo Warp MJCF scene to FlashCHORD's Newton/MuJoCo-Warp scene (contact parameters, Sharpa model, wrist collider) is unmeasured. Open-loop replay in FlashCHORD would test it.
InterMimic's quantitative claim from secondary summaries ('68% / 81% fewer pops / frozen frames') was not found in the v2 text and is not used.

ContactOpt, TOCH, D-Grasp, ArtiGrasp, DexMV, HOLD and QuasiSim were not fetched in this session. I judged them low priority because problem (4), hand-object interpenetration, is already handled by our contact-anchored retargeting with simulator collision. AGILE and MagicHOI rely on generative or diffusion shape priors (grey zone). Grasp-and-Lift (arXiv 2601.18121; CMA-ES keyframe simulation-in-the-loop refinement in MuJoCo, 71.7% vs ManipTrans 45.9% success on DexYCB) is an alternative to sampling MPC but was not evaluated further.
The H3 centre-of-mass mismatch is from reading our code, not measured: this cloud session has no trimesh / FlashCHORD venv, so I could not compute both COMs here.

verified.angle:
Fact-check of the hoi-physical-plausibility findings against primary sources. I read the full arXiv HTML for each paper and the released code at upstream HEAD. Do as I Do is at 824591b and SPIDER at 4471700, both checked with git ls-remote; the clones are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v2d-track3/8c892c5e-fd7c-57aa-abef-68d2af098e4f/scratchpad/repos. The colleague's numbers are mostly right. Five corrections matter for the plan:
(1) The SPIDER figures quoted come from v1/v2. v3 (2026-09-26) replaced success rates with ADD-AUC, and the 'RL still beats SPIDER on ARCTIC' result no longer appears.
(2) In Do as I Do's released code, objects do not collide with the floor by default (OBJECT_FLOOR_COLLISION=False). The transition reward is wired to the pedestal. The floor version of the rest gate only fires when the reference object is within 1 cm of the floor, so with our references floating 1-4 cm it would never fire. Rest-pose repair therefore has to come before any physics-search retargeting.
(3) Do as I Do itself fixes geometry. Its paper appendix 'Object Base' and resolve_pedestal.py add a flat collision-only plate under resting objects, sized to cover the centre-of-mass projection. That is the same kind of fix as our underside flattening. So 'no HOI method repairs geometry' is wrong for the support case; it holds only for object-object assembly.
(4) PhysPose's gravity cost lowers every convex part, which favours lying flat. Our ep24 boards stand on edge and the ep18 sweeper stands upright, so the cost works against both poses.
(5) RePHO code is released (MIT). A precedent the colleague missed: Co-Section (CVPR 2020, with code) completes hidden surfaces of moving objects from object-intersection and observed-free-space constraints.

checked.title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos (Paliwal, Etukuru, Liang, Abbeel, Shafiullah, Malik; arXiv 2606.19333v1, 17 Jun 2026)
checked.claim_checked: Checked: Table 3 numbers; Sharpa embodiment and MuJoCo Warp; warmup, perturbation and transition reward; pedestals and welded supports in the code; hyperparameters; MIT licence; use_pedestal=False as the way to disable pedestals.
checked.verdict: Confirmed for the numbers and method. Partly right on how the code handles rest and support, which is the part that matters for us.
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Table 3 is exact. Reconstructed in-the-wild references, success: 0.25 (annealed sampling) -> 0.66 (+warmup) -> 0.67 (+perturbation) -> 0.71 (+transition reward); position error 0.08 -> 0.05 m. OakInk2: 0.72 -> 0.77 -> 0.79 -> 0.81. Success means E_pos < 0.1 m and E_rot < 0.5 rad. The paper calls warmup the main differentiator. Embodiment is the 22-DoF Sharpa Wave on every task (UR3e arms in the real deployment). Physics is MuJoCo Warp at 200 Hz with CoACD hulls. Hyperparameters (Table 4 and the do_as_i_do override) are as quoted: 1024 samples, 32 iterations, 3 s horizon, ctrl_dt 0.5 s, penetration penalty 3000 with a 5 mm margin (the code's base default margin is 3 mm). The transition reward is described in the paper as a constant penalty for 'lack of object-floor contact during resting reference timesteps' or no hand contact while in hand, with stages set by reference hand-object distance.
Paper Appendix B, 'Object Base': 'we add a flat base plate to the bottom of the object mesh, which only has contact with the floor'.
What the code does (the colleague missed this):
(a) launch.py hard-codes OBJECT_FLOOR_COLLISION=False, USE_PEDESTAL=True and USE_SUPPORT=True as module constants, not CLI flags. By default objects never touch the floor.
(b) resolve_pedestal.py adds pedestals only at the two trajectory endpoints (frame 0 and the last frame, smoothed over 3 frames), and only when the reference hand is at least 10 cm from the object (hand_object_distance_thresh=0.1). It does not test whether the object would fall. The pedestal is a cylinder whose top sits 0.1 mm below the object's lowest vertex at its reference pose, so a floating reference gets a pedestal at the floating height.
(c) The 'support' is a thin disc fixed to the object body (a geom, not a weld constraint) that collides only with the pedestal. If the centre of mass projects outside the bottom 1 cm slice, the disc is centred under the centre of mass and widened to cover the whole xy footprint.
(d) The released transition reward is pedestal_penalty_scale=0.5. floor_penalty_scale defaults to 0. The floor gate arms only when the reference lowest vertex is within object_floor_distance_thresh=0.01 m ('floor-rest reference data is assumed accurate'). Frames that are neither rest nor in-hand are not penalised.
(e) launch.py thickens meshes and dilates hulls by 2 mm, and add_ur3_arm=True adds a 32 mm x 92 mm cylinder behind each palm.
The paper's limitations section says it 'reconstructs only the hand and an object, rather than the full scene'. Runtime is given only as 'in minutes'.
checked.code_status: Released. Repo is MIT, but retargeting/README.md says 'This codebase is built on SPIDER', and SPIDER is CC BY-NC 4.0, so assume the non-commercial terms carry over. The reconstruction stage needs SAM 3 / SAM 3D (gated Hugging Face weights). Key files: retargeting/launch.py, retargeting/pipeline/resolve_pedestal.py, retargeting/utils/mjwp.py (_rest_surface_penalty), config/override/do_as_i_do.yaml. Inspected at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v2d-track3/8c892c5e-fd7c-57aa-abef-68d2af098e4f/scratchpad/repos/do-as-i-do. The GitHub API was blocked for this repo; git clone and ls-remote worked.

checked.title: SPIDER: Scalable Physics-Informed Dexterous Retargeting (Pan et al., arXiv 2511.09484; v1 12 Nov 2025, v2 5 Feb 2026, v3 26 Sep 2026)
checked.claim_checked: Checked: the +18% from contact guidance; Oakink 0.479 (1022 trajectories) and GigaHands 0.879 (756); SPIDER vs ManipTrans 47.9% vs 39.5% and vs DexMachina 42.0% vs 67.1% (RL better); H = 1.2 s, N = 1024, 16 iterations, 100/50 Hz; residual RL (u = u_SPIDER + pi); the contact filter; 7,876 released trajectories.
checked.verdict: Partly. The figures exist, but only in v1/v2. The current v3 replaces them, and two of the colleague's conclusions no longer hold.
checked.code_status: Released, CC BY-NC 4.0 (checked LICENSE and README). Supports MuJoCo Warp, Genesis and IsaacGym. Sharpa appears in the dataset tooling; Do as I Do ships Sharpa assets.
checked.applicability:
Use it through Do as I Do, which already wraps it for the Sharpa hand; don't adopt it separately. Two corrections to the colleague's plan:
- The residual-RL route is not backed by v3. The cheap test is to swap only the reference: physics-searched reference in, FlashCHORD unchanged.
- v3's ADD-AUC (22-57%) is far below our RL tracking on easy episodes (ep12 0.79, ep27 0.94 registered AUC). Sampling MPC can improve references, but it cannot replace the policy.
Contact guidance is reported to help mainly on clean MoCap. The authors switched it off for noisy references, which is our case.

checked.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints (Malenický, Cífka, Fourmy, Montaut, Carpentier, Sivic, Petrik; arXiv 2503.23587v1, 30 Mar 2025; ICCV 2025 per the supplementary file name)
checked.claim_checked: Checked: the cost terms (anisotropic Mahalanobis pose prior, hinge collision cost on convex pieces via DiffCol, gravity cost switched off for an object in contact with another object); the YCB-V and HOPE numbers; the 0.650/0.715 with estimated geometry; the Panda results; the failure modes; that no code exists.
checked.verdict: Confirmed. The colleague missed one caveat that matters for us.
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Every quoted number is exact:
- YCB-V AR: MegaPose 0.620 -> 0.707, FoundPose 0.690 -> 0.775;
- HOPE-Video: 0.353 -> 0.395 and 0.286 -> 0.324;
- with estimated scene geometry and a support view: 0.650 / 0.715;
- Panda grasping: 0/60/0% -> 80% each.
The failure modes (object reordering along the optical axis, false detections pushing other objects) are as quoted.
What the colleague left out:
(a) The gravity cost is the average positive distance of every convex part of the object to the closest static support part ('minimizes the scene's potential energy'). It pulls all parts down, so it favours lying flat.
(b) The switch-off term fires when the object is in collision with any other object.
(c) Ablation on 10% of YCB-V: full 0.691; without gravity 0.615, about equal to the no-refinement baseline of 0.611; without collision 0.607; without the pose prior 0.540. The support term carries most of the gain.
(d) The gains are in MSSD and VSD, not MSPD, i.e. they correct depth errors of single-view RGB estimators.
(e) A known gravity direction did not consistently help.
checked.code_status: None released. The project page links only arXiv and a supplementary PDF, and a web search found no repository.
checked.applicability:
Good template for repairing rest segments: per-segment constant pose, anisotropic stereo prior, hinge collision cost on our CoACD pieces, support switched off when the object rests on another object (ep12 cup in the dish rack). Two changes:
- Replace the mean-of-all-parts gravity term with a term that makes only the lowest part(s) touch the support, then run a static-equilibrium (centre of mass over support polygon) or 1-2 s assist-off settle check.
- Restrict the free variables to vertical translation plus a small tilt. Otherwise the cost tips the on-edge ep24 boards and the upright ep18 sweeper towards lying flat.
Expect smaller gains than reported: our stereo depth error is well below single-view MegaPose/FoundPose error. Before using it, check whether our 1-4 cm float is pose error at all, or mesh-underside error.

checked.title: RePHO: Recovering Physically Plausible Human-Object Interactions from Monocular Videos (Huang, Vouga, Huang, Pavlakos; arXiv 2606.05359v1, 3 Jun 2026; CVPR 2026, Highlight per README)
checked.claim_checked: Checked: the BEHAVE and InterCap numbers, including the object Chamfer getting worse; the adaptive reset sampling and self-update; whether code is released.
checked.verdict: Confirmed numbers. The colleague's 'code release not verified' is out of date: code is released.
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Table 1 against the VisTracker initialisation:
- BEHAVE: object CD 8.73 -> 11.06 (worse); hand contact rate 0.52 -> 0.89; penetration 6.64 -> 3.91; ObjFloat 0.30 -> 0.10; ObjJerk 524.9 -> 188.5.
- InterCap: object CD 11.07 -> 12.32 (worse); contact 0.48 -> 0.81; penetration 3.11 -> 1.76; ObjFloat 0.49 -> 0.06.
The authors call the CD loss 'a slight degradation'. CD is a Procrustes-aligned Chamfer distance (cm) over 10-frame windows after aligning the combined human-object mesh, so it is not an object-pose ADD metric. ObjFloat is the fraction of unsupported frames among frames where the object is in the air. Method: adaptive reset sampling weighted by rollout length, plus forward and reverse propagation that replaces reference states with simulated ones. Contact markers are given for the hands only; ground contact is not given.
checked.code_status: Released, MIT (LICENSE present). Isaac Gym, SMPL whole body, training initialised from an InterMimic checkpoint, VisTracker inputs. It is not a drop-in for our dexterous-hand FlashCHORD setup.
checked.applicability: Ideas only: reset-frame weighting by survival length, and a self-update of the reference. The accuracy-vs-plausibility trade-off is real, but because CD is Procrustes-aligned it is only a loose analogy for our ep12 drop (0.740 with rest settle vs 0.790 without, one seed). It supports applying corrections only where an assist-off test fails.

checked.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction (Ni et al., arXiv 2404.16666, NeurIPS 2024): the 'bulges' claim
checked.claim_checked: Checked: that a physics loss applied where the surface was never observed produces bulges and degenerate shapes.
checked.verdict: Confirmed
checked.what_source_actually_says: Appendix E (Fig. 8a): 'in regions scarcely observed in the input images, optimizing with the physical loss may lead to degenerated object shapes, e.g., bulges, to maintain physical stability'. Fig. 8b: stable but disconnected parts. The ablation states that the physical loss alone 'will overshadow the rendering losses, leading to degenerated object shapes'. Their mitigation is to apply the loss only to simulated contact points, plus uncertainty-guided pixel sampling.
checked.code_status: Not checked (out of scope).
checked.applicability: Supports the plan to edit only never-observed regions, using constrained shape families rather than a free-form physics loss on our SDF.

checked.title: InterMimic (Xu et al., arXiv 2502.20390, v2 1 Feb 2026, CVPR 2025): contact labels from object acceleration, neutral bands, PSI, early termination
checked.claim_checked: Checked: reference contact markers inferred from object acceleration; three levels (promote, neutral, penalise); Physical State Initialization (PSI); termination when a required contact is lost for more than 10 frames.
checked.verdict: Confirmed
checked.code_status: Not checked in this session.
checked.applicability: A good template for stage A, with a quantitative caveat (my estimate, not measured). Second differences of stereo-tracked poses are noisy: about 1 mm position noise at 30 fps gives roughly sqrt(6)*1 mm/(1/30 s)^2, about 2 m/s^2 per frame (about 0.2 g). Smooth over 5 or more frames, or use velocity together with hand distance, before thresholding.

checked.title: PhysHOI (Wang et al., arXiv 2312.04393): contact-graph reward ablation
checked.claim_checked: Checked: BallPlay contact-graph ablation numbers 7.7/20.7 -> 84.8, 8.2 -> 88.2, 21.7 -> 70.3, 16.2 -> 71.2.
checked.verdict: Partly. All quoted numbers appear in the ablation table text. I did not re-read the row and column mapping.
checked.what_source_actually_says: The contact graph is a complete graph over body parts and objects, with binary contact labels per frame. The contact-graph reward multiplies the kinematic rewards. BallPlay contact labels come with the dataset, not from inference.
checked.code_status: Not checked.
checked.applicability: Adding table and object-object contact edges to the FlashCHORD reward is plausible. Our labels would come from stage A inference, which is noisier than BallPlay's dataset labels.

checked.title: NEW, not in the colleague's list: Co-Section, 'Where Does It End? Reasoning About Hidden Surfaces by Object Intersection Constraints' (Strecke and Stückler, CVPR 2020, arXiv 2004.04630)
checked.claim_checked: Checks the colleague's claim that object-object assembly geometry is not covered by any published method.
checked.verdict: Confirmed from the abstract only; I did not read the full paper.
checked.what_source_actually_says: Object-level dynamic RGB-D SLAM builds a dense model per object. An energy-minimisation back end then 'completes the shapes using hull and intersection constraints between the objects': observed free space bounds each object, and objects may not intersect. The authors call it the first method to put such physical-plausibility constraints into shape completion of dynamic objects. Source code is linked from arXiv.
checked.code_status: Source code is linked from the arXiv page; I did not inspect its licence or state.
checked.applicability: The closest published template for stage B with our TSDF objects: complete never-seen surfaces (undersides, filled notches) from free-space plus no-overlap evidence at co-located frames, instead of per-object patches. Limit: an intersection constraint says the 13.5 cm^3 ep24 overlap must go, but not which board loses which part. Attribution needs free-space evidence from frames before assembly, or a cross-halving prior. Not an HOI method, so the colleague's narrow claim stands, but the principle is published.

corrected_ideas: Run stage C before stage D. Do as I Do's floor rest gate only arms when the reference object's lowest vertex is within 1 cm of the table. With our 1-4 cm floats, its transition reward would never fire on ep24 or ep27 rest frames. Its default pedestal would be built at the floating height, hiding the error instead of fixing it.

Do as I Do for our setup means editing launch.py and the config: OBJECT_FLOOR_COLLISION=True, USE_PEDESTAL=False, USE_SUPPORT=False, floor_penalty_scale=0.5, pedestal_penalty_scale=0, thicken=0, dilate=0 (its 2 mm hull inflation would add a 2 mm float and mismatch our collision geometry), add_ur3_arm=False, and our own CoACD pieces. The authors never report this configuration. Hypothesis: it yields references the policy can track better. It is falsified if the policy trained on these references does not beat the current registered AUC over at least 2 seeds (ep18 0.715 with flattening, ep24 about 0.31), or if objects still leave the table at reference rest frames in an assist-off replay.

Correct the framing that no method repairs geometry. Do as I Do's own 'Object Base' (paper Appendix B; resolve_pedestal.py) is a geometry patch of the same class as our underside flattening. Reuse its sizing rule: when the centre-of-mass projection falls outside the bottom-slice footprint, centre the support under the centre of mass and widen it. For us the patch must be real mesh, because the evaluator has no collision-only geoms. Keep it inside never-observed volume, bounded by the observed side walls extended down to the table plane. Add it only to objects that fail the assist-off drop test.

Stage B template: use Co-Section's hull and intersection constraints (CVPR 2020, with code) on our TSDF objects instead of hand-made patches. Observed free space (depth and mask rays from all frames) bounds each object; co-located frames forbid overlap. For ep24 the constraint does not say which board loses the 13.5 cm^3. Attribute it with free-space evidence from frames before assembly plus the cross-halving prior: each board gets a notch as wide as the other board's thickness and about half the board's height deep. Hypothesis: falsified if the assembled-pose overlap reaches about 0 but the diagnostic registration of the boards to the public scans gets worse (public episodes only, scoring-side).

Thin planar objects (ep24 boards): fit an oriented plate (box primitive, thickness from the observed faces) plus boolean notches, instead of using the TSDF surface. Rounded edges and filled notches are TSDF artefacts, and PhyRecon shows that free-form physics losses on poorly observed regions produce bulges. Falsified if the plate mesh registers worse to the public scan than the TSDF mesh (diagnostic), or if it still cannot stand on edge in an assist-off settle test.

Find where the float comes from before fixing it. For each rest segment, compare (a) the mesh's lowest point at the perceived pose against the table plane with (b) the lowest observed stereo points of that object against the table plane. If (b) is about 0 while (a) is 1-4 cm, the mesh underside is wrong and needs a geometry fix. If (b) is also off, it is pose or table-plane error, and a PhysPose-style pose fix applies. This uses only our own data.

PhysPose-style stage C: keep the anisotropic stereo prior, the collision hinge on convex pieces, and switching support off when an object rests on another object. Replace its gravity term (mean positive distance of all parts, which pulls everything down and favours lying flat) with a term that makes the lowest part(s) touch the support, plus a centre-of-mass-over-support-polygon check. Restrict the free variables to vertical translation plus a small tilt, so on-edge or upright rest poses are not tipped over. Expect smaller gains than PhysPose's +0.085 AR: that came from fixing single-view RGB depth errors, and in its ablation the support term carried almost all of the gain.

Stage A: InterMimic's acceleration rules are verified, but stereo-tracked acceleration is noisy (estimate: about 2 m/s^2 per frame at 1 mm and 30 fps). Smooth over 5 or more frames, combine with velocity and hand distance, and keep neutral bands. Do as I Do's own in-hand gate is only 'reference hand within 10 cm', so our labeller can be stricter than theirs.

Use SPIDER v3 numbers, not v2. On the 0-10 cm ADD-AUC scale: ManipTrans 19.4 vs SPIDER 22.3; DexMachina 41.0 vs SPIDER 43.6; contact guidance 48.8 -> 56.9 on Oakink and 56.9 -> 57.7 on GigaHands. v3 drops the residual action, using SPIDER output only to initialise RL targets and as the tracking reference, and runs Sharpa without contact guidance because contacts from noisy demonstrations are unreliable. These values sit far below our RL tracking, so sampling MPC is a reference generator, not a policy replacement. First test the reference swap alone, before any FlashCHORD feed-forward or residual changes.

Licence and rules: the Do as I Do repo says 'built on SPIDER', so assume CC BY-NC 4.0 applies to the retargeting code. Ask the owner whether challenge use is acceptable before a submitted run depends on it. Never use its SAM 3D reconstruction stage: it is generative, and it conflicts with the own-mesh rule.

Validation gate for every stage: check in the collision representation the evaluator builds from our submitted mesh, with the object assist off, and change an object only if its drop test or overlap test fails. Also require that public-episode registered AUC does not drop. RePHO (object CD worse by 2.3 cm on BEHAVE and 1.25 cm on InterCap) and our ep12 result (0.740 vs 0.790, one seed) both show that unconditional physical correction costs accuracy.

found.angle:
Multi-object assembly: interlocking, nested and stacked objects, and how published work recovers mating geometry that the sensors cannot see.

**What the literature does**
1. Most assembly work never recovers it. Assembly-from-video and assembly-RL work takes CAD or scanned models as given. Examples: IKEA Video Manuals (arXiv 2411.11409), the 2BY2 pairwise dataset (2504.06961, which covers lid covering, inserting and placing), AutoMate, Factory, and DemoBot (2601.01651, human RGB-D video to simulated bimanual assembly). I found no paper that reconstructs a hidden notch or slot from observation.
2. Physics as the regulariser of unobserved geometry and poses:
   - stability or force equilibrium plus non-penetration (Zheng CVPR'13, PhyRecon, SPARCS RSS'26, CAST, PhysPose, MoreFusion);
   - bounding objects by the support surface (RICO);
   - "opposite volume occupancy": a part's mating region is the complement of its partner (Combinative Matching, arXiv 2508.09780, learned on fracture data; principle only).
3. Generative priors (SAM3D, CAST's generator). These are in the rules' grey zone.

**Verdict on our patches.** They are point fixes of three generic constraints. Flattening the sweeper's underside is static equilibrium at an observed rest. Carving the slot is non-penetration between co-located objects. Snapping to a stable pose is pose-level equilibrium. The robust version applies these constraints to the never-observed voxels of every object at every observed rest or contact. It then verifies in the simulator's own collision geometry. It should not be keyed to object names or episodes.

**Proposed stages, each with its research**
- **S0. Observation-first geometry.** Reconstruct each object from frames where it is unoccluded and not in contact. Add carving down to the known table plane and mask (visual-hull) carving. Research: visual hull / silhouette-plus-stereo fusion, and why the TSDF loses thin gaps.
- **S1. Interaction graph from our tracks, no VLM.** Edges are support, contact, nested/inserted or attached, from relative-pose stillness, distance and overlap. Research: Zheng'13 and CAST relation graphs.
- **S2. Occupancy arbitration for co-located pairs.**
  - Voxels observed inside one object win.
  - Voxels unobserved in both are split by the swept volume of the observed partner along the tracked insertion path. This rule is my own hypothesis; I found no paper that does it.
  - Research: MoreFusion free-space exclusion, combinative matching, assembly-by-disassembly.
- **S3. Physics-consistent pose and hidden shape at rests.** A PhysPose-style pose term, plus SPARCS-style equilibrium that moves only unobserved geometry. Optionally a planar refit (PolyFit) for planar objects. Research: SPARCS, PhysPose, PolyFit.
- **S4. Simulator-geometry check.** Run checks on the hulls the simulator actually collides, not on the meshes:
  - overlap at the mating pose;
  - a 2 s no-hand settle test at each rest;
  - a reverse-insertion (disassembly) sweep.

  Research: CoACD threshold behaviour, Newton SDF contacts, and what the official evaluator does.
- **S5. GPU A/B** on ep18, ep24, ep12 and ep27.

**Measured this session (synthetic, CPU)**
- Script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v2d-track3/8c892c5e-fd7c-57aa-abef-68d2af098e4f/scratchpad/scripts/slot_coacd.py
- Test object: a correctly slotted 22.9 × 13 × 2 cm board with a 2 × 6.5 cm through-slot.
- With Newton's CoACD setting (threshold 0.05) it decomposes into 3 hulls that still occupy 9.6% of the slot volume (about 2.5 cm³). At threshold 0.02, or 3 mm real-metric, it is 5 hulls and 3.8% (about 1 cm³). So even a perfect slot leaves 1–2.5 cm³ of hull overlap at the mating pose unless we add clearance or change the decomposition.
- Caveat: trimesh reported the test mesh as not watertight (its volume, 569.4 cm³, is correct).

**Code reading: our recon_mesh.py**
