- Earlier run, rot25 with W = 1.3 cm: 1 hull, 18.7 cm^3 pair overlap (the same as no slot at all), in 0.1 s. The manifold check passed, so it was not preprocessing. rot40: 1.8 cm^3 overlap and 8 % fill. pca=True undid it (0.00 cm^3).

The colleague's clean boards were axis-aligned, with notches of 1.3 cm (W/L = 0.057) and 1.6 cm in the TSDF runs (0.070). Both are best cases. I did not re-run the TSDF-like numbers (6.9-7.1, 15.4-25.2 and 2.5 cm^3).
checked.code_status: github.com/SarahWeiii/CoACD, MIT. The GitHub web and API views were blocked here; LICENSE and source were read via raw.githubusercontent. pip coacd 1.0.11 is in the scratchpad venv.
checked.applicability:
Highest value of the four. Our repo note docs/research/notes/19-collision-hulls.md (A2/A3/A13) already records the evaluator's exact call: run_coacd(threshold=0.05, preprocess auto, seed 0, pca False), applied to each collision mesh in its own frame, with each hull kept as its own shape. The --split concern does not apply. Under that call:
- Any functional gap (a board notch, a rack bay, a handle hole, the cup seat in the rack) is bridged when w < ~0.05*L_bbox of the mesh it belongs to. For a 30-40 cm rack that is 15-20 mm. This is consistent with note 19's finding that splitting the rack into parts of at most 120 mm helps, and it is a candidate cause of the ep12 cup tipping (hypothesis).
- Fixes, in order: (a) ship each mesh in a frame that minimises its bbox and aligns its faces with the axes, carrying the rotation in our tracks or in <collision><origin rpy> (note 19 C12 says FlashCHORD keeps it per hull); (b) make the notch at least the partner's thickness plus clearance, with a margin of 1.2x or more over 0.05*L; (c) if the organisers allow several <collision> meshes per object (still an open question in note 19), ship convex pieces, which turns CoACD into a no-op and makes the slots exact.
- Add a check to the gate that recomputes w/L_bbox on the float32 vertices exactly as shipped, and reruns the exact call on them.

checked.title: CRISP: Contact-Guided Real2Sim from Monocular Video with Planar Scene Primitives (Wang et al., ICLR 2026)
checked.claim_checked: EMDB RL success: TSDF 75.9 %, NKSR 79.3 %, planar 93.1 % (VideoMimic 44.8 %). Failure rate 55.2 -> 6.9 %. Throughput 15K -> 23K FPS (+43 %). PROX non-penetration 0.925 vs 0.947. About 50 primitives. 'Missing small details largely harmless'.
checked.verdict: partly (the numbers are real but two are mislabelled)
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Table 1 has an overall Success column (44.8 / 75.9 / 79.3 / 93.1 % for VideoMimic / TSDF / NKSR / Planar) and FPS (16K / 15K / 16K / 23K). The PROX(11) block gives Success 27.3 / 72.7 / 90.9 / 90.9 % and Non-Pene 0.906 / 0.925 / 0.937 / 0.947. The EMDB(20) block gives Success 50.0 / 77.8 / 75.0 / 93.8 %.

So:
- 75.9/79.3/93.1 is the combined column, not EMDB.
- +43 % is 23K vs VideoMimic's 16K (vs TSDF it is +53 %).
- The abstract's 55.2 -> 6.9 % failure drop is vs VideoMimic. Against their own TSDF variant it is 24.1 -> 6.9 %.

Success means every joint stays within 0.5 m of the reference: a coarse locomotion criterion. Primitives are RANSAC planar cuboids with a default thickness of 0.05 m, about 50 per scene. Contact completion uses InteractVLM, a learned contact predictor, on SMPL. Scenes are STATIC; 'supporting dynamic human-object interaction' is listed as future work. The quote 'missing tiny non-contact details is largely harmless, whereas extra noisy geometry produces unwanted contact artifacts' is accurate. The TSDF baseline is VDBFusion plus Marching Cubes.
checked.code_status: The project page links github.com/Z1hanW/CRISP-Real2Sim and Z1hanW/holosoma-crisp. I could not access them (GitHub 403 via the proxy; raw README 404 on main/master), so licence and contents are not verified. The paper text is CC BY 4.0.
checked.applicability: Evidence that clean planar primitives beat TSDF meshes for contact-rich RL, but only for static support surfaces at human scale, with a 0.5 m success criterion. It shows nothing about manipulated objects, so the analogy to our boards and dust-pan plate is a hypothesis. Falsify it with an A/B on ep24: refit slab boards (measured thickness, sharp edges, rectangular notches, aligned frame, W/L >= 0.06) vs the current TSDF boards, same policy budget, measuring the assembled-state hull overlap and the score. Do not port their code. Their 5 cm default thickness and learned contact model do not fit.

checked.title: SPARCS: Simulation-Ready Cluttered Scene Estimation via Physics-aware Joint Shape and Pose Optimization (Huang, Han, Ye, Pan, Hauser; RSS 2026)
checked.claim_checked: Hull vertices and poses are optimised jointly with an augmented Lagrangian, SDRS contact and quasi-static equilibrium. Separating-plane aggregation flattens unseen contact faces. SAM3D initialisation, 800 kg/m^3. Drift 0.73-3.10 vs 31-173 cm; KE 7e-4 to 1.1e-2 vs 2.1-5.7 J. 6-9 ALM iterations, about 200-540 s per scene on CPU. No code.
checked.verdict: partly (method and stability numbers confirmed; the run time is wrong by 60x)
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Method as described. Input is a SINGLE RGBD image of a static scene; tested on 5 tabletop scenes with up to 5 objects and 22 hulls. Mass is 800 kg/m^3 times the SAM3D mesh volume.

Unseen regions are regularised by a type-III term that pulls the hulls toward the SAM3D-generated mesh, plus the physics terms. Appendix A-B: one separating plane per object pair 'regularizes occluded contact regions by encouraging them to align with a common separating plane'.

Table I: KE in the first 1 s is 7.19e-4 to 1.12e-2 J vs 2.08-5.73 J; drift over 1 min is 0.73-3.10 vs 31.06-172.55 cm (confirmed). Table III: 6-9 ALM iterations; 'Wall Time (min)' is 46.1, 259.7, 224.2, 202.15 and 539.92, i.e. 0.8-9 HOURS per scene, on an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K, all CPU except texturing.

Stated limitations: high compute; mass and friction set by hand; SAM3D shapes inaccurate under heavy occlusion. The MuJoCo check settings are given (implicit integrator, dt 1e-3, noslip 10, elliptic cones, condim 4, friction 1).
checked.code_status: None. The project page rory-weicheng.github.io/SPARCS says 'Code (To be released soon)'. SDRS (Ye et al., T-RO 2025) is the underlying contact model; I did not check its code.
checked.applicability:
Infeasible as a method for us. It costs hours per static frame, needs a generative prior (SAM3D, a grey zone) for unseen shape, and is single-image with no in-hand phases. Two things are worth borrowing:
- The idea of one shared separating plane per object pair (object-table, object-object) during each rest interval, used to flatten ONLY unobserved contact geometry.
- Its MuJoCo settle-test protocol (KE in the first second, drift over 60 s) as a GT-free gate metric.
Their vertex-lumped gravity potential is crude; our gate should use the volume centre of mass.

checked.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints (Malenicky et al., 2025)
checked.claim_checked: Pose cost + CoACD-part collision hinge + gravity hinge to the nearest static support, disabled when supported by another object; RANSAC table. YCB-V AR: MegaPose 0.620 -> 0.707, FoundPose 0.690 -> 0.775; MSSD +0.13; HOPE 0.353 -> 0.395. Panda grasping 0/0/60 % -> 80 %. No code.
checked.verdict: confirmed numerically, but the headline numbers are the known-scene setting
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Method as described. [45] is CoACD. The pose prior is anisotropic, looser along the camera ray. The gravity cost is the average positive distance of each convex part to the closest static part along gravity, switched off (delta_A) while the object collides with another.

Table 1 is titled 'Results in known environments' (scene geometry known a priori, plus model-based object CAD):
- YCB-V MegaPose 0.620 -> 0.707, FoundPose 0.690 -> 0.775.
- MSSD 0.597 -> 0.730 and 0.670 -> 0.802; MSPD nearly unchanged.
- HOPE MegaPose 0.353 -> 0.395, FoundPose 0.286 -> 0.324.

Table 2, estimated scene: with a support view, 0.620 -> 0.650 and 0.690 -> 0.715. A single-view estimate DEGRADES them (0.597 / 0.658). A known gravity direction 'did not consistently enhance performance'.

Grasping: 5 trials per object; 0 / 0 / 60 % -> 80 % for all three. Limitations: joint optimisation spreads detection errors, and large initial collisions can produce the wrong ordering along the optical axis (Fig. 8).
checked.code_status: No code. The project page has only arXiv and a supplementary PDF (2025_ICCV_collision_pose_supplementary.pdf, which suggests ICCV 2025; not verified).
checked.applicability:
Good fit for problem 3 (floating 1-4 cm) in rest intervals: our stereo table plane is close to a 'known' support. Expect gains nearer the estimated-scene numbers than the headline. Three limits:
- The gravity term only closes gaps. It does not test stability (centre of mass over the support polygon), so it does NOT fix ep18-type or ep12 cup tipping. Add a settle or CoM-margin check.
- In ep24 the 13.5 cm^3 overlap comes from a shape error (missing notches). Pose-only refinement would push the boards apart, which is exactly its documented failure mode, so run it only after the shape is fixed.
- Switch the gravity term off while an object is held.

checked.title: Atlas3D (NeurIPS 2024), spot-check only
checked.claim_checked: More than 6x lower rotation deviation than Magic3D over 107 prompts; 13 perturbation angles x 100 trials; 10 deg incline and sphere; IPC cross-check.
checked.verdict: confirmed
checked.what_source_actually_says: 107 prompts (150 sampled, 43 excluded); mean TRD 'reduced by more than six times'. Perturbation test: 13 phi_max values x 100 random tests on 6 generated models; success = the maximum height stays within 3 % of its initial value. Results on a 10 deg incline and on a sphere. Every model was validated in IPC.
checked.code_status: No Atlas3D repository link in the paper (it cites threestudio and NVIDIA Warp only); not searched further.
checked.applicability: Use only the test protocol: small random tilts at the perceived rest pose, pass if the height stays within 3 %. It makes a cheap GT-free gate for ep18 and ep12. The SDS generator is a generative prior and is not needed.

corrected_ideas: NEW S0, cheapest and highest value: a 'gap law' gate. For every collision mesh, in the exact frame and float32 vertices it will be shipped in, compute L = the longest axis-aligned bbox side and list every functional clearance w: board notches, rack bays and the cup seat, handle holes, the lid seat. Require w >= 1.2 x 0.05 x L. Measured basis: a clean board with W/L 0.0483 was filled on 6/6 seeds, 0.0503 on 3/6, and 0.054 or more was kept on 6/6. If the check fails: re-frame the mesh to its minimal or face-aligned bbox (compensate in the tracks or <collision><origin rpy>), split it into separate collision meshes if the organisers allow it, or widen only unobserved clearances.

Correct the CoACD tolerance: the per-side deviation is t*L/2 (5.75 mm for a 23 cm board, 3.7 mm for the sweeper, 7.5-10 mm for a 30-40 cm rack), and a gap closes when its full width is below about t*L. The t*L/1.6 figure is the real-metric mode's conversion, which carries a 0.8 safety factor.

Re-run the colleague's slot experiments on the REAL ep24 board meshes, in our shipped frame, with the true notch width. Their synthetic boards were axis-aligned and used 1.3 cm and 1.6 cm notches for a 1.2 cm board, both best cases. A 25 deg frame rotation turned a clean 1.3 cm notch into a single hull (18.7 cm^3 overlap, the same as no slot).

Hypothesis for ep12, to falsify cheaply: the rack's CoACD hulls bridge the bay the cup sits in (L about 30-40 cm, so gaps under 15-20 mm close), which tilts the cup. Test: measure how far the rack hulls reach into the cup's perceived rest volume under the exact call, before and after splitting or re-framing the rack.

S2 (refit by shape class) stays, but judge each refit by the exact evaluator decomposition plus the gap law, not by mesh accuracy alone. CRISP supports primitives over TSDF only for static support surfaces under a 0.5 m locomotion criterion, so for manipulated boards the benefit is a hypothesis. The falsifying experiment is an ep24 A/B: slab refit vs TSDF board, same policy budget.

S4 (PhysPose-style pose refinement) should run only after the shape fixes and only in rest intervals, with gravity switched off while an object is held. Expect gains nearer PhysPose's estimated-scene result (+0.025 to +0.030 AR) than its known-scene headline (+0.085). Its gravity term fixes floating but not tipping, so pair it with a centre-of-mass-over-footprint margin or an Atlas3D-style tilt test.

Drop SPARCS as a method. It takes 0.8-9 h per static single-image scene on CPU, relies on a SAM3D generative prior for unseen shape, and has no code. Borrow only two things: one separating plane per object pair to flatten unobserved contact faces, and its MuJoCo stability metrics (KE in the first second, drift over 60 s) for the S5 gate.

S5 gate additions: confirm every hull is loaded as its own shape (the README --split warning); repo note 19 A3 says FlashCHORD already does this. Recheck the manifold flag on the float32 vertices as loaded, since note 19 C12 found it fragile under rotation. Report hull counts, because pre-convex or re-framed meshes change the contact budget.

found.angle:
Tracking with physical consistency: objects that stay put without drifting or floating above the table, contact with support surfaces, pose and shape refinement that uses physics, objects standing on an edge or leaning on each other, and turning a demonstrated object trajectory into one the simulator can execute.

Bottom line for the owner's question: no, the current fixes are not robust. Each one is built from a single observation: one episode's up vector for flatten_base, one co-located overlap for the slot carve. In the literature, an observed physical configuration is treated as a set of constraints on both the unobserved shape and the pose. Those configurations are an object resting on the table, resting on another object, or assembled with it. The constraints are:
- non-penetration with the table and with other objects;
- touching the support, with no gap;
- static equilibrium: the object stays still when nothing pushes it.

Shape and pose are solved jointly, the physics check runs in the same kind of simulator used downstream, and a passive-physics audit acts as a gate. Methods of this kind:
- SPARCS 2026: joint optimisation of convex-hull vertices and poses under force and torque balance.
- HoloScene 2025: energy with penetration, stability and touch terms, plus sampling and tree search scored in simulation.
- PhysPose 2025: pose cost plus collision and gravity costs, with a covariance stretched along the camera ray.
- Vysics 2025: geometry inferred from contacts with the table or robot ("physible" geometry).
- ARM 2020, PhyRecon 2024, Atlas3D 2024: stability losses or terms in reconstruction.

None of them was tested on egocentric human manipulation with stereo depth. Their numbers come from YCB-V, HOPE, ScanNet, Replica and DexYCB, so how well they transfer to us is a hypothesis.

Suggested stages:
- S0: segment each object's frames by contact state (held, resting on table, resting on an object, assembled) and run a passive-physics audit.
- S1: decide whether each float is a pose error or a mesh error.
- S2: complete the unobserved geometry under physics, pooling every observed rest or assembled configuration of the object across episodes.
- S3: refine poses per rest segment at scene level.
- S4: make the trajectory feasible (adaptive virtual-object-controller curriculum, or physics-in-the-loop search).
- S5: an automatic sim-validity gate for every mesh library version.

Everything except the RL validation runs on CPU.

sources.title: SPARCS: Simulation-Ready Cluttered Scene Estimation via Physics-aware Joint Shape and Pose Optimization (Huang, Han, Ye, Pan, Hauser)
sources.method: Each rigid object is a union of convex hulls, and the optimisation variables are the hull vertices (the shape) plus the 6-DoF poses. The physics constraint is quasi-static equilibrium. Gravity potential plus a separating-plane collision potential from the SDRS contact model; with friction, force and in-plane torque balance. The fit to the point cloud is an ICP-like term. Solver: an augmented-Lagrangian method with a structured Woodbury/Schur linear solver. Initialisation is SAM3D shapes, FoundationPose poses and CoACD decomposition. The unseen regions are only weakly tied to the SAM3D mesh.
sources.solves_for_us: This is the formulation of our problems (1) and (2): the shape is wrong where it was never seen, so the perceived rest or assembled pose is not an equilibrium. It works on the same representation our simulator uses (CoACD convex pieces), handles objects leaning on or supported by other objects, and adds friction. It would turn the hand-made underside flattening and slot carving into one optimisation over all rest configurations.
sources.evidence: Five tabletop scenes with up to 5 objects and 22 hulls, checked in MuJoCo over 1 minute. Max drift 0.73-3.10 cm versus 31-173 cm for the SAM3D+FoundationPose initialisation. Max kinetic energy 7e-4 to 1.1e-2 J versus 2.1-5.7 J. 6-9 ALM iterations; wall time 46-540 min per scene. PSNR stays comparable to the initialisation. Even their result still drifts up to 3 cm.
sources.code: None found (project page rory-weicheng.github.io/SPARCS has the paper and video only). The SDRS contact model (arXiv 2412.19127) has no confirmed code release.
sources.adoption_effort: A full re-implementation would take more than a week: nested separating-plane optimisation and an ALM solver. Not realistic in 13 days. A 'lite' version is feasible on CPU in 1-2 days (see ideas): optimise only a few unobserved-shape parameters, score with MuJoCo or Newton passive simulation as a black box, search with CMA-ES or a grid.
sources.rule_risk: Uses SAM3D, a generative prior: grey zone. Replace it with our own TSDF mesh and give unseen regions zero prior weight. Otherwise no ground truth is used.

sources.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints (Malenicky, Cifka, Fourmy, Montaut, Carpentier, Sivic, Petrik)
sources.method: A post-processing step after any pose estimator, minimising a sum of three costs. (A) A pose cost: Mahalanobis distance to the initial estimate, with translation variance stretched along the camera-to-object ray, because depth is the least certain direction. (B) A collision cost: hinge on the negative signed distance between convex-decomposition parts (DiffCol-style gradients) of the objects and the static scene. (C) A gravity cost: positive distance of each object's parts to the closest static part below it along gravity. Gravity is switched off for an object already in contact with another object, so stacking works. The table pose comes from a two-view MASt3R reconstruction plus a RANSAC plane.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem (3), floating objects and drops at the start, and the residual inter-object penetration, at the pose level. The anisotropic covariance fits our egocentric stereo, where error is mostly along the ray. The 'gravity off when supported by another object' rule covers ep12's cup in the rack. It does NOT fix unstable shapes. The gravity cost only pulls objects down; there is no torque balance, so ep18's rounded sweeper would still tip.
sources.evidence: YCB-V, BOP AR: 0.620 -> 0.707 with MegaPose, 0.690 -> 0.775 with FoundPose; MSSD 0.597 -> 0.730. HOPE-Video: 0.353 -> 0.395 and 0.286 -> 0.324. Ablation on 10 % of YCB-V: full 0.691; without the pose cost 0.540, without collision 0.607, without gravity 0.615, baseline 0.611. With an estimated table: 0.650 / 0.715 versus 0.706 / 0.774 with the known scene. Robot pick: 80 % on all three objects versus 0 % (cracker, sugar) and 60 % (mustard), 5 trials each. Failure mode: large initial collisions can flip the depth order of objects.
sources.code: None found; the project page (data.ciirc.cvut.cz/public/projects/2025PhysPose/) links only the arXiv paper and a supplementary PDF. The file name suggests an ICCV 2025 submission; acceptance not confirmed.
sources.adoption_effort: About 1 day on CPU. Our table plane is already known, and contact_retarget.py's MjPen already queries the simulator's distances on CoACD pieces. Implement per-rest-segment Gauss-Newton or Adam on 6-DoF, with finite-difference or MuJoCo distance gradients. No GPU needed.
sources.rule_risk: None. It uses only our own poses, meshes and table plane. Mocap may be used only to score the result afterwards.

sources.title: HoloScene: Simulation-Ready Interactive 3D Worlds from a Single Video (Xia et al.)
sources.method: The scene is a graph: one node per object, support edges forming a tree, plus 'beside' edges. The energy combines observation terms, an SDF-penetration term between objects, a 'stable' term (displacement after forward simulation, so low means the scene stays still under gravity) and a 'touch' term (supporting pairs must be in contact, measured by Chamfer distance). Stage 1 is gradient-based neural-SDF fitting with the penetration term. Stage 2 samples several complete-shape hypotheses per object from Wonder3D and picks the combination by tree search along the support tree, scored by simulated stability. Stage 3 refines appearance.
sources.solves_for_us: A template for scoring shape hypotheses by simulated stability, which is the robust replacement for picking one flattening by hand. The support tree plus touch term handles a cup resting in a rack and boards supported by each other or by the table. The SDF-penetration term between objects, applied during reconstruction, is the general form of our slot carving. Our hypotheses would come from our own geometry (cut heights, fills, notch parameters) rather than a generative model.
sources.evidence: Share of objects stable in Isaac Sim, all objects: Replica 81.7 % versus PhyRecon 5.6 % and ObjSDF++ 39.4 %; ScanNet++ 70.6 % versus 9.4 % and 28.2 %; iGibson 71.1 % versus 5.2 %. Ground-supported objects: 95.7 % on Replica. Runtime: about 4 h + 4 h + 20 min on one A6000 per scene. Static scenes only.
sources.code: github.com/xiahongchi/HoloScene (Apache-2.0 LICENSE file seen).
sources.adoption_effort: Running the full system: days and a GPU, and it targets static room scenes, so it is not worth it. Borrowing the energy terms and the sim-scored hypothesis search: 1 day on CPU with MuJoCo.
sources.rule_risk: Wonder3D and LaMa are generative priors: grey zone, avoid. The physics terms and the search use no prior and no ground truth.

sources.title: Vysics: Object Reconstruction Under Occlusion by Fusing Vision and Contact-Rich Physics (Bianchini, Zhu, Sun, Jiang, Taylor, Posa)
sources.method: BundleSDF tracks the object and reconstructs its visible geometry from RGB-D. PLL, a physics-based dynamics learner, then infers convex geometry that must exist to explain the observed motion through contacts with the known table plane and the robot ('physible' geometry). That geometry is fed back into BundleSDF as support-point and supporting-hyperplane losses on the SDF, alternating rounds. Inertia is learned as well. The key claim: contact-based reconstruction can recover the full convex hull wherever a point of the hull touched the known plane or the robot during the trajectory.
sources.solves_for_us: The principled version of 'the table hides the underside'. Every frame in which the object rests on, slides on or pivots about the table is a contact witness for its unseen bottom, and the table plane is a supporting hyperplane of the convex hull in the gravity direction. It suggests pooling all rest and contact frames, across episodes, as constraints on the unseen geometry (problem 1, board edges in problem 2), instead of one episode's up vector.
sources.evidence: Average Chamfer distance over 7 objects under heavy occlusion: 1.45 cm versus 2.98 cm for BundleSDF, and versus 2.45-3.06 cm for the learned completion methods (OctMAE, IPoD, V-PRISM, 3DSGrasp). Longer time-before-divergence in open-loop simulation and better temporal contact IoU. Needs no pretraining and no tactile sensors. Contact geometry is convex only. Friction was fixed at 0.26 for object-table and 0.15 for object-robot.
sources.code: github.com/DAIRLab/vysics. Its LICENSE text is NVIDIA's, inherited from BundleSDF, which is a research or non-commercial licence.
sources.adoption_effort: Full adoption: days, a GPU, and BundleSDF plus PLL, plus known contact geometry for the 'robot'. Ours would be MANO hands, which are noisy. Not feasible in 13 days. The idea itself (support plane = supporting hyperplane, pooled over rest frames) is about 1 day on CPU; see ideas.
sources.rule_risk: None for the principle. BundleSDF uses pretrained matchers and segmenters, which are not generative.

sources.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction (Ni et al.)
sources.method: A neural SDF scene reconstruction with a differentiable particle-based simulator. Surface points are extracted with SP-MC and dropped onto the support plane, and a physics loss penalises the motion of the points that contact the plane. A 'physical uncertainty' field marks regions that lack support and need supporting structure; it also drives which pixels are sampled. A rendering uncertainty field down-weights inconsistent monocular depth and normal priors.
sources.solves_for_us: Directly the ep18 case: an object on the ground whose support region is unobserved gets a physics loss that grows support where needed. It handles object-ground support only, so it does not help with the cup in the rack or leaning boards.
sources.evidence: Share of objects stable in simulation: ScanNet++ 78.16 % versus 26.43 % (RICO) and 25.28 % (ObjectSDF++); ScanNet 70.31 % versus 29.68 %; Replica 77.63 % versus 32.89 %. Object Chamfer on ScanNet++: 3.28 versus 4.08. HoloScene later reports that its 'all objects' stability is low (5-9 %) because only ground contact is modelled.
sources.code: Project page phyrecon.github.io (repository not checked in this session).
sources.adoption_effort: Would mean replacing our TSDF with a neural SDF: multi-day, GPU. Only the idea, a stability loss restricted to contact points with the plane, is cheap to borrow.
sources.rule_risk: Uses Omnidata monocular depth and normal priors, which are pretrained but not generative: a mild grey zone. No ground truth.

sources.title: ARM: Amodal 3D Reconstruction for Robotic Manipulation via Stability and Connectivity (Agnew, Xie, Walsman, Murad, Wang, Domingos, Srinivasa)
sources.method: Amodal voxel reconstruction with a differentiable stability loss defined on voxel occupancy probabilities. The loss is the probability that the object's centre of mass is unsupported in some direction, given which voxels exist and are themselves supported by the table or other objects. A connectivity prior is added, and inputs are multi-channel so that groups of objects are reasoned about together. The authors stress that the prior is shape-agnostic: it does not just add a base, it raises the probability of whichever voxels would make the object stable.
sources.solves_for_us: Gives a principled loss on exactly our unknown TSDF voxels: the underside (problem 1) and the edges of standing boards (problem 2). It needs no learned network if applied to our own TSDF unknown region at the perceived rest poses.
sources.evidence: Abstract and paper: Chamfer improves 28 % over the GenRE baseline across occlusion levels, and model-based grasping, pushing and rearrangement improve 42 % over GenRE. Stability of the reconstructions comes close to that of the ground-truth shapes.
sources.code: github.com/wagnew3/ARM (MIT LICENSE file seen).
sources.adoption_effort: 0.5-1 day on CPU to implement the loss alone on our voxel grid (torch or numpy). Their network is not needed.
sources.rule_risk: Their network was trained on shape datasets (a learned prior, grey zone). Using only the loss on our own voxels carries no rule risk.

sources.title: Atlas3D: Physically Constrained Self-Supporting Text-to-3D for Simulation and Fabrication (Chen, Xie et al.)
sources.method: Physics losses back-propagated to mesh vertices through Warp's differentiable rigid-body simulator (semi-implicit Euler). (1) A standability loss: rotation deviation after simulating the object placed upright. (2) A stable-equilibrium 'potential well' loss: the centre of mass must rise under 20 sampled small tilts, a cheap check that needs no simulation. (3) Normal-consistency regularisation. (4) A Laplacian loss restricted to vertices below a height threshold, which favours flat bottoms. The text-to-3D SDS term supplies the appearance.
sources.solves_for_us: Makes a given mesh stand at a given pose, which is what flatten_base does by hand for ep18 and what the boards need for standing on an edge. Replace the SDS term with a term that keeps our observed TSDF surface fixed, and let only unobserved vertices move. Our Newton venv already includes Warp.
sources.evidence: 3D-printed figures placed by 10 users, 800 trials: 92.25 % stood versus 7 % for the baseline. Simulated success under perturbation is higher with the equilibrium loss (exact values in their Table 1 were not extracted here). Standing on a 10-degree incline and on a sphere is also shown.
sources.code: Not found in this session.
sources.adoption_effort: Potential-well loss plus bottom-vertex optimisation: about 0.5 day on CPU. A differentiable standability loss through Warp: 1-2 days. We could instead use our own simulator as a black box.
sources.rule_risk: The original relies on SDS generative priors (grey zone). The physics losses applied to our own meshes carry no risk.

sources.title: VeREFINE: Integrating Object Pose Verification with Physics-guided Iterative Refinement (Bauer, Patten, Vincze)
sources.method: Interleaves short PyBullet physics steps (objects settle under gravity on an estimated support plane) with ICP or DenseFusion refinement against the observation. A rendering-based verification score drives a multi-armed bandit over pose hypotheses (regret-minimising refinement). Multi-object scenes are handled by building support-dependency lists and adding objects to the simulation bottom-up.
sources.solves_for_us: Explains our measured regression. ep12 rest settling gave 0.740 versus 0.790 without it; settling by pure simulation with an imperfect mesh or support drifts away from the observation. The authors state that simulation 'improves implausible initial estimates while being vulnerable to divergence in inaccurate simulation environments', and that interleaving with observation-based refinement limits this divergence. Also gives a bottom-up support ordering for the cup in the rack and stacked or assembled objects.
sources.evidence: Reported improvements: SIR +7.1 % AR over DF-R; regret-minimising refinement +5.1 % and +1.3 % AR at equal iteration budgets; the scene-level variant (VFb) +6.8 % AR over DF-R on YCB-V. Higher real-robot grasp success with a Toyota HSR in GRASPA layouts.
sources.code: github.com/dornik/verefine (MIT LICENSE file seen).
sources.adoption_effort: Pattern only: about 0.5 day to make rest_settle alternate a simulation step with a pull back toward the observed pose. CPU.
sources.rule_risk: None.

sources.title: HOIC: Hand-Object Interaction Controller - Deep RL for Reconstructing Interactions with Physics (Hu, Yi, Cao, Yong, Xu)
sources.method: An RL policy imitates kinematic hand-object tracking in a simulator. Besides the hand torques it outputs an 'object compensation' force and torque applied directly to the object, which stabilises training. A surface-contact model explains the part of that compensation that real hand-object contact could produce. Only the unexplained residual force is penalised by a physics reward.
sources.solves_for_us: (a) A measurement tool. The wrench a virtual controller needs to keep our object reference on track at frames with no hand near the object is a direct, per-frame infeasibility signal: geometry or pose is wrong, as in ep18's tipping, ep24's floating boards and ep12's cup. (b) A principled alternative to FlashCHORD's fixed 20-step object assist: allow assistance only to the extent that contact explains it.
sources.evidence: The authors claim faster and better imitation of complex hand-object motions without heuristic physics rules. No numbers were extracted in this session.
sources.code: github.com/hu-hy17/HOIC (GPL-3.0 LICENSE file seen).
sources.adoption_effort: The audit (a): about 0.5 day on CPU with our Newton or MuJoCo scene (a 6-DoF PD virtual controller, logging the wrench). Changing the policy (b): GPU, 1-2 days plus about $4 per test run.
sources.rule_risk: None. The official evaluation runs without assist, so any compensation must vanish at evaluation, and the audit is diagnostic only.

sources.title: Grasp-and-Lift: Executable 3D Hand-Object Interaction Reconstruction via Physics-in-the-Loop Optimization
sources.method: Turns visually aligned hand-object data (DexYCB, HO-3D) into physically executable motion. Hand motion is parameterised as cubic splines over sparse keyframes (MANO PCA-10 plus wrist). CMA-ES treats MuJoCo as a black box, optimising one keyframe at a time in a sliding window, so the object moves only through simulated contact. The objective is object pose and velocity, hand joints, contact and smoothness. Already summarised in docs/professor-package/notes/05-alternatives.md.
sources.solves_for_us: The trajectory-feasibility stage (S4) for hard segments: ep24's lift and stand-up. The same black-box CMA-ES-plus-MuJoCo pattern is also the cheapest way to search a few unobserved-shape parameters scored by passive stability (the SPARCS-lite idea).
sources.evidence: DexYCB, 120 sequences: success rate 71.67 % versus 45.93 % for ManipTrans; object translation error 0.67 versus 0.93 cm; rotation 2.97 versus 8.50 degrees; 557 s versus 1,987 s per sequence (A6000 + i7). Removing the object-velocity term worsens every metric.
sources.code: Not found.
sources.adoption_effort: 1-2 days on CPU per pattern. About 10 min per sequence with CPU MuJoCo; for the shape-parameter search each evaluation is only a 1 s passive simulation, so it is cheap.
sources.rule_risk: None.

sources.title: DexMachina: Functional Retargeting for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation (Mandi, Hou, Fox, Narang, Mandlekar, Song)
sources.method: A virtual object controller (PD on the object's base degrees of freedom) drives the object toward its reference. Its gains decay adaptively, only when each normalised reward's running mean exceeds its standard deviation, until zero. This sits alongside motion-imitation, behaviour-cloning and contact rewards. Already summarised in docs/professor-package/notes/04-lit-transfer.md.
sources.solves_for_us: ep24's measured limit is learning the lift and stand-up with the assist off. An adaptive decay replaces FlashCHORD's fixed schedule. Works only once the meshes make the end state physically possible: with the boards overlapping by 13.5 cm^3, no controller can succeed.
sources.evidence: Per our notes: curriculum on the virtual controller beats no curriculum on long-horizon tasks; ManipTrans-style physics curricula showed 'no clear improvement'; about 10 h per task on an L40S or H100 according to CHORD.
sources.code: Released by the authors (per our earlier notes; not re-checked in this session).
sources.adoption_effort: GPU: about 0.5 day of code in FlashCHORD plus about $3.5-4 per 250M-step test run (2.2 h at $1.6/h), plus repeat evaluations.
sources.rule_risk: None. Assist at training only; evaluation has no assist.

sources.title: TwinTrack: Bridging Vision and Contact Physics for Real-Time Tracking of Unknown Objects in Contact-Rich Scenes
sources.method: Real2Sim: a vision reconstruction is refined by a constant geometry residual plus physical parameters (mass, inertia, friction) fitted for contact-dynamics consistency. Sim2Real: per frame, a feature-based visual tracker anchored to optimised keyframes is fused adaptively with a prediction from a customised MJX (GPU MuJoCo) contact simulation.
sources.solves_for_us: Shows that physics prediction can carry a track through occlusion and impacts, for example boards being dropped or knocked. Our measured problems are mostly at rest, so the gain for us is small. The geometry-residual-from-contact idea parallels Vysics.
sources.evidence: Over 20 Hz on a Ryzen 5955WX with an RTX 4090. Per frame: SAM2 about 12 ms, SuperPoint about 8 ms, one dynamics step with neural-SDF collision about 5 ms. ADD/ADD-S improvements are measured against FoundationPose pseudo-ground truth, for falling objects and in-hand manipulation.
sources.code: Not checked.
sources.adoption_effort: Days plus GPU; not justified for our problems.
sources.rule_risk: SAM2 and SuperPoint are pretrained, not generative. No ground truth.

ideas: S0 passive-physics audit (CPU, about 0.5 day), from the HoloScene stable term, Atlas3D's rotation-deviation measure and the HOIC/DexMachina virtual controller. Per episode, label every object-frame as held, resting on the table, resting on an object, or assembled, using our own perception only (fingertip distance, object speed, height above the table; rest_settle already computes these). For each resting segment, remove the hands, drop the objects from their perceived pose and simulate 1 s; log drift, tilt, gap to support and maximum penetration. Also replay the whole reference with a 6-DoF PD virtual object controller and log the wrench needed at frames with no hand within 3 cm. Hypothesis: audit failures explain the hard episodes (ep18 before the fix, ep24, ep12's cup). Falsified if, over the public episodes with the current policies, the fraction of failed rest frames does not rank-correlate (Spearman < 0.5) with the registered-AUC deficit, or if the fixed ep18 (library_v3) still fails.

S1 float diagnosis, pose error or mesh error (CPU, hours). At each rest frame with a gap above 5 mm, compute the signed distance from the object's own FoundationStereo points to our posed mesh. Hypothesis A: the visible points fit within about 2 mm, so the pose is right and the mesh bottom is missing; fix the mesh (S2). Hypothesis B: the visible points sit systematically about one gap below the mesh surface, so the pose is biased up; use PhysPose-style refinement (S3). Falsified for both if the residual is mainly lateral or rotational; then the float is a tracking rotation error and neither fix applies. This decides whether lowering the pose (which would misalign the visible surface) or completing the mesh is correct.

S2a support-aware completion to replace flatten_base (CPU, about 1 day), from Vysics' support hyperplane and the ARM stability prior. Keep three TSDF states: surface, observed-free and unknown. Treat unknown voxels inside the multi-view visual hull as occupied, then clip by the table half-space at every perceived rest pose of that object, pooled across all episodes where it appears (own perception only). The base becomes flat exactly where the table blocked the view, with no per-episode up vector. Falsified if (a) on ep18 the footprint is under 5 cm^2, the centre of mass lies outside it, or passive-sim tilt exceeds 3 degrees within 1 s at the perceived pose; or (b) for any of the 11 objects, Chamfer to the public scans worsens by more than 2 mm versus library_v3, or an observed concavity (cup or pot interior, rack gaps) is filled. This is a diagnostic only, scans used after inference.

S2b physics-scored search over unobserved-shape parameters, SPARCS-lite / HoloScene-lite (CPU, 1-2 days). Parameterise only what was not seen: support-cut height per rest face; sharp versus rounded edges (for the planar boards, replace the TSDF surface by RANSAC planes intersected into a polyhedron, as in PolyFit / CGAL Polygonal Surface Reconstruction, GPL); notch width, depth and position for interlocking pairs. Score each candidate with the S0 audit at every rest and assembled frame (drift, tilt, gap, penetration) plus visible-surface fit, and search with CMA-ES or a grid as in Grasp-and-Lift. Falsified on ep24 unless the optimised boards (i) stand alone on an edge where we perceive them standing and (ii) stand as the X assembly for at least 2 s in passive simulation (drift < 1 cm, tilt < 5 degrees, overlap < 1 cm^3), while visible-surface fit worsens by less than 2 mm. If no candidate passes, the parameter family is wrong.

S2c non-penetration over all co-tracked frames as the general slot carve (CPU, about 0.5 day), from HoloScene's SDF-penetration term and SPARCS. Accumulate, across every frame where two objects are within 1 cm and both tracks are confident, the voxels of A that B occupies (and the reverse). Carve only voxels that are unknown or weakly observed in A's TSDF and occupied in at least k frames; add a symmetry tie if wooden_piece_1 and wooden_piece_2 turn out to be the same shape. Falsified if the carved notch volume differs from the scan notch by more than 30 % (diagnostic), if any observed outer surface moves by more than 1 mm, or if the assembled-pose overlap stays above 1 cm^3.

S3 PhysPose-style per-rest-segment pose refinement (CPU, about 1 day). For objects labelled resting, solve one pose per static segment. Minimise a Mahalanobis pose prior with variance stretched along the camera ray, plus a hinge on penetration over CoACD pairs (table, other objects) via MjPen or mj_geomDistance, plus gap to support. Switch the gravity or gap term off when the object is supported by another object (cup in rack). Hold the pose fixed over the segment. Falsified if rest-frame ADD against mocap (diagnostic, public episodes only, after inference) worsens by more than 2 mm on any of ep12, ep18, ep24, ep27, or if sim_vs_ref AUC with the existing base policies drops.

ep12 cup tipping 23 degrees: possibly a collision-geometry artefact (CPU, hours). Hypothesis: the CoACD hulls of the thin plastic rack fill the gaps between its bars, so the cup rests on surfaces that do not exist or is pushed out. Test at the perceived frame-0 pose: compare cup-to-rack penetration using the CoACD hulls with penetration using the full-resolution mesh SDF. If the hulls penetrate more than 3 mm where the mesh does not, re-decompose the rack with a lower concavity threshold or more hulls. Falsified if the full mesh penetrates about as much as the hulls; then the cause is the mesh or pose (S1/S3).

Gate rest settling on mesh validity (VeREFINE lesson; CPU, then one GPU A/B). Measured: rest settling helped ep18 (where the mesh could not stand) but cost ep12 (0.740 versus 0.790). Hypothesis: simulating an invalid mesh into rest drifts objects away from the observation. Apply rest_settle only to objects whose mesh passes S5, and alternate each simulation step with a pull back toward the observed pose. Falsified unless gated settling scores at least as well as both ungated settling and no settling on all of ep12, ep18, ep24 and ep27 (6 repeat evaluations each).

S4 trajectory feasibility for ep24 (GPU, about $3.5-4 per 250M-step run plus evaluations). Replace FlashCHORD's fixed 20-step object assist with DexMachina's adaptive decaying virtual controller, and optionally penalise only the part of the assist that contact cannot explain (HOIC). Precondition: the S2 meshes make the assembled X physically possible. Falsified if, at the same 250M budget and seed 42, ep24's registered AUC (6 evaluations) stays below 0.40, against the current 0.31.

S5 sim-validity gate for every mesh library version (CPU, minutes per library). Every pooled perceived rest pose must be a passive-simulation equilibrium (drift < 5 mm, tilt < 3 degrees over 1 s). Maximum penetration must stay below 2 mm with co-tracked objects in close-contact frames, and the gap below 3 mm at rest frames. This turns per-object patches into an automatic test that applies to all 11 objects and to eval episodes. Falsified as a sufficient gate if a library that passes still shows, in any public-episode RL rollout, an object falling with no hand within 10 cm; then a constraint is missing (friction, or contact with another object).
gaps: No public code was found for SPARCS, PhysPose or Atlas3D. Code for SDRS (the contact model under SPARCS) is unconfirmed. Any adoption is a re-implementation of the idea, not a port.

None of the works evaluates egocentric human-hand manipulation with stereo depth, the Sharpa hand, or our ADD-AUC after mesh registration. All reported gains (YCB-V, HOPE, ScanNet, Replica, DexYCB) are evidence for the mechanism, not estimates for us.

Not checked in the repo or data: whether any public episode shows the sweeper's or boards' undersides (lifted or flipped); this decides how much S2a must infer versus fuse. Also not checked: whether wooden_piece_1 and wooden_piece_2 are the same shape, which would allow a symmetry tie for the notches.

Unknown how the official evaluator builds collision geometry and mass properties from our submitted mesh: CoACD settings, uniform density? This decides whether centre-of-mass fixes in the style of Make It Stand (interior carving) or custom inertials could count at all. It also matters whether S2 changes alter the registration of our mesh to the hidden scan (a diagnostic is needed on public scans).

Rule interpretation to confirm with the owner: building each object's mesh from our own perception pooled across several episodes, public videos plus eval videos, never public scans or mocap. It seems within 'reconstruct the objects yourself' but is not explicitly confirmed.

Grey zone: SPARCS, HoloScene and EgoAERO all rely on generative shape priors (SAM3D, Wonder3D). The ideas above avoid them. PhyRecon and BundleSDF-based methods use pretrained non-generative networks (Omnidata, feature matchers), similar to our FoundationStereo.

GitHub API access was blocked in this session. Licences were read only from raw LICENSE files (HoloScene Apache-2.0, HOIC GPL-3.0, VeREFINE MIT, ARM MIT; Vysics carries NVIDIA's BundleSDF licence text). PhyRecon's and DexMachina's repositories were not re-checked. Atlas3D's exact perturbation-success table values and HOIC's quantitative results were not extracted.

SPARCS' own 'stable' scenes still drift 0.7-3.1 cm over 1 minute in MuJoCo. Whether our Newton/MuJoCo-Warp contact settings (friction, solver tolerance) let the true geometry stand is itself unverified. A useful control would run the public scans (diagnostic only) through the S0 audit and check they pass.

verified.angle:
Fact-check of the "tracking-physical-consistency" survey. I read the primary full texts myself through curl, using the arXiv abstract and HTML pages, GitHub raw files and the project pages; the sandbox could not use WebFetch. I checked four sources at length (SPARCS, PhysPose, HoloScene, Vysics) and two lightly (PhyRecon, SDRS).

Every number the colleague quoted for these sources matches the papers. The bottom-line framing needs three corrections.

(a) "Shape and pose are solved jointly and the physics check runs in the downstream simulator" is true of only part of the work:
- SPARCS solves shape and pose jointly, but in its own SDRS contact model, and checks the result in MuJoCo only afterwards.
- HoloScene scores a few shape samples by simulated stability in Isaac Sim.
- PhysPose refines pose only. It uses geometric hinge costs with no simulator and no torque balance, and its gains were measured with exact CAD meshes.
- Vysics needs known robot contact geometry plus dynamic contact events (sliding, pivoting, toppling).

(b) None of the methods can create a concavity such as a notch, and none models interlocking or mutual support. The two that come closest are explicitly limited:
- SPARCS shrinks objects to get a penetration-free start. Its one-separating-plane-per-object-pair regulariser rules out interpenetrating convex hulls, and an X-joint has exactly that.
- HoloScene restricts support to a tree, with exactly one parent per object. Its appendix resolves overlap by pruning SDF values inside neighbouring objects, which is the same heuristic as our slot carving.

(c) Our scorer ICP-registers our mesh to the scan before computing ADD. Pose-level physics fixes (PhysPose-style) therefore turn mesh errors into pose errors. The "S1: is the float a mesh error or a pose error" step has to come first, not as an optional extra.

The literature supports the principle that every observed static configuration constrains the unseen shape and the pose. It does not offer a ready recipe for ep24, and none of these methods is adoptable as a whole in 13 days.

I did not check the S4 sources (the virtual-object-controller curriculum and physics-in-the-loop search) because the colleague's JSON was cut off before them. I could not run GitHub search (403), so "no code" for SPARCS and SDRS means only that none is linked from the abstract or project page.

checked.title: SPARCS: Simulation-Ready Cluttered Scene Estimation via Physics-aware Joint Shape and Pose Optimization (Huang, Han, Ye, Pan, Hauser)
checked.claim_checked: Joint optimisation of hull vertices and poses under quasi-static force and torque balance; SAM3D, FoundationPose and CoACD initialisation; unseen regions only weakly tied to SAM3D; 5 scenes, up to 5 objects and 22 hulls; drift 0.73-3.10 cm vs 31-173 cm; kinetic energy 7e-4 to 1.1e-2 J vs 2.1-5.7 J; 6-9 ALM iterations; 46-540 min per scene; no code.
checked.verdict: confirmed (numbers exact), with important caveats the colleague missed
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Venue and versions: accepted to RSS 2026; v1 23 Feb 2026, v3 13 May 2026.

Numbers (Table I and Table III, read from the HTML):
- Max kinetic energy, measured over the first 1 s: 7.19e-4 to 1.12e-2 J vs 2.08-5.73 J.
- Max drift, measured over 1 min: 0.73-3.10 cm vs 31.06-172.55 cm.
- 6-9 ALM iterations; wall time 46.1-539.9 min.
- All of it on one desktop CPU (Intel Core Ultra 9 285K); only texture refinement uses the RTX 5090.

Why the baseline drifts so far: the SAM3D+FoundationPose initialisation 'always contain[s] severe inter-penetrations', so the simulation blows up. That baseline gap comes from penetration explosions, not from subtle instability.

Objective: three terms with w1 = 2e-2, w2 = 1e-1 (point cloud) and w3 = 2e-2 (SAM3D mesh used as a 'hallucinated' shape prior).

The appendix (separating-plane aggregation; Fig. 15 ablation) says that without regularisation the occluded regions converge to 'noisy or irregular geometry'.

Details that matter for us:
- SDRS is an interior-point model and needs a strictly penetration-free start. They get one by shrinking both colliding objects to an SDF iso-offset of -delta.
- CoACD is capped at 5 hulls with at most 50 vertices each, so the hull count is fixed during optimisation.
- 'Separating plane aggregation' puts ONE separating plane between each interacting object pair, so each object is effectively treated as its convex hull in that pair.
- With friction, torque balance about the contact normal is not guaranteed.
- Mass comes from volume at 800 kg/m3 and friction is set by hand to 1.0.
- The scenes are static single-view RGB-D tabletops (YCB-like objects).
- MuJoCo validation needed non-default settings to avoid slow slip: dt 1e-3, implicit integrator, noslip_iterations 10, elliptic cones, condim 4, multiccd.
checked.code_status: No code. The project page (rory-weicheng.github.io/SPARCS) has only the arXiv link and a video. The SDRS paper (arXiv 2412.19127, Ye, Gao, Wu, Pan, Komura) links no code from its abstract page. I could not run a GitHub search (API 403).
checked.applicability:
The formulation is the closest match to ep18: the wrong unseen shape means the perceived rest pose is not an equilibrium, and the representation is CoACD hulls, the same as our simulator's.

It does NOT fit ep24:
- the hull count is fixed and starts from a slotless board, so no notch can appear;
- its penetration-free initialisation shrinks both boards instead of carving;
- the one-plane-per-object-pair regulariser forbids interlocking.

Not adoptable in 13 days: no code, and hours of CPU per static scene.

Useful borrowings:
- Use our own TSDF mesh as the weak Type-III prior. Correction: the colleague's 'zero prior weight on unseen regions' contradicts the paper's own ablation.
- Use a low-dimensional shape parametrisation instead of free hull vertices.
- Check our sim's slip settings (noslip, condim, cone type) before blaming meshes. I have not verified which of these our Newton / MuJoCo-Warp build supports.

Rule risk: SAM3D is a generative prior (grey zone); our TSDF mesh replaces it.

checked.title: PhysPose: Refining 6D Object Poses with Physical Constraints (Malenicky, Cifka, Fourmy, Montaut, Carpentier, Sivic, Petrik)
checked.claim_checked: Pose cost (Mahalanobis, variance stretched along the camera ray) plus collision hinge on convex parts plus gravity hinge to the nearest static part, with gravity off when supported. YCB-V AR 0.620->0.707 (MegaPose) and 0.690->0.775 (FoundPose); MSSD 0.597->0.730; HOPE 0.353->0.395 and 0.286->0.324. Ablation 0.691 / 0.540 / 0.607 / 0.615 / 0.611. Estimated table 0.650 / 0.715. Grasping 80% vs 0% / 0% / 60%. Code not found; ICCV not confirmed.
checked.verdict: confirmed (all numbers exact); applicability overstated
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Status: one arXiv version (30 Mar 2025). The project page links only the arXiv paper and '2025_ICCV_collision_pose_supplementary.pdf'. A web search did not confirm the venue.

Table 1 (MSPD / MSSD / VSD / AR):
- MegaPose 0.728 / 0.597 / 0.535 / 0.620 -> PhysPose 0.735 / 0.730 / 0.658 / 0.707.
- FoundPose AR 0.690 -> 0.775.
- HOPE-Video: 0.353 -> 0.395 and 0.286 -> 0.324.

The authors note that MSPD (image-plane error) is essentially unchanged and the gain is in depth ('physical consistency constraints primarily aid in improving depth accuracy').

The gains are with known CAD meshes and RGB-only estimators (MegaPose, FoundPose).

Table 3 (ablation on 10% of YCB-V), AR:
- full: 0.691
- without pose cost: 0.540, below the 0.611 baseline, so physics without a strong data term hurts
- without collision: 0.607
- without gravity: 0.615

Table 2: a single-view estimated table degrades AR (0.597 / 0.658); a support view gives 0.650 / 0.715; the known scene gives 0.706 / 0.774.

Gravity rule: the cost is switched off when the object is 'in collision with any other object'.

Failure mode: large initial collisions flip depth order.

Grasping: 5 trials for each of 3 objects; baseline 0% / 0% / 60%; PhysPose '80% success rate'. That is a very small sample.
checked.code_status: No code linked on the project page or the abstract.
checked.applicability:
Good for the float and drop problem (3), but only at the pose level and only once the mesh is right.

Key caveat: PhysPose assumes the mesh is exact. With our reconstructed meshes, the collision and gravity costs move the POSE to compensate for mesh errors:
- The slotless ep24 boards would be pushed apart.
- A board with a missing underside would be pulled down into the table.
The scorer registers our mesh to the scan and then measures pose, so this would lower ADD.

The expected gain is also smaller than reported: their improvement came from fixing large RGB-only depth errors, and we have stereo depth.

No torque balance, so it cannot fix ep18.

Borrow, after a mesh-vs-pose diagnosis:
- one rigid pose per rest segment;
- ray-anisotropic sigma, estimated from our own public-episode residuals;
- a hinge on penetration of CoACD pieces, using MuJoCo distances;
- a gravity hinge to the table, off when a hand is within contact distance or the object touches another object;
- a strong data term.

Cost: CPU, about 1 day (estimate). Rule risk: none.

checked.title: HoloScene: Simulation-Ready Interactive 3D Worlds from a Single Video (Xia et al., NeurIPS 2025)
checked.claim_checked: Scene graph with a support tree; energy with SDF-penetration, stable (post-simulation displacement) and touch (Chamfer) terms; Wonder3D samples plus tree search scored by sim stability. Stable(All) 81.7 / 70.6 / 71.1% vs PhyRecon 5.6 / 9.4 / 5.2% and ObjSDF++ 39.4 / 28.2%; ground-supported 95.7% on Replica; 4 h + 4 h + 20 min on an A6000; static scenes only; Apache-2.0 code.
checked.verdict: confirmed (numbers exact); several qualifiers missing
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Table 2, Stable(All):
- Replica: 81.7 (ObjSDF++ 39.4, PhyRecon 5.6, DP-Recon 8.5)
- ScanNet++: 70.6 (28.2 / 9.4 / 9.4)
- iGibson: 71.1 (36.1 / 5.2 / 4.1)
- Stable(Ground) on Replica: 95.7.

Geometry is not best: Replica chamfer 4.05 vs DP-Recon 3.45; ScanNet++ F1 63.11 vs ObjSDF++ 70.71. The paper names a 'trade-off between scene-level reconstruction accuracy and physical stability'.

Evaluation scale: 3 Replica, 3 ScanNet++ and 2 iGibson scenes. Replica and iGibson are renders along camera paths the authors designed.

The 'stable' term is the displacement after a forward simulation in Isaac Sim. The 'touch' term is the Chamfer distance between supporting pairs.

The support edges form a tree: 'each object has exactly one such parent'.

The 'tree search' is a greedy breadth-first pass that keeps the lowest-energy sample per node, with 3 Wonder3D samples per instance.

Appendix C: after selection they 'prune the SDF value of the points if those points fall into the boundary of its parent object or the nearby objects', then optimise vertices to remove collisions. Part of the stability therefore comes from this post-hoc step.

Priors: Marigold depth and normal priors (a diffusion model), Omnidata normals, Wonder3D and LaMa.

Runtime: about 4 h + 4 h + 20 min on one A6000.

Limitation stated: 'only handles videos of static indoor scenes'. A human-manipulation replay demo uses FoundationPose tracking with no physics refinement and no quantitative evaluation.
checked.code_status: Released at github.com/xiahongchi/HoloScene. LICENSE.txt is Apache-2.0 (verified). It depends on Isaac Sim 4.2 (NVIDIA licence), Wonder3D+, LaMa, Marigold and tiny-cuda-nn.
checked.applicability:
Useful template: score a small discrete set of shape hypotheses by simulated stability (displacement after a drop) plus contact with the support. A greedy pass over 3 or so candidates is enough, as their own setup shows.

Not a model for ep24:
- the support tree cannot represent the X, where both boards stand on the table and support each other (a cycle);
- its notch-like handling is the same SDF pruning heuristic we already use.

The stability-vs-accuracy trade-off they report is a warning for us: optimising for stability can cost the pose and shape fit that ADD measures.

Running the full system is not worth it: GPU hours per static scene, and generative priors (grey zone).

Borrow the E_stable and E_touch scoring with our own CPU MuJoCo and the policy's CoACD hulls (about 1 day, estimate).

checked.title: Vysics: Object Reconstruction Under Occlusion by Fusing Vision and Contact-Rich Physics (Bianchini, Zhu, Sun, Jiang, Taylor, Posa; RSS 2025)
checked.claim_checked: BundleSDF plus PLL 'physible' geometry fed back as support-point and hyperplane losses; recovers the full convex hull where hull points touched the plane or the robot; chamfer 1.45 cm vs 2.98 BundleSDF vs 2.45-3.06 completion methods; friction 0.26 / 0.15; code with NVIDIA licence.
checked.verdict: confirmed (numbers exact); transfer to our static rest frames overstated
checked.what_source_actually_says:
Table I, chamfer in cm, 7 objects:
- Vysics 1.45
- BundleSDF 2.98
- OctMAE 2.45, IPoD 2.47, V-PRISM 2.80, 3DSGrasp 3.06

The objects are bakingbox, bottle, egg, milk, oatly, styrofoam and toblerone: mostly convex everyday items.

The data are about 10 s sessions of a Franka arm with a SPHERICAL end effector, whose location is known from proprioception, pushing, sliding, pivoting and toppling objects on a table. The table height is detected from depth.

The hull-recovery claim is conditional. It holds only 'as long as every point on its convex hull makes contact'. Otherwise the geometry is 'unobservable' and non-unique, and PLL 'can be biased to learn large geometries to increase lever arms'.

Geometry is convex only (deep support function).

Friction is fixed at 0.26 (object-table) and 0.15 (object-robot).

Limitations they state:
- it 'often cannot recover from poor pose estimates';
- shapes are 'qualitatively unappealing, with noisy artifacts'.

BundleSDF uses pretrained XMem and LoFTR (README).
checked.code_status: Released at github.com/DAIRLab/vysics, with a README and dataset links. LICENSE.txt is the NVIDIA BundleSDF licence: 'non-commercially ... research or evaluation purposes only'.
checked.applicability:
The principle transfers; the method does not.

The 'physible' signal comes from dynamic contact with a contact geometry known exactly. Ours would be noisy MANO hands. A static rest frame gives a much weaker constraint:
- the table is a supporting plane of the object at that orientation (non-penetration plus touch);
- the centre of mass must project inside the contact polygon.

Pooled over many rest segments and episodes, that is still the right replacement for one-episode flatten_base.

Watch the over-inflation bias they report: a minimum-force (or maximum-support) completion makes geometry larger. Bound fills with observed free space.

Full adoption: no (GPU, BundleSDF and PLL, known robot geometry, research-only licence).

checked.title: PhyRecon: Physically Plausible Neural Scene Reconstruction (Ni et al., NeurIPS 2024)
checked.claim_checked: Stable share 78.16 / 70.31 / 77.63% vs 26.43 / 25.28 / 29.68 / 32.89; object chamfer 3.28 vs 4.08; ground-contact physics loss only.
checked.verdict: partly: numbers confirmed, code not checked
checked.what_source_actually_says:
The numbers appear in the paper as quoted.

The stability criterion is lenient: an Isaac Gym drop counts as 'stable' within 5 deg rotation and 5 cm translation.

The physics loss is applied only to points in contact with the supporting plane.

It uses Marigold and Omnidata priors.

HoloScene's re-evaluation (Stable(All) 5.6-9.4%, Stable(Ground) 45-67%) uses a different protocol that includes inter-object contacts. That explains the gap from PhyRecon's own numbers.
checked.code_status: Project page phyrecon.github.io; repository and licence not verified.
checked.applicability: Only the idea transfers: a loss on support-contact points. Its 5 deg / 5 cm threshold is far too loose as a gate for us; at that scale an object can already have tipped. Not worth adopting.

corrected_ideas: Re-frame the answer to the owner. The literature supports the principle: each observed static configuration (resting on the table, resting in or on another object, assembled) is a constraint on the unseen shape and on the pose. It offers no ready, tested method for our case. Every quantitative result is on static scenes. PhysPose's gains use exact CAD meshes. Nothing handles concavities, interlocking or mutual support. Our current patches are not robust because each uses one observation (one episode's up vector, a fixed 8 mm band in flatten_base.py, one co-located overlap). The robust version keeps the same ideas but pools evidence from all observations and passes an automatic sim gate.

Do S1 before any pose-level physics fix. Our scorer (metric_code/track_3/AUC.py via pipeline/score_registered.py) centres our mesh at its surface centroid, scales it to the scan radius and runs trimmed ICP against the scan; ADD is then computed on pose. So if a float comes from a missing or rounded underside, snapping the pose down (PhysPose-style gravity) turns a mesh error into a pose error and lowers AUC.
Diagnostic, perception only, per rest segment:
(a) the residual along the camera ray between rendered-mesh depth and FoundationStereo depth on visible object pixels;
(b) the gap between the mesh's lowest point and our table plane.
Residual near 0 with a gap means a mesh error: fix the shape. A residual close to the gap times the ray's vertical component means a pose error: refine the pose.
Falsify on public episodes after inference: in segments labelled mesh-error, the mocap height should match our height.

Calibrate the passive-physics audit itself before trusting it as a gate. On public episodes, as a diagnostic after inference (ground truth is allowed there), run the same passive simulation with the public scan meshes at mocap poses: our simulator, CoACD settings, friction and solver.
- If scan plus mocap also drifts or tips (for example the ep12 cup in the rack, 23 deg), the fault is the simulator or contact settings, not our mesh.
- SPARCS needed MuJoCo noslip_iterations=10, condim=4, elliptic cones, multiccd and dt 1e-3 implicit to stop slow slip even at true equilibrium. Check what our Newton / MuJoCo-Warp build supports (not verified).
- Choose gate thresholds from this calibration. PhyRecon's 5 deg / 5 cm is far too loose; something like under 5 mm and 2 deg over the segment's own duration is a guess to be calibrated.

Replace flatten_base with support-plane completion pooled over every rest segment of the object, across all episodes. This is the static form of Vysics' supporting-hyperplane constraint; it uses perception only, so eval episodes are allowed.
Steps:
- For each rest segment k, take u_k (table normal in the object frame) and h_k (table offset). Cluster them by resting face.
- Disagreement within one cluster is itself a tracking-QA flag. Pooling averages out pose noise.
- Per face: clip the mesh below the plane (non-penetration).
- Add the smallest fill between the visible lower boundary and the plane that puts the centre of mass inside the contact polygon with a margin.
- Bound the fill by observed free space, so overhangs such as the sweeper handle stay empty. This avoids Vysics' noted bias toward over-large geometry.
Falsify: the ep18 footprint vs the scan's 11.7 cm2 and passive drift, both measured after the fact; registered AUC on every public episode of the object, not just ep18; leave-one-episode-out.

Add a sim-scored hypothesis search (HoloScene's E_stable + E_touch) without generative priors. Per object, keep a small discrete set: fill mode (extrude to plane / convex fill / flat cap) x cut depth x CoACD parameters.
- Score: the maximum displacement after a passive drop, over all of that object's rest and assembled segments, in OUR simulator with the policy's exact CoACD hulls (stability depends on the hulls, not the render mesh). Add a contact-gap term for supported pairs.
- Choose the smallest change that passes the calibrated gate, then check registered AUC on public episodes, because shape changes shift the scorer's centroid, scale and ICP.
- Effort: CPU, about 1 day (estimate). HoloScene used only 3 samples per object and a greedy pass, so a small set is consistent with the source.

ep24 slots need their own method; none of the surveyed papers provides one.
- SPARCS cannot add a notch: hull count fixed, shrink-to-start initialisation, one separating plane per object pair.
- HoloScene: support tree, plus the same SDF pruning heuristic we already use.
Hypothesis: carve each board with the swept volume of the other board along our tracked RELATIVE trajectory during the insertion and removal phases. That gives the notch side and depth, not just the overlap at the final pose. Add free-space carving from frames where a board is alone and its notch faces a camera.
Generic self-consistency checks, with no ground truth: each notch width close to the other board's thickness; the two notch depths sum to about the board height.
Falsify: assembled overlap drops from 13.5 cm3 to near 0; the X stands in passive simulation; ep24 registered AUC after inference.

Fix the rounded edges of thin flat objects (the boards; possibly the dust pan) at the source, with primitive refitting. Fit RANSAC planes to the two large faces and the edge faces from our own stereo points, then rebuild a sharp-edged polyhedron where the planarity residual is small. This is a hypothesis, about 0.5 day (estimate).
Falsify: the board can stand on its edge in simulation, and registered AUC on public ep24 does not drop.

Pose refinement in the style of PhysPose, applied last and only to segments S1 labels as pose errors.
- One rigid pose per rest segment.
- Ray-anisotropic covariance, with sigmas estimated from our public-episode residuals (tuning on public data only).
- A strong data term: PhysPose's ablation without the pose term gives AR 0.540, below its 0.611 baseline.
- A hinge on CoACD-piece penetration using MuJoCo distances.
- A gravity hinge to the table, off when a hand is within contact distance or the object is in contact with another object.
Expect a smaller gain than PhysPose reports, because its gains fixed RGB-only depth errors (MSPD unchanged) and we have stereo.

Do not adopt SPARCS, HoloScene or Vysics wholesale in the 13 days left.
- SPARCS: no code; 46-540 CPU minutes per static 5-object scene.
- HoloScene: Isaac Sim 4.2 plus Wonder3D, LaMa and Marigold (generative priors, grey zone); about 8 A6000-hours per scene.
- Vysics: needs known robot contact geometry and dynamic contact events; research-only NVIDIA licence.
Also correct the colleague's 'zero prior weight on unseen regions' for a SPARCS-lite: the SPARCS appendix shows unregularised occluded regions become noisy. Use our own TSDF mesh as the weak prior and a low-dimensional shape parametrisation.

Coverage gaps to state plainly to the owner. I did not check the S4 sources (the adaptive virtual-object-controller curriculum and physics-in-the-loop trajectory search) because the colleague's findings were cut off. I did not check ARM, Atlas3D or the PhyRecon code. 'No code' for SPARCS and SDRS rests on their project and abstract pages only, since GitHub search was blocked.

found.angle: Challenge and leaders. I read the organisers' own documentation and code: the FAQ PDF, the Track 3 kit README and CD-O scorer, the video_to_data repo at commit 7eb9721 (2026-10-20) including mesh_to_usd, support_recon and the FlashCHORD scene configs, the CHORD tech report and the CoRL tutorial page. I checked the live leaderboard (generated 2026-10-22 05:31 UTC) and searched for anything the top teams have published. I also looked at NVIDIA work on sim-ready assets (GATOR, Newton SDF/hydroelastic contact, SimReady, Cosmos) and at the closest Sharpa / MuJoCo-Warp group (Do as I Do). Two new measurements, both read-only and kept in scratch. (1) The CD-O floor that the kit's own 4096-face budget imposes, compared with our library_v3 meshes, measured with the kit's CD-O code. (2) Eval exposure per object, taken from the kit roster. The script is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v2d-track3/8c892c5e-fd7c-57aa-abef-68d2af098e4f/scratchpad/leaders/cdfloor.py. No repo files were changed. Bottom line: the organisers' tooling never repairs mesh geometry. It (a) makes the support fit the reference (per-object support disks), (b) checks standing with a drop test, and (c) puts a generative mesh (SAM3D) in its own video baseline. Our per-object patches should therefore become (i) evidence-derived constraints in the reconstruction plus (ii) an automatic physics acceptance gate.

sources.title: V2D official mesh-to-USD workflow with recorded-support drop test (nvidia-isaac/video_to_data, reconstruction/modules/v2d_hoi_object_reconstruction/mesh_to_usd/README.md, commit 7eb9721)
sources.method: Turns one reconstructed rigid object into a rigid USD with explicit CoACD colliders, mass (default 0.3 kg, flagged 'assumed') and inertia recomputed from the colliders. The object is then lifted, released and settled in Isaac Sim. 'recorded-support' mode takes the first stable 30-frame window in the first 90 frames of the object's own tracked poses, combines it with the fitted ground plane and infers the resting orientation; it never falls back to a geometry pose. 'principal-6-support' mode levels the largest roughly coplanar downward patch (at least 1% of max-extent squared, correction capped at 30 degrees). The workflow judges geometry but never repairs it: a failed standing test fails the job.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 1 (and the stand-up part of 2). It gives an organiser-defined, object-agnostic acceptance test to replace our hand checks. The ep18 sweeper (footprint 0.3 cm^2, centre of mass 3 cm outside) would FAIL at its recorded support pose; the flattened v3 should pass. Our 'snap to nearest stable pose' matches their recorded-support principle: orientation comes from the observed rest window, not from geometry guesses. The repair itself is left to us.
sources.evidence: Spec only, no accuracy numbers. 'Standing' requires contact, settling, support geometry within 0.02 m of the plane and final tilt of 15 degrees or less. The pose-settle window allows at most 1% of the largest extent (clamped to 1-10 mm) and 2 degrees. The lift is 0.25x the largest extent. 'Convex-hull stable-pose ranking is intentionally out of scope.' The CoRL tutorial lists 'infeasible support geometry' among the failure modes participants should diagnose.
sources.code: In the repo (SPDX headers say Apache-2.0). Local clone: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v2d-track3/8c892c5e-fd7c-57aa-abef-68d2af098e4f/scratchpad/src/video_to_data. The drop test needs the Isaac Sim 6.0.1 container and the EULA; the README says v0.2 reconstruction containers do not support RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120).
sources.adoption_effort: About half a day to port the criteria (rest-window orientation, lift, release, tilt at most 15 degrees, support within 2 cm, 2-degree settle window) to CPU MuJoCo using the same CoACD hulls the evaluator uses. No GPU and no Isaac Sim needed.
sources.rule_risk: None. It uses only our own poses and table plane, never ground truth.

sources.title: V2D support-surface reconstruction from still poses (robotic_grounding/retarget/support_recon.py) and FlashCHORD support USDA (scene/support.py, configs/scene/eval.yaml)
sources.method: Finds still runs of each object: under 1 mm and under 0.01 rad per frame. An optional hand-release gate treats fingertips within 2 cm as 'holding' and needs at least 5 released still frames. Under each run it places a 1 cm thick disk at the object's minimum vertex z, with radius equal to half the larger XY span. Disks from different bodies merge when they overlap in XY and lie within 5 cm in z. A 'phantom' disk is dropped when another body sits inside it for at least 90% of frames within 10 cm in z, i.e. a tool resting on another object, such as a cup in a bowl. Disks at or below 5 cm are skipped. FlashCHORD loads the USDA prims (Cylinder/Cube) as kinematic shapes on one static body. Its eval scene config has support: true and decompose_objects: true (CoACD default threshold 0.05) and contact_friction 1.0.
sources.solves_for_us: Problem 3 (objects floating 1-4 cm and dropping at the start). The organisers' own answer is to raise the support to meet the reference, not to move the object down. It does not fix tipping: a rounded sweeper still falls off a disk. For a cup in the dish rack the phantom filter removes the cup's own disk, so the rack mesh has to hold it, which leads back to problem 2.
sources.evidence: Code facts only; no published effect sizes. Our mkref already writes a single table disc into this same support USDA path.
sources.code: Apache-2.0 per the SPDX header. Pure numpy/trimesh/pxr.
sources.adoption_effort: A few hours, CPU only. Add per-object disks to the support USDA that mkref already writes.
sources.rule_risk: Low: official code, our own poses. Judges might view pedestals under objects as cosmetic, and if the float is really a pose error the disk preserves that error (see the ideas section).

sources.title: V2D Challenge FAQ PDF + Track 3 kit README + CD-O scorer, and our CD-O floor measurement
sources.method: Rules quoted from the FAQ: 'participants should reconstruct the objects ... and submit their own reconstructed meshes'; 'Pretrained models and external data are allowed for all tracks'; the final ranking is the lowest sum of per-metric ranks over MP-SR, SP-SR, AUC, MPPE, RPE and CD-O. Kit facts: the packer decimates every mesh to at most 4096 faces and 4096 vertices; Kaggle registers each mesh to the confidential scan once per episode-object; packer mesh warnings (planar, box-like, sphere-like, identical) are advisory only. CD-O is the symmetric mean nearest-neighbour distance (10k samples, same seed for both meshes) after surface-radius scale normalisation and trimmed ICP.
sources.solves_for_us: Rule clarity and prioritisation. Pretrained generative priors are explicitly allowed, so the 'grey zone' is settled, but public scans for eval objects are not. CD-O is one of six ranked metrics, so mesh work pays twice: once in physics, once in CD-O rank. Eval exposure from the roster (36 pairs): wooden_spoon 10, white_pot 6, blue_cup 5, plastic_dish_rack 5, beige_cup 2, mini_sweeper 2, mini_dust_pan 2, and 1 each for lid, pitcher, wooden_piece_1 and wooden_piece_2. The eval contact pairs are spoon+pot (3, 5, 6), rack+spoon or cup or pot or sweeper (14, 15, 16, 28, 30), sweeper+dustpan (19), boards (25), pot+lid (1) and cup+pitcher (20). A general fix for container/rack cavities therefore reaches more eval episodes than the board-slot fix (1 episode).
sources.evidence: MEASURED today with the kit's CD-O code. Each public scan against itself: 0.000. Against its own copy decimated by the kit's 4096-face budget: 0.084-0.269 cm (sweeper 0.084 up to rack 0.269; mean about 0.15). Against a 2 mm voxel remesh of itself: 0.14-0.31. Against our meshes/library_v3: beige_cup 0.868, water_pitcher 0.884, rack 0.572, blue_cup 0.520, pot 0.444, lid 0.418, dustpan 0.340, sweeper 0.318, wooden_piece_1 0.223, wooden_piece_2 0.216. Weighted by eval exposure over the 26 non-spoon pairs, our estimate is about 0.50 cm. Leaderboard (2026-10-22 05:31 UTC), CD-O: SoySauceChicken 0.065, Kiarash 0.088, SRL 0.239, Zihao Guo 0.313, Alcor Z 0.373, Zimo Li 0.405. INFERENCE (not verified): with full-resolution hidden references, even budget-decimated perfect scans would average at least about 0.15 when weighted by eval exposure. SoySauceChicken's 0.065 therefore points to hidden references stored at the same budget, plus meshes nearly identical to them for the 10 objects that have public scans: 26 pairs near 0 and 10 spoon pairs near 0.23 gives about 0.065. That fits public scans being used, which would give them sim-valid geometry (flat bases, slots) for free. Zihao Guo (AUC 0.831, SP-SR 0.95, CD-O 0.313) looks like the relevant own-mesh benchmark.
sources.code: Kit: metric_code/track_3/CD-O.py, v2dlb/mesh_budget.py. Our script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v2d-track3/8c892c5e-fd7c-57aa-abef-68d2af098e4f/scratchpad/leaders/cdfloor.py (scratch only).
sources.adoption_effort: None (facts). CD-O diagnostics run on CPU in about 2 min per object.
sources.rule_risk: Comparing against public scans is allowed as a diagnostic on public data. Never feed the scans into eval-episode inference.

sources.title: CHORD: Learning Dexterous Manipulation Using Contact Wrench Guidance From Human Demonstration (organisers' method; arXiv 2607.00033, tech report PDF)
sources.method: Wrench-guided RL tracking with a virtual object controller. The controller's wrench is held at scale 1.0 for a 20-step warm-up after each random-frame reset, then annealed. For two-object tasks it adds a relative object-pose reward that tracks the demonstrated pose of object 1 relative to object 0 (insert, pour, scoop). References pass a quality filter before training: rejected if hand-object penetration (capsules against the object's convex hull) or hand-hand overlap exceeds 2 cm in any frame.
